  • According to recent reports, SOLRITE, a company specializing in developing, financing, and owning Virtual Power Plant Agreement (VPA) projects, together with Sonnen, a leader in Virtual Power Plant energy storage technology, announced they will now digitally integrate VPP smart breakers, managed by ADAPT Energy, into the SOLRITE  sonnen VPP.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SOLRITE Unveils Next-Gen Virtual Power Plant Node with sonnen and ADAPT Energy, Integrating VPP Breakers to Turn Home Loads into Flexible Grid Assets.

ADAPT Energy’s control of VPP breakers will add dispatchable load flexibility to the SOLRITE sonnen VPP, while paving a simpler, faster, and lower-cost path to whole-home backup.

According to recent reports, SOLRITE, a company specializing in developing, financing, and owning Virtual Power Plant Agreement (VPA) projects, together with Sonnen, a leader in Virtual Power Plant energy storage technology, announced they will now digitally integrate VPP smart breakers, managed by ADAPT Energy, into the SOLRITE  sonnen VPP. The integration marks the next evolution of sonnen and SOLRITE’s industry-leading partnership in VPP innovation, expanding beyond battery storage by transforming residential electrical loads into flexible, dispatchable grid assets for both the VPP and smart backup power applications.

Unlike traditional approaches to whole-home backup, often requiring hard-wired circuit relocation, including exclusive loads panels, the newly expanded VPP Node combines the sonnenHub with ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart breaker technology to intelligently manage major household loads. This creates a more streamlined approach to whole-home backup while unlocking an entirely upcoming source of flexibility for the SOLRITE sonnen VPP. With homeowner permission, the VPP smart breaker—controlled by ADAPT Energy—can also participate in on-grid VPP events, enabling the same electrical infrastructure to be flexible for both backup and grid participation.

“Our work with ADAPT Energy is a meaningful step forward in how we think about residential battery storage and VPP participation,” said Regan George, CEO and Founder of SOLRITE Energy. “We have already demonstrated the tremendous value of connecting sonnen batteries together as a pooled grid asset. Now, we’re going inside the home and unlocking another layer of flexibility that has been sitting there all along. By combining the battery with additional load management made possible by the VPP smart breaker technology, we’re creating a more valuable node for the grid while also giving homeowners a clever backup solution.”.

The integration addresses one of the longstanding challenges of whole-home backup: how to provide broad electrical coverage without having large household loads drain available battery capacity too quickly or cause the nano-grid to immediately fail after an off-grid transition due to excessive inrush current. With the newly expanded VPP smart breaker technology digitally integrated with the sonnen ecosystem, the system can intelligently shed large loads without requiring those circuits to be relocated. ADAPT Energy keeps the smart breakers synchronized with the sonnen battery during backup mode and automatically restores the breakers when grid power returns. This significantly reduces installation complexity and tedious inspections for installers, allowing crews to complete more jobs per week.

For homeowners, the system provides the convenience of a whole-home electrical configuration that intelligently manages the loads that have the greatest impact on backup duration. This work is all done in the background, meaning homeowners do not have to worry about resetting individual circuits during an outage. Instead, participating homes will see more value from their VPA program in the form of an enhanced backup power experience. Furthermore, at any time in the future, if a homeowner is interested in altering which of their VPP smart breaker-controlled loads are shed during an outage, the process to make such a change is quick and easy, requiring no electrical reconfiguration.

Sources indicate that “This is about making whole-home backup work the way homeowners expect it to,” noted Troy Morgan, President of PanTech Design, the developer of ADAPT Energy. “Instead of putting the pressure on homeowners to change the way their home is wired and to manually manipulate loads during an outage, we’re putting intelligence into their energy system, which provides a seamless and automatic backup power experience for their home. Our technology empowers home loads to supply optimal backup power during an outage or provide valuable flexibility to the grid.”.

Industry observers note that the permission-based architecture aligns the interests of the homeowner, battery owner and utility. The real opportunity comes when homeowners choose to opt in to allow the breakers to participate in on-grid VPP events.

Sources indicate that when a VPP event is dispatched, the sonnen battery can discharge or charge in concert with direct load shedding via ADAPT. ADAPT Energy will strictly shed pre-approved household loads, and by using Eaton AbleEdge breakers, ADAPT achieves this right where the breaker sits, without relocation. A customer who has opted to include a pool pump, for example, can have that load temporarily turned off while the sonnen battery is discharging to the grid. That way, the VPP can respond through both energy stored in the battery and energy that would have otherwise been consumed by the home, thereby increasing the dispatched injection into the grid, by the VPP.

It has been revealed that “With the addition of ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart-breaker technology to the SOLRITE–sonnen ecosystem, we are expanding the virtual power plant from a battery-centered resource into a fully orchestrated home-energy platform,” remarked Blake Richetta, Chairman and CEO of sonnen Inc. “By synchronizing energy that has been harnessed in our battery with intelligent, real-time control of household electrical loads, we can deliver more flexible, responsive capacity to the grid precisely when it is needed most. This integration materially strengthens the value of SOLRITE’s virtual power plant—supporting grid reliability, creating greater customer value, and enabling SOLRITE to continue delivering industry-leading solar-plus-storage VPA solutions to homeowners.”.

Press release from www.sonnenusa.com.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh IEA report finds renewables are already strengthening energy security and competitiveness while cutting fuel import costs—but faster electrification, grid modernization, and greater flexibility can extend these gains across the economy.

In a recent development, spain’s rapid expansion of renewable power has strengthened its energy security and competitiveness, but faster electrification across transport, buildings, and industry will be essential to meeting the country’s energy and climate goals, according to a new IEA Energy Policy Review published Oct. 5, 2026.

Between 2015 and 2025, renewables’ share of Spain’s electricity generation increased from 35% to 56%, while emissions declined by around one-fifth. These achievements have been underpinned by the country’s strong energy and climate policy framework and its well-established approach to a just transition, which links clean energy investment with jobs, regional development, and social inclusion.

Spain’s growing share of renewable power is already helping to lower wholesale electricity prices and reduce its exposure to imported fuels. Without the vast expansion of renewable capacity, its natural gas imports for power generation would have been nearly 40%, or USD 26 billion, higher in 2024. Nonetheless, imports still provided almost 70% of Spain’s total energy consumption in 2024, underscoring the need to extend the transition beyond electricity supply.

According to recent reports, accelerating electrification of end-uses should also be a priority, the report finds. Today, electricity accounts for just 25% of Spain’s final energy consumption, well below the country’s target of 35% by 2030. Electric vehicle uptake is relatively limited, notably for corporate fleets, while fossil-fuel heating remains widespread, and the industry faces high upfront investment costs.

Sources indicate that A combination of taxes, levies, and network charges are keeping end-user electricity prices high, while fossil fuels face comparatively lower charges in Spain. The country is taking steps to address this, including by abolishing the tax on electricity production in 2026. Further rebalancing domestic energy price dynamics, while protecting vulnerable consumers, could strengthen incentives for households and businesses to electrify and help industry capture the competitive advantages of renewable power.

It has been revealed that spain has introduced reforms to accelerate storage, demand-side flexibility, and adapting grid rules to a rapidly changing generation mix. Continued progress on power system infrastructure and management, alongside a more balanced mix of wind, solar, and hybrid technologies, can help Spain integrate growing shares of renewable generation while strengthening electricity security and resilience.

The review also highlights the importance of carefully managing the planned nuclear phase-out to maintain security of supply. Following the recent approval to extend the lifetime operation of the Almaraz nuclear power plant, the report recommends implementing a transparent framework for future case-by-case decisions that considers the costs and benefits for consumers and the wider power system.

Strong progress on renewable power in Spain demonstrates that its deployment can advance energy security, competitiveness, and social inclusion. The report finds that the next test will be to turn this progress into a fully integrated, flexible, and resilient energy system. By accelerating electrification, modernizing and optimizing grids, unlocking flexibility, and carefully managing its nuclear phase-out, Spain can offer valuable lessons for other countries pursuing similar energy transformations across the wider economy.

US to install 36% more wind turbines in 2025 than previous year

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The United States is expected to add more than 7 GW of wind installations in 2025, a 36% increase over the previous year, and the five-year outlook remains unchanged quarter-over-quarter from previous forecast, according to the “U.S.
  • Sources indicate that amid a challenging market environment, the report highlights that the United States is on track to add 46 GW of fresh wind capacity from 2025 to 2029, with total projected volumes unchanged quarter-on-quarter from previous forecasts.
  • While Q3 installations came in 23% below forecast at 932 MW, the market has shown progress with 3.8 GW queued for Q4 2025 — representing 52% of the year’s total expected capacity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The United States is expected to add more than 7 GW of wind installations in 2025, a 36% increase over the previous year, and the five-year outlook remains unchanged quarter-over-quarter from previous forecast, according to the “U.S. Wind Energy Monitor” report released by Wood Mackenzie and the American Clean Power Association (ACP).

Sources indicate that amid a challenging market environment, the report highlights that the United States is on track to add 46 GW of fresh wind capacity from 2025 to 2029, with total projected volumes unchanged quarter-on-quarter from previous forecasts. However, timing has shifted, as 2026 and 2027 will deliver significant gains, at 10.7 GW and 12.7 GW, respectively, as more assets advance through the development pipeline.

While Q3 installations came in 23% below forecast at 932 MW, the market has shown progress with 3.8 GW queued for Q4 2025 — representing 52% of the year’s total expected capacity. This back-loaded installation pattern is consistent with typical project-commissioning timelines.

U.S. turbine order intake has rebounded to pre-One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) levels quarter-over-quarter, supported by 2+ GW of firm commitments in Q3, the biggest intake in the region in the last nine months and a 79% quarter-over-quarter increase. However, true visibility remains limited as OEMs increasingly withhold project details and much qualifying “start-of-construction” activity occurs through off-site component manufacturing.

The market will then see a noticeable drop off, as 2029 weakens meaningfully quarter-over-quarter following project cancellations and inactive designations for late-decade capacity, driven by permitting and broader development challenges.

“The U.S. power market is facing mounting strain after a decade of flat demand, with utilities committing to 160 GW of large-load additions. This represents a significant opportunity for wind energy, which benefits from strengthened economic fundamentals and a compelling business case driven by its competitively low LCOE,” said Leila Garcia da Fonseca, director of research at Wood Mackenzie. “However, turbine costs remain elevated due to tariffs and mid-term wind growth will depend on resolving permitting and policy uncertainty.”.

Power demand growth through 2029 is expected to average around 3% compared to just 0.7% over the previous decade, with data centers accounting for approximately 59 GW of the 90 GW total peak demand growth. This surge in baseload demand positions wind as a natural fit to meet rising power needs.

It has been revealed that the five-year capacity outlook remains unchanged at 39.8 GW of added capacity quarter-over-quarter. The 2025-2027 pipeline is fully committed with all projects having turbine orders in place. More than 60% of the three-year capacity outlook has been commissioned or is under construction.

Activity is led by western states, such as Wyoming, Newly introduced Mexico and others, that will account for 34% of activity in this time period. Major projects driving the outlook include Pattern’s 3.5-GW SunZia project in New Mexico, which will position the developer as 2026’s top installer, and Invenergy’s 998-MW Towner Energy Center in Colorado, the largest single project expected in 2027.

The market continues expanding geographically, with Arkansas bringing its first utility-scale onshore wind project online through Cordelio’s Crossover Wind.

The repowering market remains strong, as Wood Mackenzie projects that 18 projects will drive 2.5 GW of capacity additions in the next three years.

It has been revealed that wood Mackenzie expects the offshore installation pace to slow in Q4 2025 due to harsh winter weather conditions, pushing remaining capacity into 2026. Despite these near-term adjustments, Vineyard Wind has demonstrated strong execution, connecting 15 turbines in Q3 and delivering 200 GWh through nine months.

According to recent reports, “U.S. offshore wind demonstrates diverging momentum,” remarked Garcia Da Fonseca. “Projects under construction with COD estimated for 2026 continue to hit key milestones, but post-2027 developments face potential delays amid constrained wind turbine installation vessel capacity, driving delays and contract terminations.”.

The offshore sector is also experiencing significant financial pressure.

The report highlights that uncertainty around tariffs is a threat to projections. Wood Mackenzie projects that tariffs will drive up turbine costs in 2026, before moderating in subsequent years. In total, U.S. onshore wind capex is projected to increase by 5% through 2029.

It has been revealed that “U.S. wind turbine pricing is experiencing unprecedented uncertainty as conflicting market and regulatory forces interact,” remarked Garcia Da Fonseca. “Domestic manufacturing overcapacity relative to permitted project volumes, particularly after 2028, would normally place downward pressure on prices. Despite this, onshore wind costs are expected to continue rising due to tariff exposure on raw material inputs and subcomponents.”.

  • This is not a story about a construction crew failing to install a basemat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that ontario Power Generation has acknowledged that its first GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 small modular reactor at Darlington will exceed its C$7.7 billion approved budget and miss its October 2030 commercial-operation target. There is no replacement cost or completion date yet. OPG expects its engineering, cost and schedule review to be substantially complete by mid-2027.

The reason matters. In its November 10 financial results, OPG identified continuing first-of-a-kind reactor engineering and its effects on construction execution and supply-chain performance. Ontario started physical work while parts of the design governing that work were still evolving. The project is now living with the consequence.

This is not a story about a construction crew failing to install a basemat. The 2.1-million-pound reactor foundation is in place, work on the turbine building has progressed, and the cooling-water tunnel equipment has been assembled. These are real achievements. They do not settle the engineering dependencies, supplier requirements and delivery sequence for a first-of-a-kind reactor. Construction progress and schedule certainty are different things.

Sources indicate that megaproject researcher Bent Flyvbjerg calls the better approach “think slow, act fast.” Engineering, interfaces and execution plans need enough maturity that construction can advance without a succession of disruptive changes. Design and construction can overlap on controlled, ready-to-build work packages. Darlington’s own disclosure reveals that the required boundary has not been maintained.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing on Darlington’s SMR examines the November disclosure, the historical nuclear construction record and the consequences for Ontario’s four-reactor strategy.

According to recent reports, ontario is an unusually favourable test for the Western SMR industry. OPG operates a large nuclear fleet and has an experienced workforce, an established site, transmission infrastructure and public financial backing. GE Vernova Hitachi has extensive boiling-water reactor experience. Yet the BWRX-300 is still a new design, and the promised economies of repeat construction depend on its becoming stable enough to repeat.

The four-reactor programme originally carried a C$20.9 billion budget. Within that were C$6.1 billion for the first reactor, C$1.6 billion of common infrastructure and C$13.2 billion for Units 2 through 4. The financial proposition depends on the later reactors becoming cheaper after the first teaches suppliers and builders how to execute the design.

In my October 2025 assessment I applied historical nuclear construction reference-class uplifts rather than relying only on the project’s internal estimates. A 67% uplift to the Unit 1 reactor component, with shared infrastructure held unchanged, produces a C$11.8 billion first-stage cost. A 202% uplift produces about C$20.0 billion, or nearly 96% of the original budget for all four reactors. These are illustrative stress outcomes from the historical construction class, not new OPG estimates. They show how much of the programme’s financial margin depends on getting the first design and subsequent learning right.

Sources indicate that the uncertainty has already reached Ontario’s electricity planning. In its November 10 filing to the Ontario Energy Board, OPG withdrew the Darlington SMR generation forecast from its 2027–2031 rate application. Previously planned production of about 0.5 TWh in 2030 and 1.9 TWh in 2031 is no longer included. The filing does not announce a post-2031 commissioning date. It shows that the earlier production assumptions cannot support the regulatory request.

Sources indicate that ontario does not need to suspend other electricity decisions while it waits for a revised reactor budget. The Independent Electricity System Operator’s May 2026 LT2 energy procurement secured 1,115 MW of new wind and solar contracts, with expected annual generation of about 2.37 TWh and a weighted average fixed price of C$88.84/MWh. That is approximately the annual electricity a 300 MW reactor would generate at a 90% capacity factor. Ontario also contracted 640 MW of battery capacity at C$563.48 per MW-business day.

Wind and solar provide energy on a different hourly profile from a nuclear reactor. The battery procurement buys capacity services, not 640 MW of round-the-clock generation. Ontario’s decision is to assemble a reliable portfolio from the newly introduced energy, existing nuclear and hydroelectric generation, storage, interties, transmission and flexible demand. The whole-system cost of that portfolio is the relevant comparator for the next three SMRs, not a claim that a wind farm is a nuclear reactor with a different name.

Industry observers note that this distinction also matters for the C$127/MWh comparison in my longer analysis. That figure allocates the renewable contracts’ initial energy payments and separate battery capacity payments across expected renewable production. It establishes a useful procurement spending benchmark. Additional charging, integration, transmission and dependable capacity requirements must be assessed to establish a comparable delivered system service.

Before Ontario commits to Units 2 through 4, it should require a credible outside-view update of the first unit’s cost and schedule, disclosure of outstanding design packages and their interfaces, measured evidence of construction learning, and a system-level comparison against resources that can be delivered during the same period. Each proposed later reactor is an investment decision, not an automatic entitlement created by spending on the first.

Sources indicate that ontario’s existing nuclear fleet is a valuable low-carbon resource. Keeping it productive and refurbishing it where justified remains key. The problem is treating a first-of-a-kind nuclear construction programme as reliably cheap future supply before engineering and costs support that conclusion.

Recent findings suggest that read the full Darlington assessment for the reference-class cost exposure, financing sensitivities and the investment gates Ontario should apply. The linked Flexibility Mesh report develops the system-services and grid-utilisation side of the comparison.

Industry News: Arista takes aim at the next AI network battleground: distributed inference

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1343 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.
  • Awareness of the network’s role in artificial intelligence has steadily increased, with much of the focus on the back end – larger clusters, faster ports and scale-across fabrics that stitch graphics processing units together across data centers.
  • Recent findings suggest that this week at SC26, Arista announced a shift in focus to the other side of the network.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 12:57 EST / NOVEMBER 17 2026.

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.

Awareness of the network’s role in artificial intelligence has steadily increased, with much of the focus on the back end – larger clusters, faster ports and scale-across fabrics that stitch graphics processing units together across data centers. Arista Networks Inc. has seen continued, accelerated growth and has been one of the biggest winners of that buildout.

Recent findings suggest that this week at SC26, Arista announced a shift in focus to the other side of the network. The organization also announced a fresh set of Etherlink R4 routing platforms designed for what it calls distributed inferencing, along with a pluggable optical line system for data center interconnect. The lineup includes:.

Industry observers note that all are based on Broadcom’s Jericho and Qumran silicon, designed to deliver up to 60% lower power consumption than competing 7-nanometer and 16-nanometer platforms. Everything is available now, except the 7020HR4, which ships in early 2027. The speeds and feeds always make headlines, but the implications of the launch point to where AI infrastructure is heading.

During a pre-briefing, Brendan Gibbs, Arista’s assistant vice president of product line management, argued that the forces driving training across multiple sites will have the same effect on inference. Gibbs also said that roughly 30% of Arista’s AI business is now scale-across, indicating that distributed AI is rapidly becoming commonplace.

Inference will be distributed for three reinforcing reasons:.

The implication is that the front-end network, long treated as plumbing, now needs back-end attributes: deep buffers, traffic engineering, multi-tenancy, and encryption, because traffic now leaves the building.

Industry observers note that this launch is the opposite of the descriptors we typically associate with Arista. Recent announcements focused on dense 800G, 1.6T, and liquid cooling. The products introduced at SC26 are smaller and less expensive. Arista dominates big iron and is now rounding out its portfolio. Arista’s customers range from hyperscalers to neoclouds to enterprises building local AI. The front end needs rich features, not massive bandwidth, and Arista hasn’t had a viable option for that tier until now.

These routers are designed as entry-level but ship with 400G uplinks, which may seem like overkill today but offer investment protection. Gibbs remarked the goal is a 10-year life cycle, with customers swapping optics rather than chassis. No one knows what agents will do to traffic volumes, and I suspect companies that consider this overkill today will think differently in three or four years. Headroom is cheaper than a forklift upgrade at a remote site. Also notable: Arista co-designed the 7280R4 with a hyperscaler seeking a gray-to-coherent bridge, a sign that it’s building with its biggest customers.

Recent findings suggest that the most intriguing product is the hardened 7020HR4, built for 5G and AI-RAN cell sites. Telcos have largely sat out the AI buildout, yet they own the last mile and real estate near users, exactly what low-latency inference requires. This gives a carrier the backbone to offer a managed AI factory.

In a recent development, my view is that this performs better outside the U.S., where enterprises don’t trust carriers beyond connectivity. In Europe and Asia-Pacific, managed services are far more common, and providers such as BT, NTT and Telstra have the footprint to make it work. With sovereignty requirements, the opportunity for telcos to move up the stack has never been better. Telcos have never been a core market for Arista, so any growth from that audience is additive to its already massive market.

Since 2019, Arista has reported a far lower CVE count than competitors, even after the surge in AI-assisted discovery following Anthropic’s Mythos. I’m skeptical of CVE comparisons because counts depend on testing rigor, installed base and reporting practices, and some vendors now bundle multiple issues into a single CVE.

The more relevant benefit is operational. Customers often don’t apply patches because upgrades cause downtime and break things. If they trust the software, they patch faster, and the risk window shrinks. With Mythos accelerating the retirement of end-of-support gear, quality and longevity become buying criteria, not nice-to-haves.

It has been revealed that on the call, Gibbs agreed it’s hard to draw conclusions from CVE counts but explained that CVE counts were a measure of Arista’s software quality. This has been Arista’s calling card since it was a startup. While CVEs provide one metric, the bigger proof point is its historical track record of quality software.

According to recent reports, also, wire-speed MACsec and IPsec on every port is a differentiator because AI brings different security requirements. However, integrated security does not replace firewalls. I asked Gibbs about this, and he remarked that Arista has no intention of replacing firewalls and expects Palo Alto Networks Inc. to continue to sit behind it in the line. I’d like to see that formalized into validated designs for distributed inference, like what Nvidia Corp.-validated designs did for the back end.

The optical line system is a similar simplification play. Arista isn’t an optical firm and is reselling these products, but offering dark fiber customers a turnkey, EOS-integrated way to move 25.6 Tbps across a metro network removes a real headache.

Recent findings suggest that customers have responded positively to Arista’s entry into this market. Douglas Fast Net Chief Technology Officer Jon Vradenburg mentioned the firm needs “a compact platform that supports the services our business and carrier customers rely on.” Takayuki Sakou of Japan’s STNet cited “higher throughput and improved power efficiency while maintaining the quality of the EOS software we trust.”.

Considerations for network professionals.

It has been revealed that the back end of AI networking is largely a solved architecture at this point. The front end is not, and that’s where the next round of competition will play out. With R4, Arista is betting that its routing credibility, built quietly within hyperscaler backbones, can make it the default there as well. Given how much traffic agentic AI is likely to generate, that’s a bet that, like most Arista bets, will likely pay off.

It has been revealed that zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scout Motors, the revived American brand now focused on off-road capable and affordable electric trucks and SUVs, has apparently produced its first validation build vehicles at its factory in South Carolina.
  • Industry observers note that we’ve seen many EV startups come and go, including ones that revived old, historic car brands — like Detroit Electric.
  • It has been revealed that oh, also, the company has a $2 billion factory in South Carolina, and it’s real.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scout Motors, the revived American brand now focused on off-road capable and affordable electric trucks and SUVs, has apparently produced its first validation build vehicles at its factory in South Carolina. This is a significant step forward toward mass production for the Volkswagen Group subsidiary.

Industry observers note that we’ve seen many EV startups come and go, including ones that revived old, historic car brands — like Detroit Electric. However, in this case, Scout is 1) offering something unique on the market, 2) focused on affordability combined with usefulness, 3) backed by automotive giant Volkswagen Group, and 4) at the moment has more than 200,000 reservations on the books! Reportedly, there are 212,000+ reservations for Scout EVs.

It has been revealed that oh, also, the company has a $2 billion factory in South Carolina, and it’s real. I’m sure there’s a lot to do there to get it filled out and operating as desired, but getting to factory production of validation build vehicles is a notable achievement that implies we are fairly close to getting actual production vehicles delivered to customers. The validation builds are of the Traveler SUV and Terra pickup truck.

The organization is now able to do stamping, welding, and painting at the factory in Blythewood, South Carolina, and CEO Scott Keogh claims the factory is actually 85% complete already.

After validation builds, the next phase will be pre-production vehicles. Keogh forecasts that actual production of consumer cars will begin in 2027, and deliveries will then commence in 2028. (So, customer vehicle production must be slated for the end of next year.) Construction on the factory began in 2023.

Recent findings suggest that scout was initially only going to produce 100% electric vehicles. However, it pivoted to also producing extended-range electric vehicles (vehicles that always run on electricity from a battery but whose battery can be recharged from a gas engine while driving). According to the firm, 87% of those 212,000+ reservations are for the range-extended versions of the Traveler and Terra. Buyers are also heavily favoring the SUV, the Traveler, which has pulled in 75% of the reservations so far.

Sources indicate that keogh thinks the tech giant could reach 400,000 reservations by the time it starts producing customer vehicles. It was at 160,000 in March and 50,000 in January. The factory is supposed to have an annual production capacity of 200,000. Having reservations for two years worth of production would be a strong, helpful boost for the company.

All of that said, one warning on the reservation tally is it has one of the same issues as the Tesla Cybertruck had — reservations are fully refundable and only cost $100. That makes it very hard to know how many people will actually go ahead and buy the vehicles once they are on offer. We will see.

#30198. A Radically Different Approach to AI

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2388 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica ↗ Open Full Page

A Radically Different Approach to AI

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2388 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • About forty years ago, I decided I would develop artificial intelligence in my spare time.
  • Sources indicate that I wanted to produce real AI, a type of thought that might take some effort for a human being to figure out.
  • My goal, I believed, would best be reached by first inventing something I called Artificial Cognition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

About forty years ago, I decided I would develop artificial intelligence in my spare time. I knew about the Turing test, and I believed that a computer tricking people into thinking it was human did not indicate intelligence. There was a program called ELIZA that did that already, and it was clearly not intelligent at all.

Sources indicate that I wanted to produce real AI, a type of thought that might take some effort for a human being to figure out. Maybe I would have to ask the computer how it reached the conclusion it did. But it would do so using logic a human could follow, examining each step. It would be a process a person could examine.

My goal, I believed, would best be reached by first inventing something I called Artificial Cognition. This would be a native way for computers to deal with data in the form of bit-fields, which were native data for computers, as translations of human words, in the same way that computers use IEEE bitwise representations of real numbers. Once this step was done, it would be easy to string words together in sentences, which could be directly translated into and out of human language. And the sentences would tell computers things they could “understand.”.

With such translations, a computer could translate a work, such as Shakespeare’s Henry V, into its own language. Then it could translate the text into whatever language we might want. Some subtleties would be lost, but human translators do the same thing.

Industry observers note that my idea was that computers should be able to work on ideas natively. At first, I thought this would require a very wide CPU, with registers that might be 256 bits, or even wider. In time, I came to believe that it would be best to stick to CPUs that were in use. As 64-bit CPUs were clearly coming soon, when I was working on this in 1986, I decided to use that data size. I also thought I might have to design a CPU with an additional instruction set, but I never got to the point of needing one.

So my design goal ended up having a word to translate almost any word (or even phrases) of English, occupying 64 bits of memory. And these could be understood and manipulated in standard registers of a standard computer.

I believe that I did achieve that goal, though the project never went into commercial use. A patent on the final design was issued by the US PTO, but that was long ago, and as I understand it, the whole thing is now in the public domain.

My reason for writing about this is that AI is a very contentious glitch today. Anthropic has even warned potential stockholders in its IPO documents that its product could have catastrophic effects if things go wrong, possibly to the point of terminating all human life. I think it even points out that a major part of the value of its stock would be lost if there were no human beings left to buy it.

It has been revealed that so I started to work on what I called Artificial Cognition in about 1986. Doing this in my spare time was a long slog. I went through a bunch of design iterations, starting, as I remarked, with 256-bit words. I won’t go through the work that had to be done determining how many designs there were and why each would not work. Each attempt took about a year or more, but eventually I got to the point of having a design in my fifth try.

I will give a simple explanation of the design in this article. Before I do, I will describe what the design could do at the time the patent was applied for, over twenty years ago. To reiterate, it could do these things:.

Recent findings suggest that eventually, I defined about 10,000 words for this design. Doing this was a full-time project that took two years, during which I also tested the design. At a point where I had about 2,500 words, I built a simple program that took two inputs of English words, translated them into the computer words, compared them to see that they were valid for compares, and held them for the record. Then it went through the entire vocabulary, taking each word (or set of words) in turn and finding any word that compared to it in precisely the same way the first two words compared.

In a recent development, this might sound like it did far more work than it needed to do. Because most words are not comparable, most compares produced faults and were rejected immediately. So the process did not have to do the millions of compares one might imagine. This was even easier than one might suppose, because whole huge sets of words could be rejected together. So if the input words were a pair like “train” and “airplane,” all words for colors or pieces of clothing could be rejected as sets.

One thing about this that is interesting is how it is done in the computer CPU. With a pair of 64-bit registers loaded, an XOR instruction will result in the difference between the two, or it will produce a fault. The XOR requires a single clock cycle. Then, with the word from the dictionary loaded into a register, a single XOR with the difference produces the word that gives the analogy, or it will produce a fault.

If there is a fault, we go on to the next word in the vocabulary. Otherwise, we have an analogy. In practice, for example, I ran this using original inputs of “car” and “small passenger plane.” The results came back, including the examples following, for “as a car is to a small passenger plane” (please note that each set of words in quotes is a single 64-bit word for the computer):.

Sources indicate that there were many other results, but the combination of lion and eagle stood out so clearly that I looked specifically to see what the comparison entailed. Why “lion” and “eagle,” but not “tiger” and “owl,” or “house cat” and “hawk”? There were about half a dozen predatory land animals and at least four predatory birds in that small dictionary, but “lion” and “eagle” were the only pair returned by the program. What gives?

According to recent reports, it turned out that things had gone precisely the way they should have. The reason that “lion” and “eagle” were chosen while others were not is that the definitions of these two had connotative values as symbols of authority. That information was in their 64-bit definitions. You can do a lot with 64 bits, if you know how.

This work was done in a 32-bit machine, simulating the 64-bit machines just about to come to market. With registers loaded (in a 64-bit machine), each compare would take one clock cycle. So the whole thing, with computers pre-loaded, would take two clocks. In a 2-GHz machine, the set of compares took one billionth of a second. One billionth of a second in a 64-bit machine anyone could buy. One billionth of a second in a Raspberry Pi costing $45.

It has been revealed that AI companies are bringing products to market that they warn could end the lives of all human beings. Anthropic notes its IPO, which comes out on Thursday, will establish the value of the organization at $1.5 trillion (NOTE: with a “T”). But Anthropic is warning that a risk for stockholders is that it could kill all humanity, including you, and your entire family, even if you live in a modest home and get no benefit from the company in any way. And everyone else could go with you. That, I read, is what the IPO papers say, but some people believe it could be very worthwhile to do.

Industry observers note that I believe this is not artificial intelligence. It might be artificial neglect. Maybe even artificial willful ignorance. Maybe, with artificial rational thought, we could produce artificial due diligence, but AI is not known for rationality.

According to recent reports, I wonder how high the value of Anthropic stock will go if only computers could buy it because there were no people left. Of course, without a Fed made up of humans, they might figure out a way to have infinite money to play with.

Sources indicate that the iteration of my invention that works depends on 64 bits being divided into categories, each represented by 8 bits. These are organized into eight supersets (3 bits), each with four groups of subsets (2 bits), with each group having eight basic subsets (3 bits). The total is 8 bits per set value, so there are 256 categories.

Of the eight supersets in each category, one is “agent.” This is anything that does anything. It is divided into four groups of subsets, two of which are “living thing” and “mechanism.” These are divided by type into subsets, so “living thing” includes “animal” and “plant,” among others.

According to recent reports, the category “location and time” is similar. This is divided into groups of subsets, one of which is “geography.” Within this are eight subsets, among which are “air,” “land,” “water,” “space,” and four others.

In a recent development, we can see the basic way the vocabulary works by taking these for the most significant 8 bits in a word, the field I call “BAS,” and the next most significant field, which I call “ALT,” because I seem to be unable to come up with a better 3-letter name for it. (Sorry, I do get a bit dull sometimes. Often.).

In a recent development, using just these two fields, we can see that a car, a train, a taxi, a bus, and a bicycle are all in a group, “land vehicle” (for ALT and BAS). An airplane of any type is an “air vehicle.” So are a blimp and a kite carrying prayers to the clouds asking them to make rain.

Similarly, a lion, tiger, bear, or dog would be a “land animal,” and most birds are “air animal.” Please note that I say “most birds.” They are not divided into biological groups, but according to where they function. Some birds only function on land. Similarly, a bat is an “air animal.” And Melville was right, Moby Dick was a “water animal,” just like any fish.

This broadly divides our dictionary into potential word values using 16 bits. This would limit us to just 65,536 potential words, if they were 16 bits long. Fortunately, we are only a quarter of the way through the 64 bits of our potential word definitions.

The next parts of the definition use 8 bits for each of several fields. A SRC field could represent where something comes from, why it has come into existence, or even what fuels it. For a car, this could be a value that decodes as “chemical,” or a value meaning “electricity.” For a sail-powered car, this field might mean “air.” For just “car,” with no motive force specified, this would be left to the value 0, meaning “any” or “whatever.”.

Industry observers note that an MTD field represents how it is operated. For a car, this could be decoded by a word meaning “engine” or “motor.” That is, unless the car is powered by sail, in which case neither of these values would work, but something other than 0 would be used, because 0 could mean a superset that engines and motors would match to. In the case of a buggy, this field would say “animal.”.

Recent findings suggest that A DST field may mean a destination or purpose. For a car, this could be a value meaning “human being,” for what it carries.

In addition to these, there is a CXT field, which can carry context. In the case of a lion or eagle, this is a value meaning “authority,” which is why they matched to each other but nothing else in the test.

Recent findings suggest that so far, I have described six fields. They provide us with far more potential words than any human language has by a huge factor. That should be enough, but there are other uses for bits. For example, I decided some time ago that there should be eight bits assigned to negation bits, each corresponding to a single field in the word.

Clearly, the values that make up the fields in the word are very fuzzy in their meanings. However, in the design, applying how these are to be interpreted has to be done strictly according to the sets of words involved. Implementing such a design means rules have to be developed according what part of the vocabulary is being worked on.

It has been revealed that altogether, I had a bit over 10,000 words defined about twenty years ago. I believed that these could be built up just a bit for software that could read a dictionary. As it happened, no one was willing to look at the invention to evaluate it, so funding of my invention ceased.

According to recent reports, before I finish up, I should mention that this sort of AI does not do images or other types of jobs that require pattern matching. That isn’t what I set out to do. I always assumed that such things would come from people interested in them. But I wasn’t interested.

I have a problem with the AI being produced commercially today. All of it looks to me like it is based on the same sort of pattern matching that is done by a human mind to some extent. And this is a problem because human beings are not naturally rational creatures. So AI companies are basically building irrational products.

Recent findings suggest that as for Anthropic and the other organizations that claim to have products that threaten human life, that looks like artificial insanity requiring artificial restraint. Or artificial constraint. At least until someone can develop artificial ethics and artificial caution. I don’t think Anthropic has that yet. But I think there is a way to do it.

The facility will manufacture high-efficiency solar cells using advanced automation, Industry 4.0 technologies, and comprehensive digital traceability.

Nextnova celebrates the inauguration of its new solar cell manufacturing facility in Oklahoma City. Credit: Nextnova.

Designed for maximum quality and reliability, the facility features fully integrated manufacturing execution systems (MES), automated inspection technologies, advanced process control, and a dedicated analytical laboratory supporting continuous quality verification throughout production.

Nextnova notes that its commitment to transparent sourcing, manufacturing excellence, and scalable production provides customers with high-performance solar cells that support the continued growth of a secure and competitive U.S. solar industry.

  • Patent-pending vertical PECVD/PVD architecture doubles wafer throughput over NAED’s previous platform and is designed to produce perovskite/HJT tandem cells targeting 30% efficiency.
  • According to recent reports, NAED Energy Holding Inc.
  • In a recent development, in PV-1, wafers travel upright on a shared carrier through every PECVD and PVD stage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Patent-pending vertical PECVD/PVD architecture doubles wafer throughput over NAED’s previous platform and is designed to produce perovskite/HJT tandem cells targeting 30% efficiency.

According to recent reports, NAED Energy Holding Inc. (“NAED”), the U.S. aerospace, engineering, and utility-energy company behind NAED Nexus Core™, last week unveiled PV-1 PECVD-V, a vertical in-line deposition platform for high-volume solar cell manufacturing. PV-1 combines plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) and physical vapor deposition (PVD) on a single shared-carrier line. It is designed for a throughput of 96,000 wafers per hour, double the 48,000 wafers per hour of NAED’s previous XL-class platform.

In a recent development, in PV-1, wafers travel upright on a shared carrier through every PECVD and PVD stage. To reach the second side of the wafer, the system never flips the substrate: the entire carrier is lifted and turned 180 degrees as a unit. This keeps wafers seated in the same carrier from first deposition to last, cutting direct wafer handling between process steps. The PV-1 production line, its 180-degree carrier turn, its wafer-retention carrier, and the T2X tandem cell are the subject of pending U.S. patent applications assigned to NAED Energy Holding Inc. NAED’s intellectual property portfolio has been independently appraised at $179 million under an ASC 820 Level 3 fair-value methodology, as of November 11, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that PV-1 was engineered from the start for tandem solar. The full line, including perovskite top-cell process tools, is designed to produce NAED’s T2X two-terminal perovskite/heterojunction (HJT) tandem cell, which targets 30% cell efficiency. NAED aims to bring T2X cells to both terrestrial and space solar markets, alongside a family of glass-glass T2X modules starting at 600 W.

Sources indicate that every PV-1 tool is designed in-house by NAED and machined in its own aerospace-grade CNC shop in the United States. The first six of PV-1’s thirteen process tools are complete, and the remaining seven are in production. Engineering and design for the full PV-1 line and its production facility are complete.

In a recent development, “Going vertical, let us double throughput and build the line around tandem cells from day one, rather than retrofitting tandem onto a platform designed for something else,” noted Malcom Longair, Media & Development Lead, NAED Energy Holding Inc. “With PV-1, manufacturers anywhere in the world can reserve U.S.-engineered deposition equipment built for the next generation of solar cells.”.

NAED is now opening reservations for PV-1 production tool slots to solar cell manufacturers in the United States and internationally. Manufacturers can request specifications and reserve a slot at NAED. energy or through the media and partnership contact below.

News release from NAED Energy Holding, Inc.

It has been revealed that WUHU, China — Following the 2026 Chery International User Summit, Chery Auto is pressing ahead with its new energy ecosystem strategy. Entering the Globalization 3.0 phase, the firm is deploying a mix of energy solutions to meet mobility energy needs around the world. As electric vehicles integrate with power grids, Chery Auto is developing a smart energy ecosystem that transforms new energy vehicles (NEVs) into dispatchable distributed mobile energy nodes, supporting grid management, sustainable urban development, and local energy resource utilization.

Unlike conventional charging, which can increase peak demand, V2G offers a flexible alternative. Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) enables bidirectional flow, allowing vehicles to store off-peak electricity and return power during peak demand. For users, this creates opportunities to participate in energy management and potentially generate value. With participation depending on commercial feasibility and user confidence, Chery Group’s global user base exceeding 21 million provides a foundation for V2G deployment.

Sources indicate that chery Auto is validating its energy ecosystem across homes, communities and industrial parks. Its household Energy Cube integrates solar, storage and bidirectional charging to support electricity supply during exceptional conditions. In Wuhu, a large-scale AC V2G demonstration station enables private vehicles to support grid management through onboard chargers with limited modifications. In Spain, an industrial park microgrid uses green electricity to reduce energy costs, fossil fuel dependence, and carbon emissions.

Chery Auto’s Volt-dragon Ultra-Fast Charging technology targets 500 km of range in five minutes. Its hybrid engine has achieved 48.57% thermal efficiency, while the planned Rhino S solid-state battery targets 400 Wh/kg energy density. Chery’s Rhino Battery prioritizes fast charging, longevity and safety, addressing battery degradation and thermal management concerns associated with V2G charging cycles.

Sources indicate that chery Auto is developing modular solar, storage, charging, and V2G solutions tailored to regional infrastructure. In Europe, electricity markets provide opportunities for distributed energy participation. Mature markets integrate vehicles into grid management, while regions with weaker infrastructure can prioritize microgrids before introducing V2G.

Industry observers note that through applications spanning households, communities, and industrial parks, Chery Auto is extending automotive-grade engineering into energy infrastructure. Its approach supports distributed energy networks using locally generated electricity and managing energy flows, positioning Chery to participate in future smart cities.

Sources indicate that antalya, Türkiye — The COP31 Leaders’ Summit concluded today, with several new announcements and speeches from heads of state and the UN Secretary-General. Developments included country endorsements of the COP Presidency’s 35×35 electrification pledge, growing support for the transition away from fossil fuels, and new pledges from philanthropies to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, among others.

Following is a statement from Ani Dasgupta, President and CEO, World Resources Institute:.

“One message came across loud and clear from world leaders: climate action has shifted from an environmental movement to a core economic and security imperative. The conversation is moving beyond high-level commitments to the practical challenges of how to transition away from fossil fuels while supporting workers and communities and how to put entire economies on a cleaner, more resilient path.

“Electrification and the transition away from fossil fuels rightly took center stage. These are two vital, intertwined goals, and progress on one must reinforce the other. Early support for the 35×35 electrification pledge is encouraging, but many more countries need to endorse it and turn their commitments into credible national prepares backed by concrete policies and investment.

“President Lula deserves credit for keeping the transition away from fossil fuels at the top of the international agenda and delivering a global roadmap that countries can adapt to their own circumstances. Australia and Türkiye now have an opportunity to lead by example, putting forward their own transition intends and encouraging others to follow.

Recent findings suggest that “Vulnerable countries delivered an equally clear message: access to affordable finance is critical to them implementing their climate ambition. High borrowing costs and unsustainable debt are holding back investment in the very countries that need it most. With the $1.3 trillion finance goal established, the focus is shifting to how all sources of finance can work together to deliver investment at scale and how we ensure affordable capital reaches those who need it most. There are encouraging signs, including an influx of pledges from philanthropies for the Brazil-initiated Tropical Forests Forever Facility.

“Adaptation and early warning systems received much-needed attention after a year of crushing heatwaves, fires, and floods. But that attention now needs to turn to the investment in systemic resilience as the best way to make economies and societies stronger and improve people’s lives. Building more resilient cities was a major focus and will take deep collaboration between national governments, cities, and states. Cities are on the front lines of delivering the climate solutions and essential services that make people’s lives better, and demonstrating these benefits is critical to accelerating the transition. Local leaders are on the front lines of climate impacts and the delivery of essential services that make communities safer, healthier, and more resilient, yet too often lack the resources to respond. Cities and local communities especially need greater access to adaptation finance.

“It was disappointing to see no dedicated ocean event at the Leaders’ Summit, despite over 90% of countries including ocean action in national climate intends. The ocean is on the front lines of the climate crisis, but it could also be one of our greatest allies in tackling it. Ocean-based solutions can provide up to one-third of the emissions cuts needed by 2050 to keep 1.5°C within reach. This ambition for ocean action must be reflected in any COP31 cover decision and translate into concrete progress, especially for vulnerable coastal and island nations.

“Some leaders also delivered a resounding defense of multilateralism, even amid deep geopolitical tensions. International cooperation on climate may be changing shape, but it is still alive and needed now more than ever. Even in a fractured world, leaders recognize that no country can secure its economic future, build resilience, or prosper without working together on shared climate and environmental challenges. That spirit of cooperation must now carry through the negotiations and deliver a strong, ambitious outcome at COP31.”.

Industry News: Dell puts a single gateway between enterprise AI agents and the data they crave

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Data intelligence is becoming the deciding layer of the enterprise AI factory as companies learn that racks of graphics processing units deliver little value when agents lack trusted, governed context.
  • Industry observers note that neocloud providers built the first wave of large-scale AI systems, and core enterprise customers now want the same capabilities inside their own organizations.
  • It has been revealed that “The bottom line is if you feed the wrong data, you get the wrong outcomes,” Alapati stated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 13:19 EST / NOVEMBER 17 2026.

Data intelligence is becoming the deciding layer of the enterprise AI factory as companies learn that racks of graphics processing units deliver little value when agents lack trusted, governed context.

Industry observers note that neocloud providers built the first wave of large-scale AI systems, and core enterprise customers now want the same capabilities inside their own organizations. Dell Technologies Inc. recently extended its AI Data Platform with semantic and knowledge graph features aimed at that market shift. But both the challenge and the opportunity lie in pairing structured and unstructured data so agents get full context while maintaining guardrails and human oversight, according to Srinath Alapati (pictured, right), senior director of product marketing for AI Data Platform at Dell.

It has been revealed that “The bottom line is if you feed the wrong data, you get the wrong outcomes,” Alapati stated. “What we’ve found is in our own testing — by giving the right context — you can improve the accuracy from roughly 60% to like 94%.”.

Alapati, Alison Biers (center), senior director of product marketing for compute, networking and global industries at Dell, and Adam Glick (left), senior director of AI solutions product marketing for compute at Dell, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Dell is tying data, infrastructure management and validated designs together to move enterprise AI factories into production. (* Disclosure below.).

According to recent reports, enterprises can’t give agents unfettered access to their systems, which is where Dell’s newly announced Agentic Data Gateway fits. The gateway sits in the orchestration layer as a single point of control, backed by a Model Context Protocol server, Alapati explained. Storage intelligence tells customers what data they hold, who owns it and how large it is, while Dell’s newly introduced data intelligence capabilities track lineage and provenance. Hybrid workflows extend that model across the edge, the cloud and the data center, where companies can struggle to meet the data consolidation requirements of other data platform providers.

Sources indicate that “They want you to bring all the data to wherever the platform is. That’s not always possible,” Alapati said. “Number one, it’s super expensive. Two is data is always being generated. It’s a never-ending game. You can’t always keep bringing in data, consolidating data. What we do is we only send metadata … That way your data stays where you want to be.”.

In a recent development, on the infrastructure side, Dell OpenManage Rack Scale extends management beyond compute endpoints to the network fabric, power and cooling. That gives operators a single operational plane from day zero through day two, according to Biers. A rebuilt, intent-based Dell Fabric Manager replaces the tech giant’s SmartFabric Manager, and Dell’s PowerRack systems treat the full rack as the unit of deployment.

“It is literally six hours from the time it hits your loading dock to full production,” Biers stated. “Something that used to take maybe months and months [is] now cut in half, maybe even less.”.

Sources indicate that more than 6,500 customers now use the Dell AI Factory, and a growing share are core enterprises asking for help putting AI to work, Glick noted. Validated designs built with Nvidia Corp. and other partners cover both the hardware and the full software stack, and Dell is expanding its labs to keep pace with independent software companies joining the ecosystem. Compute still draws most of the attention, but that is only one part of a larger system.

Recent findings suggest that “If you’ve got a factory, compute is your assembly line. It’s the notable part,” Glick said. “It’s what you think of when you think of ‘factory’, but that assembly line doesn’t run if you don’t have a warehouse that’s feeding it the raw materials — that’s the data that goes into it.”.

Tech Report: 5 Exciting Ways to Invest in Real Estate

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth.
  • In recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it.
  • According to recent reports, not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

In recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

According to recent reports, not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing fresh opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

With digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

Recent findings suggest that the approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

According to recent reports, REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

Industry observers note that if you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech tech giant could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

Sources indicate that investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.

Latest Update: Cummins Told Electrolyser Customers to Stop. Who Keeps the Hydrogen Plants Running?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, cummins is withdrawing from upcoming electrolyser sales, but its customers have a problem that cannot be handled by closing a sales office.
  • Sources indicate that cummins had a substantial position in the PEM electrolyser business.
  • In a recent development, the timing makes the situation consequential.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, cummins is withdrawing from upcoming electrolyser sales, but its customers have a problem that cannot be handled by closing a sales office. In September, its Hydrogenics subsidiaries recommended that customers stop using HyLYZER electrolysers following a review of operating data. The company disclosed the recommendation in its November quarterly report, stated that it had not launched a recall, and was still assessing what modifications might be needed for equipment to return to service. It had not established the cost of resolving the issue and warned that the eventual financial effect could be material.

Sources indicate that cummins had a substantial position in the PEM electrolyser business. Accelera reports more than 45 HyLYZER 500 systems and more than 20 HyLYZER 1000 systems rated at 5 MW each. Using those minimum reported system counts and equipment ratings, its historical deployments represent roughly 145–213 MW, equivalent to 11–16% of the IEA’s projected 1.3 GW global PEM installed base at the end of 2026. Cummins has not published the number of HyLYZER plants covered by its September recommendation. The tech giant is leaving a sizeable equipment estate requiring expert maintenance, field engineers and potential safety modifications.

In a recent development, the timing makes the situation consequential. Cummins declared in February that it intended to cease new commercial electrolyser activity, while continuing existing customer commitments. Its 2025 Accelera restructuring and impairment charges reached $458 million across several actions, including the electrolyser retreat. It is reducing specialist capacity at the same time as installed equipment needs engineering attention. Revenue from new orders can disappear faster than warranties, service obligations and safety responsibilities.

Industry observers note that my TFIE Strategy Briefing on Cummins’ hydrogen hangover examines the HyLYZER warning, the customer projects and the financial implications of manufacturers leaving shrinking markets. The underlying evidence and project comparisons are in the full analysis.

It has been revealed that the problem now moves from selling hardware to keeping it safe and serviceable. Investigating field data, testing modifications, certifying repair procedures and maintaining proprietary controls requires specialist teams. Those teams must remain capable long after the sales pipeline and the business unit built around it have contracted.

Estonia’s Stargate Hydrogen has taken over Cummins’ legacy HySTAT alkaline electrolyser platform and supplies replacement stacks and service for a fleet of more than 400 installations. That handover demonstrates how intellectual property, manufacturing capability and field-service expertise can survive an OEM exit. Cummins’ HyLYZER PEM fleet needs its own engineering and aftermarket solution.

For owners, the financial question also depends on the purpose of the hydrogen. Air Liquide’s 20 MW Bécancour installation and Linde’s 35 MW Niagara Falls project serve companies with industrial hydrogen customers and alternative supply networks. Interruptions can mean lost sales, replacement purchases and costs of maintaining customer commitments. An owner with contracted industrial demand has a commercial reason to restore production, provided the equipment can meet the required safety standards and the replacement supply costs justify it.

Sources indicate that florida Power & Light’s Cavendish project presents another decision. Its 25 MW HyLYZER installation converts electricity to hydrogen for limited blending into natural gas used in power generation. Even without a stop-use issue, that application has to compete with using electricity directly or obtaining reliable grid services by other means. At an illustrative 55 kWh/kg of electrolyser electricity and 60% combined-cycle generation efficiency, about 36% of the original electricity returns after converting it to hydrogen and burning it, before compression and storage. Input power at $50/MWh would cost roughly $138/MWh of recovered electricity before equipment and operating expenses. Repairing the electrolyser would not change that conversion arithmetic.

The economic difference appears again at Hysolar’s Nieuwegein installation. A 2025 KWR H-Flex evaluation documented project delays, higher costs and hydrogen demand expanding more slowly than planned. Its electrolyser, dedicated pipeline, refuelling station and vehicle customers are linked by a common demand forecast. Better equipment performance helps only when enough customers will buy the hydrogen at prices covering production and delivery. The same distinction applies to demonstration projects combining buses, heating, electricity and gas blending: several proposed uses do not guarantee several profitable markets.

According to recent reports, manufacturers face the cost of retaining the people and intellectual property to support complex equipment long after the expected growth market has contracted. Cummins’ separate exit from its low-pressure fuel-cell business illustrates the potential bill: in March 2026, it made a $175 million net payment as part of a sale, cancellation of commitments and claims settlement, producing a $199 million accounting charge. Those are fuel-cell transaction figures, not estimated HyLYZER repair costs. The PEM matter remains unquantified.

The customers’ cost can exceed the repair bill. Owners need a safe restart route, long-term supply of stacks and controls, a price for replacement hydrogen during outages, and buyers able to pay for the output afterward. Lenders face a thinner resale market for specialised plants when their OEM leaves. Public funders face grant, regulated cost-recovery and guarantee liabilities when projects stop operating.

The wider hydrogen market makes these questions urgent. The IEA’s Global Hydrogen Review 2026 finds that global demand still sits overwhelmingly in traditional industry and refining. Only about one-fifth of newly signed low-emissions hydrogen offtake volumes in 2025 had firm contractual commitments. A producer, refuelling-station operator and vehicle buyer can each invest on the assumption that the other two will grow. That is one demand risk distributed across three balance sheets, not three independent investments.

Sources indicate that the next investment decision needs a safe route back to service, contracted customers, dependable parts supply and a costed exit alternative. Governments should direct support toward industrial customers who need hydrogen and can pay for it, rather than finance energy-carrier applications that lose to direct electricity. Cummins is exposing the long tail of earlier commitments. Other suppliers, buyers and lenders still control their next decisions.

In a recent development, the complete Cummins analysis compares industrial-gas plants, fuel-substitution pilots, refuelling systems and legacy equipment obligations. The earlier Cummins–Alstom assessment reveals how similar service liabilities can persist in fuel-cell transportation.
