#30130. Tech Report: BMW In South Carolina: A Free Trade Success Story

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2215 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Cleantechnica ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: BMW In South Carolina: A Free Trade Success Story

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2215 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I recently attended BMW’s “Beyond The Machine” event in South Carolina.
  • It has been revealed that beyond the vehicles and manufacturing, which I proposal to cover in more detail in future articles, one of the most striking aspects was the human impact.
  • According to recent reports, the area around Greenville, South Carolina the rose to prominence in the 1870s on the textile industry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I recently attended BMW’s “Beyond The Machine” event in South Carolina. The largest facility of the German company globally is Plant Spartanburg in Greer, South Carolina. As part of the event, I saw the opening of BMW’s new battery plant in nearby Woodruff. We stayed in the nearby city of Greenville, which was transformed by BMW and the businesses that followed.

It has been revealed that beyond the vehicles and manufacturing, which I proposal to cover in more detail in future articles, one of the most striking aspects was the human impact. From the “Woodruffian” Mayor fighting back tears at the opening of the battery plant to the plant employees to the people I met exploring the town, they clearly appreciate what BMW has done for the community. Throughout the presentations and discussions, there was support for free trade along with the local benefits. People in the area pride themselves in their resilience. They have reason to be proud. And they were optimistic about the growth of the increasingly clean manufacturing and electrified products from this global manufacturer.

According to recent reports, the area around Greenville, South Carolina the rose to prominence in the 1870s on the textile industry. Cotton from throughout the South that had previously been shipped to other areas for processing was processed in Greenville and Spartanburg counties. However, as global competition increased in the 20th century, the mills became less competitive. The last textile mill closed in Greenville in 1977, although a few textile operations continued in the region into the 1980’s. As that industry left, the local economy declined. If the story ended there, many might use it as an argument against free trade.

Sources indicate that when BMW came to South Carolina in 1992, they saw a lot of potential. Michelin had already started making tires there in 1978. Local leaders were enthusiastic to work with BMW. The people were also enthusiastic to receive training for the new jobs. The deep-water port of Charleston on the other side of the state facilitated shipping, while nearby rail links connected to much of the US.

Since 1992, BMW has invested over $15.8 Billion. The newly introduced Woodruff battery plant is their most recent major investment. In the process, an area that could have been considered a casualty of global trade became one of its greatest beneficiaries.

The first model, an E36 3 series, rolled off the line in 1994. BMW also produced the Z3 in the plant, including the first “German” car driven by James Bond on camera. However, the big breakthrough came with the introduction of the X5 in 1999. At the time, relatively few SUVs were being sold in Europe. BMW Spartanburg as the center of SUV production was intending to largely for the US. However, global markets shifted.

Now, Spartanburg is the “Home of X.” It currently produces the X3, X5, X6, X7 and XM, including electrified versions. It is the sole manufacturing plant for a number of those SUV models globally. A little over half of their production is exported, which also makes it consistently the top US overseas automotive exporter. Export volume topped $9 Billion in 2025 over roughly 200,000 X vehicles.

BMW designed those vehicles to be able to use ICE, PHEV and BEV powertrains. While some may want them to make just pure BEV, the approach gives BMW the ability to shift rapidly with the market. The different models also give the plant a level of market resilience. However, to fuel that resilience they need a very flexible supply chain that can respond swiftly. Suppliers being close to the plant creates greater resilience.

Recent findings suggest that BMW is designing its vehicles to be globally competitive. While 400+ miles of EPA range and charging speeds approaching 500 kW may be at the top of the US market, they are also competitive in global markets. While BMW developed the cells and packs, they use multiple suppliers to manufacture the cylindrical cells to their specifications. Packs at the plant currently use AESC cells, but they will shift to LG in the future and use other suppliers in other markets.

BMW also worked with the state of South Carolina to develop people. Nearby Clemson University provides a source of engineering talent, and BMW partners with the university on the Clemson University International Center for Automotive Research, where both students and BMW benefit from the development of newly introduced innovations. They are also developing potential future suppliers with the BMW Venture funds. One such company will be supplying flax-based composites to future M models.

Industry observers note that A heavy emphasis is placed on technical training at the factory. In addition, they collaborated with community colleges to provide technical training. But the development programs start much earlier, with a heavy emphasis in middle school and sponsoring the First Robotics Competition for elementary school students.

Recent findings suggest that BMW also worked with the South Carolina Department of Transportation to build infrastructure to support the plant and its suppliers. Moving forward, that infrastructure will increasingly include electrification and EV charging. BMW also worked with the SC Ports Authority to develop an “inland port,” which is essentially a direct rail link to the Port of Charleston. By moving freight by rail, emissions are greatly reduced. In addition, a lot of emphasis is going into transferring freight rapidly, as every minute a truck sits idling is also wasted emissions.

According to recent reports, while BMW employs 11,000 workers, over four times as many jobs are supported by the plant, according to a Clemson economist. That multiplier is much higher than most companies due to how BMW operates. Part of the impact on the local economy beyond employee count comes from the strategy behind the manufacturing. Overall, more than 70% of the value of the vehicles comes from outside suppliers.

Plant Spartanburg receives 3.3 million parts per day delivered by 1200 truckloads and 50 sea containers, 6 days per week. All those parts then go into over 1500 vehicles produced per day. The plant is laid out a bit different than some other manufacturing plants to facilitate the supply chain. Multiple fingers go up off the main line, along which parts are delivered to be assembled nearby. There isn’t much in the way of warehousing. Trucks come to the plant each day and the parts can end up on vehicles driving off the line the same day.

In the initial stages of manufacturing, more of the supply base came from overseas. However, as the plant established itself, more suppliers localized. That growing supply chain then attracted additional companies to the region, like Mercedes, Volvo and Scout. Those companies then create greater scale for the suppliers, who can reduce costs and expand operations.

Recent findings suggest that overall, for heavy, bulky components, localization will tend to  happen naturally. For a company that relies on suppliers to consistently and almost constantly deliver parts, that localization tends to increase. The more localized the supply chain, the more capable it becomes to respond to market dynamics. Once scale is attained for heavy, bulky components like batteries, that production will naturally become more localized.

According to recent reports, BMW has a growing supply chain footprint across the Americas and especially across the Southeastern US. There will be over 850 Tier 1 supplier locations in the Americas by 2027, with multiple times as many Tier 2 and Tier 3 suppliers providing materials, parts and components. BMW focuses on value creation, competitiveness and collaboration in their supply chain. In addition, while they are bringing economic benefit, they are also focused on decarbonization.

Of course, all this economic activity has brought “green” in terms of money to the local communities. As I was stranded in Greenville due to flight interruptions, I had time to walk around the town and speak to some of the locals. Streets that were once desolate and unsafe are now vibrant with shops and restaurants. An area that people once wanted to leave is now growing rapidly and attracting people from around the world. I started conversations  with several friendly people in town about trade. I heard stories of transformation from past struggles to current successes.

Even though it was clear that they were benefitting from the economic impact, I was still surprised how strongly and openly they supported free trade and realized the benefits. A local guide pointed out major buildings and businesses that were new. Downtown is now pleasant and walkable. Part of that is due to the restoration of a river that runs through the city, surrounded by shops and artwork, where I saw some locals fishing in the clear water. This gets to the other kind of “green.”.

While there are a lot of trucks transporting materials and components, shortened travel distances and efforts to streamline intermodal transfers reduce emissions. The proximity enables packaging to typically be sent back to the supplier to be reused. BMW is also putting a lot of effort into reduced CO2 emissions steel produced locally, which I blueprint to follow up on. Over half the steel in their vehicles is reduced CO2. Solar panels and landfill gas provide power for their facilities.

As the company relies heavily on its supply chain, the supply chain is a major focus of its decarbonization strategy. While EVs reduce emissions overall, the proportion of emissions from the manufacturing phase tends to be higher than for ICE vehicles, adding emphasis to decarbonization of manufacturing. At the same time, they strive to create regional strength, resilience and value creation while reducing emissions. Close collaboration is the key to meeting these goals. BMW looks to have net zero CO2 emissions throughout their supply chain by 2050 at the latest.

Industry observers note that the new Woodruff plant will produce their sixth-generation battery. BMW develops the batteries first and then outsources the cell manufacturing, but they will now be manufacturing the packs locally. Initially, this will be for the iX5, to be delivered domestically and to global markets. However, additional EV models may benefit in the future.

Overall, politicians in the 1970’s could have tried to block global competition to protect the textile mills. That might have extended the life of those plants for a few years. However, in the process, those plants would become less globally competitive and less globally relevant. Protectionism would have only extended a slow, painful decline.

Industry observers note that however, by keeping the market open and staying open to latest business opportunities, Greenville, Greer, Spartanburg and Woodruff created the circumstances for their current success. People were open to new companies from other countries. They were open to industries that were new to the area. And they were open to investing in retraining to better take advantage of the new opportunities.

Recent findings suggest that in the initial site selection, South Carolina could have imposed strict regulations and tried to force localization before the factory was built, production was ramped up and scale was attained to support that localization. If that happened, the plant would have undoubtedly been built elsewhere, and the economic benefits would have gone to someone else. By taking a more collaborative approach, rather than being confrontational, both BMW and local suppliers benefitted greatly. Building on that approach, more companies came to the region, building scale and amplifying the benefits.

BMW is not being hypocritical in their support of free trade. They are not promoting free trade just when it benefits them and then putting up barriers for other competitors. They are not shying away from global competition. They are seeking to make globally competitive vehicles for global markets. While global competition is fierce, by facing that competition, rather than hiding from it, their products become more competitive.

In the process, one of the brightest spots in US automotive trade globally, as well as one of the leaders in electrified product and supply chain decarbonization, comes from a German manufacturer.

Change and globalization can be scary things. Especially in the short term. The transition to EVs can also be scary, especially for those tied to the past. However, hiding behind political and trade walls rarely works out in the long run. A willingness to be open and collaborative with people who might come from within different lines on a map or sound different than you can have long term benefits. And the courage to engage with the technology transition and compete globally can put you ahead of many established competitors. That cannot only transform how we power our vehicles, but also transform the lives of people in communities for generations to come. As Woodruff Mayor Kenneth Gist put it at the battery plant opening:.

BMW and the City of Woodruff wanted the same thing. Success in business, success in our community, and success in building the next generation of BMW electric vehicles to be the best in the world….

…When I think about this plant, I think about our children, our grandchildren. Educational partnership that will open the doors for them, the career that will be waiting for them, and a Woodruff they would be proud to call home for decades to come. BMW, you have been a true partner to me personally, to every person in this community.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

V10 engines are the ultimate metaphors for what gearheads love about performance cars — relics of a bygone era where noise, power and absolute combustion were the go-to recipes of kings. The Lexus LFA and Porsche Carrera GT – arguably two of the greatest road-going supercars ever – used them. So too did the Sesto Elemento, which was Lamborghini's answer to the very essence of track-day hoonery. They even featured in the E60-generation BMW M5 – a perhaps ugly but elegant grand tourer that made a mockery of purpose-built, seven-figure unobtanium thanks to an unrestricted 200-mph-plus top speed.

According to recent reports, but aside from the actual cylinder count, what these cars all have in common is substantial displacements. The LFA's V10 is the smallest of the bunch, and even that measures in at 4.8 liters. You'd think, then, that all V10s must surely have to be meaty by nature to work, but you'd be wrong. Say hello to the Connaught Type D concept: a sports car conceived in 2004 and equipped with a pipsqueak 2.0-liter V10. Yes, two liters.

For some perspective, many passenger cars these days use 2.0-liter four-cylinder engines, including the Honda Civic hatchback, which is the platonic ideal of economy cars. Now imagine constraining yourself to such a small surface area, with the added complication of having to manage an extra six cylinders. The result would be ... amazing, actually.

The standard Connaught used a naturally aspirated V10 and a Lynch electric motor for 162 hp. Yes, hybrid technology was being tested as far back as 2004 with this car, long before the hypercar Holy Trinity was formed and crowned. However, in the top-spec "Syracuse GT" version, the Type D's V10 engine was instead paired with a supercharger for a healthy 300 hp. The Connaught Type D Syracuse GT's 0 to 60 mph was projected to be in the low-four-second range, and popular publications cited a top speed of roughly 171 mph. This thing also tipped the scales at just 1,874 pounds.

Sources indicate that those are some serious numbers and would be enough to trouble many four-cylinder sports cars that, dare we say, could be called super. Even today's fleet of racey four-banger metal wouldn't be safe. The Honda Civic Type R, which is a rowdy teenage dirtbag, takes about a second longer to get to 60 mph, while the 2026 Ford Mustang RTR (with its 2.3-liter engine) only just edges it by two-tenths of a second (via Car and Driver). Unfortunately, the Type D never made it past the concept stage and into production due to funding issues.

The brand was acquired in 2016 by a British automotive design company called Bevan Davidson International (BDI), and in 2021, it came up with a wild idea to revive Connaught with a 20-cylinder supercar called the X20. We'll give you a moment to rub your eyes and re-read the final part of that sentence.

That 20-cylinder engine would be made up of two horizontally opposed and mid-mounted 2.0-liter V10s. It would also blow its waste gases out of no fewer than 20 exhaust pipes, rev all the way up to 10,000 rpm, and, as far as the company's calculations go, produce more than 500 hp. That sounds less like a car, and more like a miniature steam train from the 17th century, but no word on whether any have been produced yet.

According to recent reports, whether BDI chooses to also bring the original Type D back to life remains to be seen, but just think about it for a second: A tiny-displacement, supercharged V10-powered sports car built to comply with the ever-growing regulations posed on the industry by lawmakers. Wouldn't that be just marvelous?

Artificial intelligence-driven disease detection and intelligent care platform Viz.ai declared Monday a strategic partnership with Wolters Kluwer Health to integrate the Viz.ai One platform into UpToDate Expert AI.

Through the partnership, providers caring for patients with complex conditions will be able to ask detailed questions and receive evidence-based answers relevant to clinical context from UpToDate directly within existing workflows.

“The greatest leap we can achieve in healthcare is to make the best medical evidence always available, applied automatically to every patient, at the moment it matters,” mentioned Chris Mansi, Viz.ai CEO and co-founder, in a statement to Fierce Healthcare.

Mansi continued, “Bringing UpToDate’s trusted evidence into Viz.ai’s workflow takes us closer to that vision: an AI safety net that detects disease, helps clinicians identify who needs care and empower them to act on the evidence. Our goal is to close the gap between what medicine knows and the care each patient receives, so no patient is left behind.”.

The companies say it is the first integration to bring UpToDate into AI-driven care coordination workflows.

Wolters Kluwer CEO Greg Samios said in a statement that one of healthcare AI’s biggest opportunities is "to help clinicians see more of the patient's full picture when making healthcare decisions.".

“Viz.ai's technology can proactively flag signs of disease and alert care teams, even before a condition is suspected,” Samios said. “Paired with UpToDate's trusted clinical intelligence, clinicians have more of the information they need, directly in their workflow, to help inform care decisions.”.

The BLUETTI Apex 200 Expandable Portable Power Station — CleanTechnica Tested

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1273 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • BLUETTI continues to innovate, finding fresh ways to move its portable power station technology into meaningful new formats that provide owners with additional capability, portability, and utility.
  • Industry observers note that they recently reached out about a fresh stackable portable power station format based around the Apex 200 power station.
  • Disclaimer: BLUETTI provided the Apex 200, B300K, and a pair of solar panels to the author for the purposes of this review.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BLUETTI continues to innovate, finding fresh ways to move its portable power station technology into meaningful new formats that provide owners with additional capability, portability, and utility.

Industry observers note that they recently reached out about a fresh stackable portable power station format based around the Apex 200 power station. It packs in a meaningful 2.5 kilowatt-hours (kWh) of storage capacity by itself, but the real magic is that it was built to be modular and can be linked up with additional storage modules to be stacked underneath, connecting directly to the main unit.

Disclaimer: BLUETTI provided the Apex 200, B300K, and a pair of solar panels to the author for the purposes of this review.

This modular format is a game changer because it means you don’t need an installer to bolt 300 pounds of batteries to the wall of your house. Instead, you can order them in manageable formats and add more as you need them. Among other things, this capability allows the owner to assemble and disassemble the battery pack that meets their needs when they need it.

Industry observers note that if you’re heading out to camp for a week in your RV, you can grab an Apex 200 and one of BLUETTI’s B300K expansion batteries and bring 5.5 kWh of capacity with you on the road. When you get home from the trip, you can put them back into the garage and add that back into the battery capacity for your home.

The BLUETTI Apex 200 serves as a head unit or master controller for the battery stack, while the other battery modules are effectively servants to it. For example, when you’re setting the unit up to charge from a wall outlet or from a set of BLUETTI’s solar panels, which can wire directly into the Apex 200 with MC4 connectors, you simply plug one set of connectors or one AC charging cable into the Apex 200 and it automatically balances the energy storage across however many additional battery packs are plugged into the unit.

Industry observers note that that really simplifies the charging structure and allows you to use the battery exactly how you want to. If you want to just head to the park with two solar panels that are portable, you can do that and have a much more manageable power system, effectively bringing a mini-grid with you on the go.

In a recent development, we tested the BLUETTI Apex 200 out on a wall charger and, much like most of the other portable power stations on the market, it effectively maxes out the capacity you can actually draw from a wall outlet, which is around 1,600 watts continuous. Even with the best charging cables, you’re going to notice some heat building up in the cable, and BLUETTI has made some concessions for this. The Apex 200 has a switch that allows you to select from different charging modes:.

When it comes to solar, the BLUETTI Apex 200 can plug in to solar arrays through either an XT60 connector or the MC4 connectors that wire directly into the unit on the side. Between the MC4 connectors and the XT60 solar input, the unit can pull down 3,000 watts of solar, though you will need to make sure the voltage on your panels lines up with what each of the ports on the unit can handle. When we initially wired our two Bluetti 100-watt solar panels into the unit, we had them wired in parallel, which resulted in just 40 volts being pushed into the unit.

Stacking them in series gave us 80 volts, which pushed it over the minimum 60 volts for the MC4 connectors and allowed the BLUETTI Apex 200 to start charging from the panels. Pushing 2,000 watts maximum of solar power into a 5.5 kWh battery stack is going to take some time to get it charged up, but it’s easy to manage scaling the input power system up to an impressive 2,000 watts to really deliver some meaningful power.

The flexibility is pretty impressive, because it means you can dial the system in to exactly what you need, whether that’s bolting an array to the top of your RV or installing solar panels on the side of your house and then wiring them in a way that’s the most convenient for you.

BLUETTI also makes a larger B500K battery, so you can really pick and choose exactly the right level of storage that you need for your house and the right size battery packs that you want to be able to move around.

It has been revealed that the MC4 connectors for solar panels are a little bit troublesome on the BLUETTI Apex 200 because they require a special tool to release the locks that connect the male and female ends of MC4 connectors together. That means if you have your solar panels wired up and plugged into the unit, you’ll need an MC4 connector release tool to disconnect the solar panels from the Apex 200 before you move on. Alternately, you can wire the solar panels up through an XT60 connector, which is a simple plug-and-play adapter for lower voltage solar setups.

Recent findings suggest that when it came time to use the stored power from the BLUETTI Apex 200 and the B300K battery pack, we had to pick up some more high-draw appliances to really put them the the test. We bought a 1,500-watt electric fireplace and 1,500-watt portable heater for a total draw of around 3,000 watts by. We also grabbed an an Instant Pot from the kitchen to pull a bit more juice from the battery stack.

The BLUETTI Apex 200 handled both of the heaters running full blast without a problem. It shared a continuous power output capacity of 3,200 watts. This gets bumped to 3,600 watts when you attach a B300K extension battery. Beyond that, you can even pull a little bit more power, pulling peak usage up to 4,800 watts for a few seconds, because of its peak power handling capacity.

Keeping the larger heater unit attached, we added an Instapot to the the mix, and again the unit had no issues no matter what power levels we used. It’s a solid stack with impressive stats that actually deliver when you need them to the most.

Sources indicate that BLUETTI has really built an impressive system here with the Apex 200 and its different expansion battery options. A single BLUETTI Apex 200 can be expanded up to 33.3 kWh, and they can even go bigger than that if you need something with more storage.

Industry observers note that BLUETTI allows you to link three Apex 200 battery stacks together through their Hub 1 accessory for a total of just under 100 kWh of storage capacity. That can be accomplished by stacking three Apex 200s with a bunch of BLUETTI’s 5kWh B500Ks and then linking them all together through the Hub 1.

It’s a massive system that shows BLUETTI isn’t just building products for a quick sale, but building a much more comprehensive, flexible storage system that you can build at home into the right configuration for your needs with components that act more like LEGO building blocks.

The ability to wire in solar via XT60 connectors and MC4 connectors is exciting, giving homeowners even more options to produce power from the sun for them to run their lives on. The BLUETTI Apex 200 retails for $1,399 USD.

For more information about the BLUETTI Apex 200, the B300K, B500K expansion packs, or their solar panels, head over to their official website.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Testing at all Louisiana coal plants found unsafe groundwater contamination.
  • It has been revealed that BATON ROUGE, La.
  • Coal ash is generated when coal is burned, and massive quantities are stored at coal-burning power plants near Baton Rouge, Alexandria, and Shreveport.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Testing at all Louisiana coal plants found unsafe groundwater contamination.

It has been revealed that BATON ROUGE, La. — The Sierra Club, Earthjustice, and the Alliance for Affordable Energy Louisiana decried the Trump administration’s final decision today to put the State of Louisiana in charge of oversight of toxic coal ash waste. The Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality (LDEQ) has repeatedly allowed coal plants to violate federal coal ash protections.

Coal ash is generated when coal is burned, and massive quantities are stored at coal-burning power plants near Baton Rouge, Alexandria, and Shreveport.

At all three active Louisiana coal plants (Significant Cajun 2, Brame Energy Center, R S Nelson), and the state’s one retired plant (Dolet Hills), monitoring data demonstrates that coal ash is contaminating groundwater at levels above federal safe drinking water standards. These toxic chemicals include arsenic, boron, cobalt, lead, lithium, radium, sulfate, and thallium. More than 61% of Louisiana’s population relies on groundwater for all or part of their drinking water supply.

Recent findings suggest that “Louisianans know all too well that we can’t trust our state regulators to hold polluters accountable, so it’s nonsensical that the Trump Administration just gave LDEQ even more authority to handle something as dangerous as coal ash,” said Darryl Malek-Wiley, a Sierra Club senior field representative in Louisiana. “It’s clear this decision is meant to favor wealthy coal-owning utilities at the expense of our health.”.

“The Trump administration chose polluters over the people of Louisiana,” said Earthjustice senior attorney Mychal Ozaeta. “An alphabet soup of toxic chemicals from burning coal is contaminating groundwater in locations across the state. The right thing to do is make the polluters clean up their toxic mess, and protect sources of drinking water. Instead, the Trump administration is handing over authority to Louisiana’s state government which won’t lift a finger to clamp down on the concerning levels of contaminants poisoning the state’s groundwater.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Our state regulators are dangerously inadequate in their oversight and enforcement of polluting industries, which has already cost Louisiana our safe air and water. We simply don’t think LDEQ can handle even more responsibilities they won’t take seriously,” said Logan Burke, Executive Director of the Alliance for Affordable Energy.

Public interest groups submitted formal comments to EPA urging the administration to reject Louisiana’s request to handle coal ash oversight in the state.

Coal ash contains arsenic, mercury, chromium, lead, lithium, radium, and other heavy metals, which have been linked to numerous types of cancer, heart and thyroid disease, respiratory illness, reproductive failure, and neurological harm.

According to recent reports, as an example of the state’s abysmal track record on coal ash, LDEQ has allowed power plants to close coal ash dumps with ash in groundwater, ensuring that the dumps will contaminate groundwater with toxic chemicals indefinitely. LDEQ should not be in charge of issuing permits that let coal plants continue to violate the law. These permits will shield power plants from federal enforcement and prevent Louisiana residents from stopping coal ash pollution.

It has been revealed that LDEQ is a severely understaffed and extremely lenient environmental regulator. In addition to its coal ash failures, its air monitors are far away from Louisiana’s heaviest air-polluting facilities, and the agency has for years been criticized for approving permits for wealthy polluters, including LNG terminals and a massive Formosa plastics factory. Louisianans know all too well that LDEQ does not protect low-income communities of color, and creates a lax regulatory environment that has enabled disasters like the recent Smitty’s Supply explosion and spill.

Please see the Earthjustice Louisiana coal ash page.

HLTH 2026: Suki unveils agentic OS to automate complex healthcare workflows" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Ambient clinical intelligence platform Suki declared Monday the launch of an agentic operating system designed to connect fragmented healthcare technology.

The operating system—dubbed Suki OS—is built on three core pillars, the company claims: a partner ecosystem, unified artificial intelligence agents and a performance guarantee. It prepares to expand the capabilities beyond its Suki for Clinicians platform over time.

Suki is introducing two initial AI agent initiatives as part of its goal to reduce administrative work.

Suki Prior Authorization will streamline the process by identifying requirements and gathering supporting clinical documentation. Its Clinical Documentation Improvement (CDI) Agent will focus on identifying documentation gaps, improving accuracy and supporting downstream coding and revenue cycle workflows.

Additional agents are planned across clinical, operational and financial workflows as part of the organization’s broader strategy to develop agents that can execute complex workflows with human oversight.

Suki’s Partner Ecosystem is comprised of its Insight Partners, which integrate intelligence with Suki patient context, and Platform Partners, which let health tech companies embed Suki’s AI directly into their products.

The Suki Guarantee offers eligible customers up to a 100% refund if agreed-upon performance targets aren't met, the tech giant says.

Suki CEO and Founder Punit Soni told Fierce Healthcare that healthcare has an "execution problem" rather than an AI shortage.

Recent findings suggest that "We've spent years building technology that can understand clinical conversations, but understanding is only the beginning," Soni said. "The real opportunity is to turn that intelligence into action, connecting the systems, people and workflows that make healthcare run.".

That’s the motivation behind Suki OS, according to Soni.

"Nearly a decade ago, we pioneered ambient AI, and today, our technology is trusted by more than 450 healthcare organizations, with independently validated clinical and financial outcomes," Soni said. "We've built deep clinical intelligence, integrations across EHRs, and an expansive partner ecosystem. That foundation uniquely positions Suki to move beyond documentation and help automate the complex work that surrounds patient care.".

Industry observers note that soni mentioned that the next generation of AI tools have to "do more than save time" as health systems face mounting financial pressures and workforce constraints. "It has to deliver meaningful clinical and financial outcomes," he said.

Soni continued, "Ultimately, the measure of AI's success won't be how many agents we build. It will be how much complexity we remove from healthcare, how much time we give back to clinicians and their patients, and how much measurable financial value we create for the organizations delivering care.".

In October, the manufacturer secured $90 million in series E funding to accelerate its growth and continue expanding its AI capabilities.

The company has raised more than $250 million to date, executives say. Patient encounters supported by its tools grew more than 190% year over year in 2026, with revenue doubling in 2025 and on track for similar growth this year.

  • According to recent reports, that comparison indicated me how the GR team's gradual tweaks positively impacted the experience of driving a GR Corolla, and last week I got the chance to try out their latest creation.
  • According to recent reports, full disclosure: Toyota wanted me to sample an array of its upcoming offerings for 2027 so badly that it flew me out to Texas, put me up in a hotel for a few nights, and kept me fed so I could drive its cars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Toyota shook up the compact performance car space when it introduced the GR Corolla back in 2022, and perhaps even more remarkably, it has continuously improved the car each year since. I had the distinct pleasure of hucking the 2026 GR Corolla around Sonoma Raceway last year at the press launch, and in a rare turn of events, I actually got to compare its driving dynamics to a 2025 car as well as a 2024 model.

According to recent reports, that comparison indicated me how the GR team's gradual tweaks positively impacted the experience of driving a GR Corolla, and last week I got the chance to try out their latest creation. Toyota let me loose the limited-production 2027 GRMN Corolla around Eagles Canyon Raceway in Texas to experience what is the ultimate Corolla — for now, at least. Again, the changes are small, but the resulting improvements are immediately palpable.

According to recent reports, full disclosure: Toyota wanted me to sample an array of its upcoming offerings for 2027 so badly that it flew me out to Texas, put me up in a hotel for a few nights, and kept me fed so I could drive its cars. I only got to drive the GRMN Corolla on the track, so I cannot offer on-road impressions.

It has been revealed that the GRMN Corolla earned those last two letters while lapping arguably the most iconic race track on the planet, the Nürburgring. The MN in GRMN represents the fact that this version of the GR Corolla was tuned by the "Meisters of the Nürburgring," and that's not just marketing jargon. The GR team made suspension, aerodynamic, cooling, and drivetrain tweaks. They also swapped some metal body panels for carbon-fiber ones, all with the goal of making the GRMN Corolla the most track-focused GR Corolla yet.

Recent findings suggest that suspension-wise, Toyota changed the bump stops because it found the GR Corolla's standard suspension would hit the bump stops on certain corners of the Nürburgring, causing sudden understeer. Aerodynamically, Toyota added a larger hood duct, bumper side splitters, fender ducts from the Super Taikyu hydrogen-engine GR Corolla development car to reduce front-end lift, and that adjustable rear spoiler for increased stability. The entire hood, both front fenders, and the rear spoiler are made from carbon fiber, and the rear seat was removed in order to save weight, making the GRMN weigh 66 pounds less than a standard GR Corolla.

Moving to the drivetrain, Toyota added a supplemental AWD transfer case oil cooler that will also be available for other GR Corollas but comes as standard on the GRMN, which keeps the system cool even after repeated laps in high temperatures. There's also a standard intercooler sprayer to keep it and the turbo working hard in high temperatures, too.

Engineers retuned Track Mode in the GRMN's GR-Four all-wheel-drive system to make it more rear-biased, and they managed to increase the turbocharged 1.6-liter three-cylinder engine's torque output by 7 pound-feet while also making maximum torque available at lower engine speeds, so it now produces 300 horsepower and 302 lb-ft. The changes are definitely palpable on the track, with my favorite upgrades being the GRMN's sticky Pilot Sport Cup 2 tires, the retuned steering rack with increased feedback, and the close-ratio transmission from the Morizo Edition, all of which heightened the GRMN Corolla's dynamics.

It has been revealed that toyota so graciously let the media go hog wild on Eagles Canyon Raceway before, which I had never seen or driven before, and luckily I was in the perfect car to attempt to learn the 2.7-mile "Italian Canyon" course's 15 corners, 20 apexes, and 150 feet of elevation change. We weren't allowed to do any consecutive laps — we had to enter the pits on each lap — but we were allowed to do as many laps as we pleased. I drove both the GRMN Corolla and a 2026 GR Corolla to see if I could tell the difference, and the answer was a resounding "hell yeah!".

Industry observers note that taking off from the pits, the GRMN Corolla's inputs immediately felt more taut and communicative, from the snickety shifter to the talkative steering. Once I left pit lane and got to wring out the powertrain, the GRMN's extra mid-range torque and lighter weight made it feel like it had noticeably more shove than the standard GR. Cornering is where the GRMN really shined, though.

When I first entered a corner, the GRMN's reworked steering felt sharper and more direct, and the more rear-biased all-wheel-drive tune in Track Mode made its nose feel like it could change direction like a greyhound weaving through the slalom at the AKC National Agility Championship. Compared to the GR, the GRMN felt markedly more agile and more eager to rotate rather than understeer.

According to recent reports, the GRMN's retuned engine pulled its lighter weight out of corners stronger than the GR, and its Cup 2 tires made it cling to the road with what felt like merciless ferocity. Naturally, since this was my first time on this track I made my fair share of corner misjudgments, but even when I overcooked a decreasing radius turn, a dab of brakes made the GRMN dive toward the apex, expertly turning "oh crap" moments into drama-free learning experiences. Chief Engineer for the GR Corolla Naoyuki Sakamoto called the GRMN, "a car you can confidently push the limits in," and Sakamoto-san was absolutely correct.

The GRMN Corolla is an extremely limited-production vehicle, with just 730 units planned globally, so the U.S. market will get even fewer than that. Exclusivity paired with the GRMN Corolla's other driving experience enhancements and proven track-oriented capabilities make it a rare special edition that truly feels special. That said, it's set to cost $65,665, so it had better be pretty damn special to make you pay $65k for a freakin' Corolla.

According to recent reports, the interior is all Corolla, but at least it has more aggressive bucket seats and a flocked instrument panel and A-pillars. You also forgo the opportunity to bring more than one passenger along for the ride, since the GRMN has what looks like a lap bar from a roller coaster rather than a back seat. Perhaps the biggest glitch I had with the GRMN Corolla was that its rear windows do not roll down. The driver's window control panel has just two switches, one for the driver's side front door and one for the passenger side window, which I can imagine will cause horrendous wind buffeting for anyone who enjoys driving with the windows down.

In case you couldn't tell, I was totally taken by the GRMN Corolla. I already loved driving the GR Corolla, but the GRMN Corolla's sharpened inputs, hardcore style, and delightful driving dynamics take that love even further. I truly hope this was not the last time I can drive one.

Driving The Scion By Toyota KEI-01 Will Make You Giggle And Jiggle In Places You Didn't Know Could Jiggle

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I was just as shocked as you all were last week when Toyota confirmed the launch of the Scion by Toyota brand in the United States with a right-hand-drive kei truck.
  • I was baffled by Toyota's choice to bring such a niche product in the United States, its choice to do so under the name "Scion by Toyota," and by its choice to make it available to fleets only.
  • Full disclosure: Toyota wanted me to sample a smattering of its new and updated models, so it flew me out to scenic Frisco, Texas, kept me fed and housed in a hotel for a few days.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I was just as shocked as you all were last week when Toyota confirmed the launch of the Scion by Toyota brand in the United States with a right-hand-drive kei truck. The KEI-01 is limited to 25 mph in order to conform to low-speed vehicle (LSV) regulations, and as of now it's exclusively limited to fleet buyers. Though final details about the dinky little hauler remain slim, I did get a briefer-than-brief chance to whip around a prototype KEI-01 while attending the press event in Texas at which the truck was revealed, and the experience left me exceedingly tickled and slightly baffled.

I was baffled by Toyota's choice to bring such a niche product in the United States, its choice to do so under the name "Scion by Toyota," and by its choice to make it available to fleets only. I was tickled by the opportunity to contort my comically long limbs in order to squeeze my 6-foot-8-inch tall body behind its wheel and take it for a spin. The result? A truly unique automotive experience that is all but guaranteed to make you giggle.

Full disclosure: Toyota wanted me to sample a smattering of its new and updated models, so it flew me out to scenic Frisco, Texas, kept me fed and housed in a hotel for a few days. I got to witness the announcement of the Scion by Toyota brand there, and drive the KEI-01 a few hundred feet.

Recent findings suggest that the KEI-01 is not a brand upcoming vehicle — in fact, it's based on the Toyota Pixis Truck, which is a rebadged 10th-generation Daihatsu HiJet Truck that itself was introduced 12 years ago now. We are only getting the "extended cab" version of the kei truck, generously called the Jumbo on the Daihatsu HiJet, which adds a taller roof and about an iPhone's length of room behind the two seats for storage — I used that space to store my shoes, since I couldn't fit behind the wheel while wearing them.

According to recent reports, in its U.S. specification, the dinky KEI-01 will only be offered with a mid-mounted 660cc three-cylinder engine that sends its power to all four wheels via a CVT automatic transmission. Toyota didn't make power figures public, but it's almost certainly the same 660cc three-cylinder used in the other kei trucks that share the platform, which produces about 50 horsepower and 47 lb-ft of torque. The standard four-wheel-drive system features a lock mode that should make this little pickup rather capable on unpaved roads, but that's only if your spine is up to the task.

They will all come standard with a weird mix of modern and throwback features, like dual front airbags, automatic emergency braking, push-button start, traction control, parking sensors, and an engine start/stop system. The standard climate controls are operated using horizontal levers like the ones in my grandfather's 1991 F-150, and the overall appearance of the interior looks like it belongs in a car that's being shown at Radwood, minus the substantial tacked-on infotainment screen. I didn't get to experience any of these technology features on my abridged drive, except the start/stop system that I instantly turned off because it cut the AC and was unsurprisingly annoying.

This was my first time driving a kei car, and I solely got to drive the KEI-01 on a short gravel loop, but the instant I started moving I was aware that it was not a refined vehicle. The suspension that gives it a 600-pound payload capacity also felt like it faultlessly transmitted even the smallest surface detail of every single piece of gravel I drove over directly to my butt. It jiggled parts of me that I didn't know could jiggle, and sounded very crashy going through dips and bumps. I wouldn't want to ride in one if I had a bad back. Though Toyota didn't release a spec sheet for the KEI-01, the Daihatsu Hijet has a truly puny wheelbase of 74.8 inches and laughably small tires, so no one should expect it to ride like a limousine.

As for its powertrain, the three-cylinder engine and CVT combination were more than enough to get the KEI-01 to its top speed of 25 mph, but the truck I drove did not have the limiter yet, so I saw as high as 40 mph. The CVT created a typical momentary lag between throttle pedal inputs and actual engine response, but discussing powertrain responsiveness in a kei truck that'll be limited to 25 mph is about as useful as discussing a newly introduced hyperpop album with an octogenarian.

In a recent development, if you didn't catch it upon first mention, I'm 6-foot-8, so I drew a bit of a crowd when I first tried inserting myself into the KEI-01. I'm all legs with a 40-inch inseam, and my first entry attempt was foiled by the immovable steering wheel. Once I took my shoes off and swung my left knee under the wheel first, I was able to finagle myself into a comfortable driving position, with about an inch left between my right knee and the hard plastic cupholder.

Headroom in the KEI-01 was downright impressive, though. Using the automotive industry's standardized headroom measurement, I had room to put one, maybe even two magician's hats on top of my head and still fit comfortably in the KEI-01. The cargo bed strangely protrudes a bit into the cab space, so the floor of the extended cab's rear storage area sits at about the same spot where the rear side window ends. It's a diminutive and awkwardly shaped and accessed space, but it allows for a bit of seat recline and is better than nothing.

Annoyingly, Toyota hasn't released pricing for the KEI-01 as of yet, but as we already know it will be limited to fleet buyers initially anyway, so it's not like anyone can go to a Toyota dealer and buy one off the lot. Car and Driver estimates that the KEI-01 will cost around $28,000, though, which would be a really tough sell. I love that American fleet buyers are getting access to a brand fresh genuine kei truck — especially one that's built in the U.S. — but I am left to grapple with the point of it, especially considering that anyone can go out and find a derestricted imported kei truck for a rather low price.

The so-cute-it-hurts Fiat Topolino is another recently unveiled U.S.-bound LSV, and I think it makes more sense than the KEI-01 since it will mainly be a cheeky electric neighborhood runabout for rich people. Its only competition are golf carts, where the KEI-01 will compete with a sea of UTVs that have served U.S. campuses, ranches, and other all-terrain hauling needs for ages. Who knows, maybe the fleet market will fall in love with the KEI-01, jiggles and all.

Despite Americans’ Disapproval, Data Centers Rush to Build Climate-Threatening Projects.

In a recent development, washington, D.C. — Sierra Club has released a newly introduced report that shows that without swift, critical guardrails, artificial intelligence data centers in the United States could undo 15 years of climate progress.

In a recent development, the power demand brought on by data centers combined with utility companies’ rush to fossil fuels has severe and threatening climate impacts. The Artificial Intelligence, Real Pollution report indicates that between data centers connected to the electrical grid and those that are building their own on-site power supply, these projects could add 680 million tons of greenhouse gas emissions into the atmosphere.

It has been revealed that sierra Club’s Dirty Truth Report, released in September 2026, reflected the alarming rate at which utility companies are building new methane gas power plants to power artificial intelligence data centers. Today’s report shows that additionally, data center projects are building massive amounts of on-site power sources that are subject to more lenient guardrails and reporting standards.

It has been revealed that this report comes on the heels of the 2026 midterm elections, in which voters across the country overwhelmingly supported candidates who promised more guardrails and accountability on data center projects. Voters also passed nearly every ballot measure that would slow the breakneck speed at which data centers are developing. Artificial Intelligence, Real Pollution does not just outline the real climate risk that the industry’s current growth trajectory poses, it shares substantive and impactful strategies that states can implement right now to prevent harmful emissions from gas plants while protecting ratepayers from rising costs caused by data center demand.

In response, Sierra Club Chief Program Officer Holly Bender issued the following response:.

“For twenty years, the Sierra Club has led the environmental movement’s most successful campaign—the Beyond Coal Campaign—with a clear-eyed vision that a clean power grid is the backbone of any climate strategy. Millions of people have contributed to this work, advocating for clean air, clean water, and investments in clean energy across the country. We face an unprecedented risk to our hard-won progress, as the picture of the climate impact of artificial intelligence data centers and their power demand becomes clear. We now know that as currently planned, this industry could put all of our progress at risk.

Industry observers note that “Artificial Intelligence, Real Pollution highlights the staggering amount of greenhouse gases that would be emitted into our air if we allow data centers and utility companies to continue their rush to fossil fuels. More pollution will worsen the extreme weather families are facing, cause illnesses, and drive up the cost of healthcare and disaster recovery. Just two weeks ago, Americans unequivocally demanded more accountability, more transparency, and more guardrails on AI data centers. With this report, the Sierra Club has not only clarified what’s at stake, but shared a menu of strategies that can be implemented right now to protect consumers, communities, and the climate.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that according to the ad, the first owner of today's Nice Price or No Dice Europa owned the car for more than 51 years. That's some dedication, and the car reveals the love they obviously had for it. We'll have to decide if we love the price the current owner has set for its sale.

In a recent development, at some point in one's life, it's best to take the road less traveled. The well-beaten path may be the safest, but the less popular way might just offer unexpected, memorable adventures. The 2004 Nissan 350Z we looked at on Monday is probably not everyone's first choice when it comes to used sports cars with a semblance of panache. The easy answer is Porsche's Boxster or a Mazda Miata, but that's part of what makes the 350Z such a rogue option.

Capable and seemingly in as-newly introduced condition, our 350Z came with a six-speed stick, a top that drops, and a $12,500 asking price. That's plumb right in the middle of 986 Boxster territory, but offering more power and potentially cheaper running costs. That concept didn't escape you all. Comments on the car ranged from "not for me, but a good deal for someone," to "if it were closer to me..." In the end, the vote went the Nissan seller's way, too, earning the Z a solid 76% 'Nice Price' win.

Nissan has never offered a mid-engine car for sale here in the States. In fact, of the major Japanese manufacturers, only Toyota and Honda (through Acura) have gone the (rear) mid-engine route here.

Recent findings suggest that in the early 1960s, mid-engine layouts were all the rage in racing, with F1, Indy, and GT classes moving to place the driver ahead of the drivetrain. Britain's Lotus was at the forefront of this movement, debuting the mid-engine Type 18 Formula 1 racer in 1960. That car brought Lotus its first F1 checkered flag and World Champion title.

It has been revealed that lotus also dallied with mid-engine GT racers, designing a chassis and body that the company hoped would be bought by the Ford Motor Company (Lotus had a close relationship with Ford at the time) for the Americans' assault on Le Mans. Ford chose the already race-tested Lola Mk 6 chassis for its GT40 racing program, leaving Lotus with significant engineering expense and little to show for it. Instead of initially building a race car from the proposed chassis, Lotus took the more lucrative route and built a road car: Hethel's first mid-engined model.

The resulting Europa leveraged a design first used on the Elan: a stiff, folded and welded center backbone with the drivetrain and suspension bolted in place, and a fiberglass body mounted atop that in saddlebag fashion. The earliest cars had Renault engines and transmissions, while later cars, like this 1973 Europa Special, used the Ford Kent-based Lotus Twin Cam engine.

Not only does this Europa have the most powerful engine offered in Federalized form, but that 115-horsepower 1,557cc four-cylinder is backed by a standard five-speed manual, still sourced from Renault, originally designed for the French company's 16 model.

Sources indicate that this isn't just a "Significant Valve" (denoting a reworked twin-cam head) Europa; it's also one of 100 John Player Specials built to commemorate Lotus's 1972 F1 Championship win. The cars were wrapped in black paint with gold trim, emulating the cigarette pack design of the racer's sponsor, Nottingham, England's John Player & Sons. It's an iconic bit of 1970s chic, and very British. This car still wears its commemorative dashboard plaque, indicating it's number 90 of the 100 cars built.

According to recent reports, while the basic Europa design is a bit odd with its bread van back end, this one appears to be in exceptional condition. Also, being a later edition (dubbed Type 47 by Lotus), it has a reworked engine cover and rear end providing better visibility out the back and slightly improved proportions.

Not only does this Europa appear to be in near-show car condition, but it comes with extensive documentation from the moment it was built (March 1973) to the present day. That paperwork details title transfers between all three owners (the second owner held on to the car for more than half a century), along with all the work that has gone into keeping it on the road and winning awards at car shows. As far as turnkey classics go, there's not much to complain about with this Lotus.

On the exterior, the black-and-gold color scheme still looks as elegant as ever, right down to the original gold anodized alloy wheels. All the badging, lights, and chrome are present and in excellent shape, which is a plus since parts are getting increasingly hard to find. The interior is just as nice, showing just some scuffing on the driver's seat side as evidence of the car's age.

According to the ad, the engine underwent an extensive rebuild and documentation just 2,000 miles ago, and now runs well when warm. Both the engine and gearbox are numbers-matching for the car. How cool is that after all these years?

Recent findings suggest that the ad notes a clean title and mileage documented at 34,526. It also touts the car as a "once in a lifetime chance to own a fully documented Lotus." It should be noted that, while advertised in the Los Angeles Craigslist classifieds, the car is actually located a few hundred miles away on the California/Oregon border.

Some classic cars come with a story. Some come with a past veiled in mystery. This Europa comes with a dossier that would make a CIA agent proud. Not only that, but it's a prime example of a significant model in its final, some might argue, most desired form. What might something like that be worth?

According to recent reports, the seller has set a price of $27,000, and since the ad for the car has been posted for almost a month, we now need to give that asking price some thought. What's your take on this original mid-engined marvel out of Hethel and the seller's cash-and-carry price? Is it really worth $27,000? Or is a fairer price yet to be documented in the car's records?

Los Angeles, California, Craigslist, or go here if the ad disappears.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Measles update: US loses measles elimination status; more deaths reported" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The United States has lost its measles elimination status, and has now exceeded 5,400 cases and 10 total measles-associated deaths in 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the status determination from the Pan American Health Organization, which is part of the World Health Organization, was made late last week and first reported by the Wall Street Journal before being confirmed by other outlets. (Editor's note: The public health body made its official announcement on Nov. 17).

The U.S. had notched elimination status, reflecting no continuous spread of the disease for at least 12 months, in 2000. Regaining it similarly requires the country to stop continuous spread for 12 months. PAHO recommends countries that have lost elimination status submit and enact a corrective action plan that includes immunization and surveillance.

The decision landed shortly after the country hit 5,412 confirmed measles cases, per a Nov. 13 upgrade from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The federal public health body also lists 591 hospitalizations (11% rate) and six deaths—though it has been hesitant to outright confirm states' reports of measles-associated deaths, of which there have now been 10.

Health groups and public health professionals have pointed to lagging vaccination rates and checked endorsement of routine childhood vaccines from current leadership at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, namely Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., as fueling the country's outbreaks.

The Wisconsin Department of Health Services on Thursday reported its first measles-outbreak associated death since 1990.

The deceased was an infant whose case was among many in the southwestern part of the state, for whom the coroner listed measles as immediate cause of death. As of Nov. 3, the department has reported 431 cases across 13 counties in 2026, the highest number of cases in over 35 years. All but three of those are among individuals who were not vaccinated, and nine have involved hospitalizations.

"Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease," Kirsten Johnson, secretary of the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, said in the announcement. "Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is key for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family.".

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone stated they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a upcoming standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles.".

The New York State Department of Health on Monday afternoon reported its first measles-associated death in 30 years.

Sources indicate that the state has counted 210 total cases this year as of Nov. 3. The reported death was a child in the northern Lewis County, according to the department. No information was given about the child's specific illness or the role measles infection may have played in their death.

Sixteen confirmed cases of measles have been reported in Lewis County as of Tuesday, the department said. Many of Newly introduced York's cases are located among upstate counties, and just eight are in New York City, according to the department.

Sources indicate that in a statement, Newly introduced York Governor Kathy Hochul—who on Oct. 5 declared a Disaster Emergency in response to rising measles case rates—expressed her sympathies to the child's family and told residents that "vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease.".

"This is Latest York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses," the statement reads, echoing criticisms of federal health leadership voiced by Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro regarding measles-associated deaths in his own state.

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone stated they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a latest standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles.".

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services told Fierce Healthcare that it had deployed epidemiologists and other experts to Latest York after receiving a formal request for support. The support is currently scheduled to run through Nov. 13, and includes on-the-ground "surveillance, data analysis, strategic planning and other outbreak response support," they remarked.

Of the roughly $100 million in additional measles and vaccine-preventable diseases funding the department has provided via the CDC since August, nearly $2.4 million has gone directly to Upcoming York State and $2.1 million to New York City, they noted.

"Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles," they added.

It has been revealed that the U.S. is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 4,000 cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of early October and a sixth measles-associated death disclosed by local Pennsylvania officials on Monday.

In a recent development, the vaccine-preventable disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. back in 2000—meaning that there was no endemic spread of the disease—but has resurfaced in force during recent years as declining childhood vaccination rates have pushed most states below the 95% coverage bar for school-age herd immunity.

The CDC had counted 2,289 cases across the entirety of 2025, which had been the country’s highest total since 1990, and several public health officials have warned for months that number would likely be surpassed based on the scale and frequency of early-year cases.

Measles-associated deaths have also accompanied the higher case counts, though just how many is a subject of dispute. While three deaths were confirmed in all of 2025, this year logged its first in late August with Pennsylvania, which hosts more than a quarter of the total cases, now reporting six measles-associated deaths as of Oct. 13. The CDC, however, lists two deaths alongside a note that its count is subject to change, and has promised more broadly to develop a new, standardized case definition to be used across all reporting states.

That discrepancy is an example of friction between federal health leadership and the broader public health community that experts say has contributed to this year’s outbreaks.

Pennsylvania’s initial death announcements in August were contested by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who accused Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro of withholding sufficient information for the CDC to confirm the deaths and using his press conference announcing them as “gaslighting the public” for political purposes.

During an ensuing social media feud, the governor and the secretary described a heated phone call in which Shapiro (at the time) rejected federal assistance and accused Kennedy of fueling the outbreaks with only lukewarm endorsement of the MMR vaccine and a broader concurrent campaign to scale back other routine childhood vaccinations.

Numerous state public health officials and experts have lobbed similar criticisms of Kennedy, who is affiliated with anti-vaccine groups, and federal health agencies under his purview.

In a recent development, the CDC, for its part, has reportedly infused at least $100 million of extra public health funding to states for immunization programs and surveillance, and leading officials including Kennedy and newly introduced CDC Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., have described the MMR vaccine as safe and effective when asked directly. Still, the agency has not launched the type of broader vaccine messaging and awareness campaigns that it would have in years past, critics are quick to note.

Pennsylvania isn’t alone in raising alarms over rising measles cases. Newly introduced York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in early October, the first such declaration in recent years.

Industry News: Idle, then spiking: Why AI agents are breaking Kubernetes resource planning

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (866 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI agents are changing the economics of cloud infrastructure, and autonomous orchestration is becoming the way platform teams keep up.
  • Container orchestration for AI is fast becoming the backbone of production AI, and agents are adding a new layer of strain.
  • “Agents and all the agent workloads pretty much made everything way more complex when managing infrastructure,” Shafrir mentioned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 15:35 EST / NOVEMBER 17 2026.

AI agents are changing the economics of cloud infrastructure, and autonomous orchestration is becoming the way platform teams keep up. Agentic workloads sit idle and then spike without warning. That pattern leaves static resource settings either wasteful or likely to fail.

Container orchestration for AI is fast becoming the backbone of production AI, and agents are adding a new layer of strain. Compute costs are climbing and reliability problems are harder to contain because everything an agent does ultimately runs on CPU and memory, according to Yodar Shafrir (pictured), founder and chief executive officer of ScaleOps Inc.

“Agents and all the agent workloads pretty much made everything way more complex when managing infrastructure,” Shafrir mentioned. “Eventually, all the complexity that existed before just got much worse. Today, the compute cost has grown dramatically. Everything that agents execute eventually runs on compute.”.

Sources indicate that shafrir spoke with theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how autonomous orchestration lets ScaleOps adjust resources in real time as AI agents spike, cutting both costs and crashes. (* Disclosure below.).

Agents behave differently from traditional microservices. An agent waits for a human or another agent, checks with a large language model and then runs its task in a burst. Teams must provision for the highest spike while the agent holds its memory the whole time, Shafrir explained. When resources fall short, a crashed step has to rerun and burns tokens all over again.

“We actually see that agents crash due to not having enough resources 80% more often compared with traditional microservices,” Shafrir said. “The reliability is much harder to manage.”.

For ScaleOps, the answer is to make resource decisions in real time. It adjusts allocations, replicas and node placement for every application, agent and Model Context Protocol server, which the company states cuts cloud costs by 70% to 80%. Customers such as Adobe Inc. and Salesforce Inc. build trust by first running the platform in read-only mode on their hardest environments, according to Shafrir.

“We understand for every application: What is it connected to? What does it communicate with? What is the business state of every application?” Shafrir mentioned. “We learn from historical patterns.”.

Sources indicate that scaleOps has also added a capability that lets other workloads use an agent’s resources while it sits idle. It also uses memory swap so an agent gets memory only when it needs it. The firm claims this makes running agents 90% more cost-efficient without moving off Kubernetes. Given the cost of always-on agents, Shafrir sees autonomous orchestration as the only workable model.

“We are now in a phase where humans and all the traditional scaling capabilities that existed in the past are pretty much irrelevant for today’s world because they’re too static and they require a human to go and configure them,” Shafrir remarked. “When things are so dynamic, it no longer works the same way.”.

When Less Is More: Rewilding as a Strategy for Nature Recovery

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1397 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Can we bring nature back from the brink of collapse?
  • In fact, with vertebrate extinction rates up to 100 times the natural background rate, some scientists believe we are at the onset of a sixth mass extinction.[4] But perhaps we should not be surprised at this precipitous decline in the health of our living planet.
  • The drivers of nature loss are many, including climate change, overexploitation of resources, pollution and invasive alien species, but the largest is land-use change, primarily for agriculture.[6] Research by UNEP and Chatham House goes so far as to identify agriculture as a threat to 86% of species at risk of extinction.[7] So, is regenerative agriculture the answer?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Can we bring nature back from the brink of collapse? That may sound melodramatic, but the evidence is sobering: the Planetary Health Check 2026 demonstrates that we have crossed 7 of the 9 science-based planetary boundaries;[1] the Living Planet Report 2026 finds that wildlife populations have declined 73% on average since 1970;[2] and around 1 million animal and plant species are threatened with extinction, with 75% of the land surface having been significantly altered by human activity, according to the IPBES, the leading intergovernmental body for assessing the state of biodiversity.[3].

In fact, with vertebrate extinction rates up to 100 times the natural background rate, some scientists believe we are at the onset of a sixth mass extinction.[4] But perhaps we should not be surprised at this precipitous decline in the health of our living planet. After all, around $7.3 trillion is spent every year on activities that harm nature ($4.9 trillion by companies and $2.4 trillion in government subsidies), while only $220 billion goes towards protecting or restoring ecosystems (2023 figures).[5] In other words, for every $1 we spend on taking care of nature, $33 is spent on activities that degrade the environment.

The drivers of nature loss are many, including climate change, overexploitation of resources, pollution and invasive alien species, but the largest is land-use change, primarily for agriculture.[6] Research by UNEP and Chatham House goes so far as to identify agriculture as a threat to 86% of species at risk of extinction.[7] So, is regenerative agriculture the answer? That is certainly one approach that would help, as I explored in a previous CleanTechnica article. But there is another, more direct—and some would say more radical—solution that is gaining popularity: rewilding.

As with regenerative agriculture, rewilding is more a collection of ideas and practices than a well-defined science. Nevertheless, experts convened by the IUCN define rewilding as the process of rebuilding a natural ecosystem, following major human disturbance, by restoring natural processes and food webs.[8] The Global Rewilding Alliance puts it even more simply, as “helping nature heal”.[9] In practice, this can mean anything from leaving areas of nature undisturbed to actively introducing keystone species such as beavers, bison and wild boar.

Perhaps the most cited rewilding experiment is the reintroduction of wolves into Yellowstone National Park in 1995–96, after they had been eradicated there by 1926. This resulted in a so-called trophic cascade, whereby elk numbers fell, scavengers such as eagles, ravens and bears gained a year-round food supply, and willow and aspen began to recover in places.[10] The strength of that recovery, and the extent to which the wolves were the primary driver, has been contested,[11] but few dispute the overall positive effect on biodiversity and the ecosystem.

The Yellowstone case is rewilding on a large scale, but it is still dwarfed by the rewilding work of Tompkins Conservation, created by the late Doug Tompkins, co-founder of The North Face and Esprit, and his wife Kristine McDivitt Tompkins, former CEO of Patagonia. Working primarily in Chile and Argentina, they have helped create or expand 16 parks protecting over 45 million acres of land and sea, and reintroduced 14 species, including around 50 wild jaguars.[12] Besides the ecological benefits, ecotourism is boosting local economies.[13] In Chilean Patagonia, every dollar the state invested in the national parks along Chile’s Route of Parks in 2024 returned US$6 to local communities,[14] while visitors to Argentina’s Iberá Park, partly degraded by cattle ranching in the past, have doubled in a decade to 60,000 a year.[15].

According to recent reports, at a more local scale, the Knepp Estate in the UK has become another well documented case of rewilding. In her book Wilding: The Return of Nature to a British Farm, Isabella Tree tells the story of how she and her husband, Charlie Burrell, converted their 1,400-hectare farm from intensive dairy and crop agriculture, which was losing money, into a thriving “wild farm,” with free-roaming herbivores such as cattle, ponies, pigs, and deer.[16] A 20-year review reveals an incredible rejuvenation of biodiversity, including a 916% increase in breeding bird abundance in the southern block, a 132% rise in bird species richness, a near-ninefold increase in dragonflies and damselflies, and a doubling of butterfly species in some areas.[17] There are climate benefits too, with 5.2 tCO2e/ha/yr sequestration, comparable to new native woodland.[18].

Industry observers note that critics of rewilding often frame it as a trade-off: more nature means less food; more wildlife means fewer jobs; more biodiversity means lower economic growth. These arguments can (and should) be tested, for in many (but not all) cases they will prove to be a false choice. My view is that it should be about balance. I saw this pragmatic approach at a rewilding site in Norfolk, England, called Wild Ken Hill, where they have designated separate areas for regenerative farming, coastal conservation, and rewilding—including 30 or so wild Exmoor ponies, 6 very inquisitive and vocal Tamworth pigs, and a small herd of Red Poll cattle.

It has been revealed that my conclusion on rewilding is that it can certainly help us to reach the global goal of reversing biodiversity loss and becoming nature positive. It is by no means the only strategy, but it is one of the most direct and impactful. As I noted in the chapter on nature restoration in my book Thriving: “We know that nature is on the ropes, bruised and battered by dumb agriculture and dumber economics. But another thing we know is that, given half a chance, nature bounces back. Ecosystems are resilient and designed to flourish. The most powerful and effective action we can take is to step back and give nature space and time to recover.”[19].
