📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Most nonprofit hospitals' tax breaks outpaced their community spending in 2023: Lown Institute" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Just over half of the country’s nonprofit hospitals have charity care and community benefit investments that fall short of their tax savings, according to the latest of the Lown Institute’s analyses on more than 3,000 hospitals’ tax filings.

Recent findings suggest that in 2023, the most recent year in which Internal Revenue Service Form 990s were available for review, the think tank identified $38.8 billion of industry-wide tax exemptions, or $12.8 million per hospital and 3.8% of total expenses on average. About $37.1 billion was collectively spent by the same hospitals on various community benefits, as reported in the IRS forms matched to other filings such as Medicare cost reports.

While the total exemption handily outpaces the benefits investments by Lown’s measure, the group underscored that these "fair share” deficits or surpluses also vary widely between facilities, and that some of the industry’s biggest names are on the wrong side of the divide.

Here, Mayo Clinic Hospital led the pack with a $366 million deficit, according to Lown’s analysis, followed by Tisch Hospital (-$294 million deficit), Stanford Hospital (-$255 million deficit), New York-Presbyterian Hospital (-$248 million deficit) and Massachusetts General Hospital (-$219 million deficit).

"Some of America's wealthiest hospitals fall hundreds of millions short of giving back what they receive from their communities, leaving those with fewer resources to pick up the slack," Vikas Saini, M.D., president of the Lown Institute, mentioned in a release on the fresh analysis, released Tuesday.

Among those leading the latter group were North Shore University Hospital ($167 fair share surplus), Rochester General Hospital ($146 million surplus) and Englewood Hospital ($142 million surplus). Lown’s analysis includes a searchable hospital-by-hospital breakdown of the tax exemptions and community investment totals.

When splitting the 52% of deficit hospitals apart from the surplus hospitals, the former group logged about $15.5 billion above their reported community benefits—a deficit Lown remarked could wipe the medical debt of 12 million Americans. Fair share surplus hospitals outpaced their exemptions by $13.8 billion.

Total tax exemptions were also “very unevenly distributed” among the hospitals, Lown said. The 30 hospitals, or about 1% of all hospitals, with the largest tax exemptions collectively avoided $6.8 billion, or about 18% of total exemptions. The 607 hospitals, or about 20%, accounted for three-quarters of the country’s hospital tax exemptions.

Sources indicate that lown’s measure of nonprofit hospitals’ tax breaks includes exemptions from federal and state corporate income taxes, state and local sales taxes, property taxes, tax-exempt bonds, tax-exempt charitable donations and federal unemployment tax exemptions. Not included are other benefits provided to many nonprofits, like Medicaid disproportionate share payments, 340B discounts or profits from indirect tax arbitrage.

Its tally of community benefit includes spending on patient financial assistance, subsidized care, payments to other nonprofits to improve health or various community health or social determinants of health investments.

Of note, it excludes Medicaid shortfall—the difference between hospitals’ costs and revenues when treating Medicaid patients—and spending on professional education and research. The hospital industry typically points to these billions of dollars of exclusions when discussing their tax breaks, with Medicaid shortfall alone accounting for nearly half of their preferred community benefit spending totals. Lown noted in its methodology that these accounting losses are often offset by other discounts and supplemental benefits and don’t always have a direct impact on community health, among other objections.

It has been revealed that lown said the disparities between hospitals and the outsized benefits being delivered by some are a call to amend, not eliminate, nonprofit status exemptions. The think tank accompanied its analysis with calls to increase reporting transparency and set spending targets for hospitals tied to variables such as size, exemption value, financial health and prior spending.

“Tax exemptions aren't a gift—they're an expectation, and regulators need to make sure all hospitals hold up their end of the bargain," Saini said.

In a recent development, lown acknowledged the impending financial pressure hospitals will face with upcoming H.R. 1 policy changes and mentioned such changes should be accompanied by “short-term” financial protections.

In a recent development, still, the group isn’t alone in drawing scrutiny to the tax breaks. Lawmakers and policy advisors have pointed to, and questioned the justification for, nonprofits’ exemptions when questioning health system leaders on collections policies or high prices.

Academics and researchers have also called for greater transparency or other overhauls of how community benefits are reported or calculated. Of note, a research article published earlier this month in Health Affairs reviewing hospital filings between 2013 and 2022 outlined a disconnect between different hospitals’ listed charity care eligibility thresholds and their relative spending, which more closely aligned with community need than their stated policy.

It seems like only a few months ago that we told you BMW is working on an electric i4 convertible (and a new 4 Series coupe, too) to sit alongside the already revealed i3 in the lineup, and that's because it was only a few months ago. Now, just hours after the first prototype reviews of the electric M3 have been published, our spies in Germany have caught the i4 droptop testing in high-performance M4 guise. Its quad motors and 800-plus horsepower will be perfect for silently messing up the broccoli haircuts of the M4 convertible's typical owners and the three friends they bring along for the ride.

Sources indicate that we have yet to see the regular i4 convertible make its debut, but since the four-door M3 is almost here and this M4 prototype looks fairly close to production-ready, once the standard model is revealed we shouldn't have to wait too long for the M4 to be shown off. We know the electric M3 will be sold alongside an M3 with a gas inline-6, and the same should be true for the M4, though as of now internal-combustion prototypes haven't been spied.

This prototype is still covered in camouflage, and it doesn't seem like the M4 bumpers has been fitted because it's missing things like the M's square LEDs in the corners, but there are a few tells we're looking at an M4. There are wider flares tacked onto the front fenders, and the rear fenders seem wider than the ones on previously spied i4 prototypes. The wheels look massively wide, and this car is fitted with pretty big drilled brake discs with blue calipers. It has camo paneling on the hood, which is probably to obscure the vent we've seen on the M3.

Like its four-door counterpart, the electric M4 convertible should get a quad-motor powertrain with well over 800 horsepower that will make it drive and feel like a proper M car. There will be fun noises that you can turn off if you're boring, simulated gear shifts and other performance technology features, alongside actual mechanical changes like upgraded suspension and better steering. We don't yet know how much of a range hit you'll take when going for an M4 instead of an i4, but given how fast the Neue Klasse cars charge, long road trips should be no problem.

We don't have concrete details on when the i4 will be revealed or go on sale, not to mention the timeline for the M versions, but it seems like a sure bet that the standard model will be shown at some point in 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that WASHINGTON, D.C.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FY 2027 Transportation Proposal Puts EV Charging Investments at Risk.

Sources indicate that WASHINGTON, D.C. — On Monday, Senate Republicans released an Appropriations package that proposes to take back nearly $2 billion in federal funding already allocated to states to build out electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and repurpose it for general transportation uses, putting critical clean transportation investments at risk.

Industry observers note that republicans already clawed back roughly $500 million from the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) Formula Program in the FY 2026 appropriations bill. Now, they are proposing to further divert these funds, even as all 50 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico have approved prepares for their use and are working to deliver critical charging infrastructure to their communities. More than half of available NEVI funding has already been committed to projects, and the proposal threatens to upend additional awards that states continue to make to charging developers.

For example, Texas recently made an announcement of $226 million in awards that will support 321 stations. The Senate proposal would threaten Texas’s remaining NEVI funding, along with funding for states like Ohio, which has one of the largest numbers of operational NEVI-funded stations in the country.

In response, Clean Transportation for All Director Katherine García released the following statement:.

Recent findings suggest that “It is unacceptable for Senate Republicans to once again seek to claw back critical EV charging investments. Trump’s day-one freeze of NEVI set states back, and they are only now back on track after we successfully challenged that freeze in court. This latest proposal threatens affordable transportation for American families, clean air for communities, and states’ efforts to build the infrastructure of the future. We have successfully defended NEVI against the Trump administration’s attacks, and we will continue fighting to protect the program and ensure these investments reach communities across the country.”.

The NEVI program, established through the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law in 2021, provides funding to states to build a nationwide network of EV fast-charging stations. Protecting that investment is essential to expanding charging access, supporting EV adoption, reducing dependence on volatile gasoline prices, and cutting transportation pollution.

Since the Trump administration’s unlawful freeze of the NEVI program was lifted following successful litigation by Sierra Club, its partners, and a coalition of states, hundreds of millions of dollars in NEVI funding have been committed to charging projects.

Congress must preserve funding for EV charging infrastructure while providing dedicated resources for passenger rail, public transit, and other clean transportation priorities.

#30094. Are There Any V12 Engines That Could Be Called 'Dependable?'

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

Are There Any V12 Engines That Could Be Called 'Dependable?'

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1205 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A V12 engine under the bonnet is a symbol of automotive decadence, telling the world that you've made it and who cares about fuel consumption.
  • It has been revealed that V12s are installed in high-end sedans and limousines, in mid-engined supercars, and in a handful of opulent SUVs and 4x4s.
  • Sources indicate that one of the first uses of the V12 came in 1913, when, in the UK, Louis Coatalen, the chief engineer of Sunbeam Motor Car Company, stuffed a fresh type of aircraft engine called the Mohawk into one of the company's race cars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A V12 engine under the bonnet is a symbol of automotive decadence, telling the world that you've made it and who cares about fuel consumption. Sure, there are plenty of engines that deliver as much performance, but few that exude extravagance and luxury in quite the same way. Still, can V12s be dependable? You might assume not, given their specialized nature and low-volume production.

It has been revealed that V12s are installed in high-end sedans and limousines, in mid-engined supercars, and in a handful of opulent SUVs and 4x4s. But they're not that numerous in the grand scheme of production vehicles.

Sources indicate that one of the first uses of the V12 came in 1913, when, in the UK, Louis Coatalen, the chief engineer of Sunbeam Motor Car Company, stuffed a fresh type of aircraft engine called the Mohawk into one of the company's race cars. Subsequently, "Toodles V" was born: a machine which, after a few hiccups, went on to set eight world speed-over-distance records at Brooklands racetrack.

After Toodles and before WWII, V12s grew in popularity for their smoothness and power, with the North American auto industry providing the bulk of them, even during the Great Depression of 1929: think Packard Twin Six, the Auburn 12, the Cadillac V-12, and the Lincoln series K.

But when Lincoln ceased production of the V12 in 1948, that was that for American V12s. No car company has made one in the U.S. since, and production was mainly left to Europe. Ferrari made its legendary "Colombo" V12, Lamborghini's 1963 V12 would eventually underpin the gorgeous Miura, and even Jaguar brought a 5.3-liter V12 engine to the E-Type in 1971.

In a recent development, there are still a few V12s in production today that you can buy with a fresh-car warranty, which are likely reliable, but what about those of yesteryear? Here's a look at the most dependable.

According to recent reports, if you're after a V12 that's about as widespread and dependable as can be, then the Mercedes M120 is the one to seek out. Mercedes had been working on the idea of a passenger car with a V12 since the 1950s (and considered putting one in its 600 Pullman limo), but it was beaten to the punch by BMW's adoption of the 5.0-liter V12 in 1987's E32 750i. Mercedes didn't get its M120 V12 to market until 1991 in the W140-series S-Class. The 600 badge was given to the W140-series S-Class, the related CL coupe, and the R129 Mercedes SL due to the engine's displacement.

The M120 was a considerably more advanced engine than BMW's V12. It featured an aluminum-alloy block, a forged crankshaft, and LH-Jetronic fuel injection, along with dual throttle bodies, mass airflow sensors, and ECUs. Producing 402 horsepower and 428 pounds-feet of torque, the M120 had enough grunt to push the heavy 600 SE and SEL models from 0 to 60 mph in around six seconds.

What makes the M120 so desirable today, though, is its dependability. There are a few known weak points, such as oil leaks around the valve covers, the front timing covers, the lower oil pan, and the front crank seal, along with worn engine mounts. But aside from these relatively minor concerns, this V12 is known for its reliability and solidity. Furthermore, owners of such high-end Mercs are likely to have kept up with their maintenance.

One final seal of approval comes in the form of the M120's subsequent use in the middle of the Pagani Zonda, a supercar classic we'll always love: a 7.3-liter development of the V12 powered various iterations, culminating in a near-800-hp final edition.

Japan is a country that has not wholeheartedly embraced the V12 engine. In fact, it has made but one road-going engine of this configuration in history, although it turns out to be one of the most reliable V12s you could imagine. It's called the 1GZ-FE, a naturally aspirated 5.0-liter lump with variable valve timing, two ECUs, and enough redundancy built in that it can run on one bank of six cylinders if necessary. The engine powered the second-generation Toyota Century.

A big plus point of the 1GZ is that it's not what you'd call a stressed V12. In its original 1997 incarnation for the Century model, the Japanese "gentleman's agreement" put in place to prevent a horsepower war meant that Toyota claimed a peak power output of just 276 horsepower, with torque rated at up to 355 pounds-feet. It was never going to be one of the most powerful JDM engines ever made, even if its horsepower was higher than the domestic advertising suggested.

Recent findings suggest that if that's not a massive enough perk, know that like so many Toyota engines, the 1GZ-FE would accommodate a heck of a lot of tuning. In fact, the notorious Smokey Nagata – founder of Top Secret and the man who pushed a Supra to 194 mph on a British motorway in 1998 – later built another Supra with a Century's V12 in it. Only that was adorned with a pair of HKS GT2540 turbos, liberating 930 hp and a top speed of over 220 mph.

When the engine was debuted, Toyota published an engineering paper stating, amongst other things, that the 1GZ-FE was more reliable than its competitors, and though the sample size is small, it has been proven to be a dependable V12, with nothing other than age-related failures of minor parts generally reported.

According to recent reports, the original BMW V12, the M70, started an entire line of engines that went into the 7 Series as well as the 8 Series. BMW's M70 successor, the M73, was employed by Rolls-Royce starting in 1998 with the Silver Seraph. Rolls began using a V12 in its Phantom III (1936-1939), but after trying that 7.3-liter monster out for size, it eventually dedicated itself to inline-6 and V8 engines. Rolls-Royce did not use a V12 again until the 1998 Silver Seraph.

Industry observers note that perhaps the most famous application of a BMW V12 was the S70/2, designed by Paul Rosche, which was the incredible engine that powered the legendary McLaren F1 with 627 horsepower. Though maintenance costs are high, the engine itself is robust.

It has been revealed that both Ferrari and Lamborghini's V12s are highly tuned, and of course, they're installed in the sorts of cars that command huge fees on the used market. Nonetheless, the 5.5-liter engine in the Ferrari 456 GT, for example, is supposed to be fairly dependable, as long as it is subjected to regular (and expensive) maintenance.

Industry observers note that aston Martin has been making production V12s since the DB7 Vantage of 1999, and while these "AML" units were not just two Ford Duratec V6s welded together, there was plenty of Ford-derived DNA in the British engine courtesy of Ford's advanced powertrain division. It's generally dependable, so long as owners keep up with maintenance. Oil starvation to the crankshaft is one of the more common problems.

Finally, Jaguar had a good array of V12s in such cars as the E-Type and XJ models. While the mechanicals are reasonably durable, these engines are frequently let down by their electrics.

#30093. For decades, we were told to avoid full-fat dairy. Fresh research says otherwise

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1333 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

For decades, we were told to avoid full-fat dairy. Fresh research says otherwise

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1333 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For years, people have been encouraged to choose low-fat or fat-free dairy products to protect their hearts and manage their weight.
  • A new Canadian study led by University of Toronto professor Harvey Anderson adds to that evidence.
  • Even more surprisingly, participants who consumed more dairy highlighted improvements in blood pressure and obtained greater amounts of several crucial nutrients.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For years, people have been encouraged to choose low-fat or fat-free dairy products to protect their hearts and manage their weight. But growing scientific evidence suggests that full-fat dairy may not carry the health risks many have come to expect.

A new Canadian study led by University of Toronto professor Harvey Anderson adds to that evidence. Researchers found that adults who consumed three servings of full-fat dairy each day for 12 weeks did not experience harmful changes in body weight, body composition, energy metabolism, or blood cholesterol levels compared with participants following a diet containing little dairy.

Even more surprisingly, participants who consumed more dairy highlighted improvements in blood pressure and obtained greater amounts of several crucial nutrients.

The findings, published in The Journal of Nutrition, raise upcoming questions about longstanding dietary recommendations and suggest that the health effects of dairy may be more complicated than its saturated fat content alone would indicate.

Why Full-Fat Dairy Has Been Discouraged.

For decades, nutrition guidelines in Canada and many other countries have recommended choosing low-fat or fat-free milk, yogurt, and other dairy products. The main concern has been saturated fat, which can raise levels of LDL cholesterol in the blood.

Recent findings suggest that often called "bad" cholesterol, LDL can contribute to fatty deposits in the arteries. Over time, this buildup can increase the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and other cardiovascular problems.

Because full-fat dairy contains more saturated fat than reduced-fat alternatives, health authorities have traditionally encouraged people to limit their intake.

However, research examining what happens when people actually consume full-fat dairy has produced a more complicated picture.

Anderson, a professor of nutritional sciences at the University of Toronto's Temerty Faculty of Medicine, points out that numerous studies involving humans have failed to find a clear association between full-fat dairy consumption and poor health outcomes.

Other research has even identified potential protective effects. That includes a recent study led by Temerty Medicine professor Kozeta Milliku, which found an association between whole-fat milk consumption and a lower risk of childhood obesity.

These findings have prompted scientists to investigate whether dairy foods behave differently in the body than their individual nutrients might suggest.

What Happened When Adults Ate Full-Fat Dairy Every Day?

To explore the question, Anderson and his colleagues conducted a 12-week study involving 74 adults with overweight or obesity.

In a recent development, participants were randomly assigned to one of three dietary approaches. The first group followed a calorie-restricted diet containing little dairy. The second consumed three daily servings of dairy while maintaining an energy-neutral diet, meaning their calorie intake was intended to match the energy their bodies used. The third also consumed three servings of dairy each day but otherwise ate without specific calorie restrictions.

All participants received guidance based on Canada's food guide, and the researchers supplied full-fat dairy products during the study.

At the end of 12 weeks, the team compared several measures of metabolic health, including body weight, body composition, and cholesterol levels.

Industry observers note that the results challenged expectations. Participants who consumed three servings of dairy daily did not show meaningful differences in weight gain, body composition, or blood cholesterol compared with those who ate little dairy.

It has been revealed that the higher-dairy groups also experienced improvements in blood pressure and consumed more calcium, protein, and vitamin D. These nutrients play essential roles in maintaining healthy bones, supporting muscle function, and regulating numerous processes throughout the body.

"Those that had three servings of dairy didn't have adverse levels of blood cholesterol or lipids or evidence of insulin resistance," says Anderson.

Blood lipids are fats and fat-like substances circulating in the bloodstream, including cholesterol and triglycerides. Insulin resistance occurs when the body's cells become less responsive to insulin, making it harder to regulate blood sugar and increasing the risk of type 2 diabetes.

It has been revealed that although the results are encouraging, the study was relatively small and lasted only three months. Longer and larger studies are needed to determine whether the findings translate into lasting health benefits or changes in cardiovascular disease risk.

The Surprising Science Behind Dairy Fat.

Why might full-fat dairy have different health effects than researchers would predict from its saturated fat content?

One possible explanation is the dairy matrix hypothesis, an idea that emphasizes how the physical structure of food influences the way the body processes its nutrients.

Rather than treating milk, cheese, or yogurt as simple collections of fat, protein, vitamins, and minerals, this theory considers how those components interact within the food itself.

"With dairy products, it's got two proteins -- casein and whey -- that are bound together with fat and with nutrients mixed in," states Anderson.

According to recent reports, casein and whey are the two major types of protein found in milk. Both provide amino acids that the body uses to build and maintain tissues, but they are digested and absorbed at different rates.

According to Anderson, the complex arrangement of proteins, fats, and other nutrients in dairy products can help regulate how quickly those nutrients are released during digestion.

This means the body's response to eating a whole dairy food may differ from its response to consuming an equivalent amount of saturated fat on its own.

The broader implication is that a food's health effects cannot always be predicted by examining a single ingredient. Its structure, nutritional composition, and interactions among nutrients may all matter.

Why the Findings Could Be Notable for Older Adults.

The researchers believe these results could be particularly relevant for older people, who often need to obtain sufficient protein and essential nutrients while consuming fewer calories.

As people age, their overall energy requirements frequently decrease. However, maintaining muscle mass, bone strength, and other notable bodily functions still requires adequate nutrition.

That can make it difficult to meet nutritional needs, particularly for people with smaller appetites.

Anderson explains that dairy products offer a familiar, convenient source of concentrated nutrition. They provide protein, calcium, and other nutrients in foods that many older adults already enjoy and regularly consume.

The new findings suggest that including full-fat dairy in a balanced diet may help people meet these nutritional requirements without necessarily worsening cholesterol levels or markers associated with diabetes risk.

However, the study did not directly establish whether long-term consumption prevents or increases diabetes, heart disease, or other chronic conditions.

Rethinking Nutrition Advice Beyond Individual Nutrients.

Beyond the debate over dairy fat, the research highlights a broader challenge in nutrition science: judging the health effects of entire foods rather than focusing exclusively on individual nutrients.

In a recent development, traditional dietary advice has often emphasized reducing specific components, such as saturated fat. Although these recommendations are grounded in evidence about cardiovascular risk, researchers increasingly recognize that different foods containing the same nutrients may not have identical effects on health.

The University of Toronto findings contribute to this discussion by showing that full-fat dairy can be incorporated into certain diets without the unfavorable short-term metabolic changes that might be expected from its saturated fat content.

Industry observers note that that does not mean saturated fat is harmless or that everyone should switch to full-fat dairy. Instead, it suggests that the overall food, its nutritional structure, and the broader dietary pattern deserve consideration.

For people trying to navigate changing nutrition recommendations and conflicting health messages, Anderson favors a practical approach rather than complicated dietary rules.

"Keep it simple, eat a variety of foods and not too much of anything.".

This research was supported by Dairy Research Cluster 3 under the Canadian Agricultural Partnership AgriScience Program, and the Mitacs Accelerate program.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Slate, maker of the barebones $26,400 electric truck that I desperately want to see succeed despite my worries about its competition, is all about simplicity.
  • The automaker is selling these atlases for $30, and on the website it's currently marked as sold out.
  • According to recent reports, rand McNally, for the younger readers out there, makes books of maps that it calls its road atlases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Slate, maker of the barebones $26,400 electric truck that I desperately want to see succeed despite my worries about its competition, is all about simplicity. Simple truck, simple purchase price, simple construction, simple accessories. So what happens when buyers want something more complex — something like GPS, which requires satellite connections, maps, screens, and code? Well, the company does it the old fashioned way by stamping its brand on a Rand McNally Road Atlas and selling it as "Screenless GPS.".

The automaker is selling these atlases for $30, and on the website it's currently marked as sold out. The product description reads, "This is the original navigation system — no signal required. Spiral bound, large print, and ready for wherever your Slate takes you. Covers the US, Canada, and Mexico. Limited edition." This particular book is the 2027 Rand McNally EasyFinder Road Atlas, and it includes "7 curated Rand McNally road trips.".

According to recent reports, rand McNally, for the younger readers out there, makes books of maps that it calls its road atlases. I grew up with a road atlas wedged between the driver's seat and center console of my mom's car, and I certainly remember thumbing through its pages while bored — behavior my mom encouraged, so I'd know how to read a map by the time I started driving myself. It's certainly a skill the average Slate buyer has, and maybe the folks that appreciate a simple truck will likewise appreciate a simple way to navigate it around.

Recent findings suggest that paper maps have had a bit of a renaissance as we all get ever more tired of our constantly-increasing screentime. Backcountry Discovery Routes has worked with Butler Maps for years to create paper maps of its BDR routes for those looking to go screenless on the trails, and it seems Slate is hoping to bring the same enthusiasm to road maps with its Rand McNally tie-in. I'm just hoping the promotion Slate is doing for its map, like the Instagram post above, is all tongue in cheek. If the company really means "analog pinch to zoom" is a feature, it comes off a bit I HATE WIFE AND PHOEN.

For most of us, a phone mount suction-cupped to the windshield will make a better navigation solution than a Rand McNally shoved next to the center console. For Slate's target market, buyers who actively miss simpler, older cars and want a return to that kind of design, the bent and worn pages of a worn Road Atlas may provide a bit of the nostalgia they're looking for in an all-electric truck. After all, they probably had one in their old Ranger all those years ago.

HHS finalizes updates to HIPAA privacy rule to ease patient access to health information" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration finalized a major revision to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Privacy Rule designed to give patients easier, faster access to their health records and streamline care coordination.

The final rule, issued by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office for Civil Rights (OCR), strengthens and clarifies the right of an individual to access their protected health information and reduces regulatory and administrative burdens, the agency said.

Industry observers note that the proposed rule was issued more than five years ago, in January 2021. An unpublished version of the final rule is available here.

Recent findings suggest that under the final rule, healthcare organizations must respond faster to patient requests for copies of their health records. HHS stated covered entities will have no more than 15 calendar days to respond to a request, reduced from the current 30-day period. Organizations are allowed one extension of no more than 30 calendar days, HHS said in the final rule.

The rule also establishes that patients can access their protected health information through personal health apps when the covered entity has the technical capacity to deliver the records in that form and format.

The rule also expands circumstances when patients must receive copies of their health records for free, requires advance notice of fees and modifies identity verification requirements.

To make it easier for healthcare organizations to share data for care coordination, the final rule clarifies that health intends may use and disclose protected health information for care coordination and case management for individuals. The rule also expressly permits covered entities to disclose PHI to social services agencies, community-based organizations and similar third parties for care coordination and case management for individuals.

To reduce regulatory burden, OCR eliminated the requirement for providers with direct treatment relationships with individuals to make a good faith effort to obtain an individual’s written acknowledgment that they have received a copy of the health care provider’s Notice of Privacy Practices. The final rule also permits disclosures to Telecommunications Relay Services (TRS) communications assistants for persons who are deaf, hard of hearing, or deaf-blind, or who have a speech disability, and excludes TRS providers from the definition of business associate.

Industry observers note that “Americans should never have to fight for access to their own health records,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr in a statement. “Under President Trump’s leadership, we are putting patients in control, requiring faster access to their information, and cutting red tape that gets in the way of coordinated care. This rule modernizes HIPAA to serve patients and help providers spend more time delivering care and less time navigating bureaucracy.”.

Provisions in the final rule will become effective 60 days after publication in the Federal Register, and compliance will be required 180 days after that date, according to HHS in a fact sheet.

During a Monday fireside chat at the HLTH 2026 conference in Las Vegas, CMS Deputy Administrator and Chief Product Officer Amy Gleason remarked the updates to the privacy rule "remove friction from the patient experience.".

Gleason said there are three main components of the rule: the designation of a "personal health app," identity verification and speed. "It should be almost instantaneous with electronic data, and it also says that this information is free to the patient," she said.

Recent findings suggest that “This final rule provides Americans with faster and easier access to their health information, which is critical to them being able to take control of their own health and health care,” said Office for Civil Rights Director Paula M. Stannard in a statement. “Consistent with the Trump Administration’s deregulatory goals, the rule also reduces regulatory burdens on health care providers and other regulated entities and decreases costs for the health care system.

While the Trump administration moved forward with changes to the HIPAA privacy rule, federal regulators delayed a major overhaul of the HIPAA Security Rule, pushing back final action on the rule by a year. HHS had proposed a May 2026 release for a final rule that makes significant changes to the HIPAA Security Rule and marks the first major update to the 23-year-old rule in more than 10 years. The U.S. Office of Management and Budget (OMB) website was updated in July and indicates that the final rule was pushed back to July 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Now live in Las Vegas, with Los Angeles to follow.

In March 2026, we declared a multi-year partnership between Zoox and Uber to bring our robotaxi experience to Uber’s growing autonomy platform in select cities.

In a recent development, now, beginning today, Uber riders in Las Vegas will have the opportunity to be matched with a Zoox robotaxi on eligible trips. Zoox will also continue to offer rides through the Zoox app. In addition, Zoox and Uber are the official robotaxi and rideshare partners of MGM Resorts’ Las Vegas properties. Together, they’re working with MGM Resorts to make pickups and drop-offs easier and more intuitive, with improved on-property wayfinding, in-app guidance, and infrastructure improvements designed to support smoother traffic flow.

The Zoox purpose-built robotaxi gives riders the agency to create a space all their own, with design elements for enhanced socialization and safety not possible in a traditional car. Bringing this experience to Uber will help introduce the benefits of purpose-built autonomy to new, curious riders.

Within the Zoox and Uber apps, riders can take a Zoox to popular resorts and venues on and around the Strip, as well as rides in the Downtown & Arts District. More destinations will be added soon.

We will continue to offer our service through the Zoox app, in addition to rides being available through Uber in those cities.

Zoox was founded in 2014 on a bold belief: if you’re going to reinvent mobility, you have to start from scratch. Instead of retrofitting cars with autonomous technology, we designed the world’s first purpose-built robotaxi: fully autonomous, all-electric, bidirectional, and intentionally engineered around the rider experience. Since the very beginning, we’ve been focused on our vision of delivering safe and enjoyable mobility.

Industry observers note that like Zoox, Uber was founded in San Francisco with a vision to improve urban transportation. Uber started in 2010 as a ridehail app connecting riders with cars, but quickly evolved. Over the past decade, it expanded into shared rides, food delivery, freight logistics, micromobility, and is now building an autonomous vehicle network, consistently redefining how people and goods move through the world. By leveraging smartphone technology, dynamic pricing, and real-time data, Uber helped catalyze the on-demand economy and reshape how people get from A to B on a global scale. This partnership is a testament to Uber’s dedication to advancing transportation within the ridehail space.

It has been revealed that zoox has always taken a measured, step-by-step approach by starting small, learning rapidly, and scaling responsibly. This launch with Uber mirrors that approach. We’re beginning with a small fleet with the potential to expand as we refine our operations, technology, and customer experience.

Uber and Zoox will launch in Los Angeles next year, after Zoox opens service on the Zoox app.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While we're yearning for another generation of the legendary Chevrolet Camaro, our best bet is to look back at its golden era — and one of the most pristine restomods we've found on Hemmings. This Ontario orange 1969 Camaro SS, listed by a Clarkston, Michigan dealer for $58,900, shows 10,000 miles on the odometer and a body-up restoration. Its 396 big-block raises a fair question: How did that engine really stack up against its rivals back in '69?

Neither the Hemmings listing nor the dealer's YouTube walkaround gives horsepower or torque figures, but this clearly isn't a stock motor. The 396 wears an Edelbrock Performer aluminum intake, ceramic headers, a mild camshaft, and a Flame Thrower high-energy-ingition distributor, with chrome valve covers and an air cleaner on top. Behind it, a Turbo-Hydramatic 400 automatic sends power to a 10-bolt rear axle with 3.23 gears.

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j-bnQtJsNGQ].

According to recent reports, for context, Chevrolet offered three 396s in the 1969 SS, rated at 325, 350, and 375 horsepower, with torque between 410 and 415 pound-feet. The 375-horsepower L78 sat at the top, peaking at 5,600 rpm. So without a dyno sheet, there's no telling where this restomod example lands among them.

On paper, the L78 outgunned most of its competition. Its 375 horsepower beat the 345 claimed for Pontiac's Ram Air IV Firebird or the 335 rated for Mustang Mach 1's 428 Cobra Jet — one of the most powerful powertrains the Mach 1 ever came with. Even the base 325-horsepower SS 396 sat within 10 horsepower of the Cobra Jet.

Testing was less flattering. Car Life's figures (per Curbside Classic), recorded in showroom-stock trim, have a Camaro SS 396 L78 reaching 60 mph in 6.8 seconds and covering the quarter-mile in 14.77 seconds at 98.7 mph. The Mach 1 428, meanwhile, managed 5.5 seconds and 13.9 at 103.3 mph. Two other 375-horsepower rivals also ran quicker quarter-miles: the Plymouth 'Cuda 440 at 14.01 seconds, and the Boss 429 Mustang at 14.09, despite a slower 7.1-second run to 60. Traction was the usual culprit, since bias-ply tires struggled with substantial-block torque, so gross ratings didn't settle the pony car argument.

The Camaro's paint is Ontario orange metallic with a black hockey stripe, and there are front and rear spoilers, a cowl hood, and dual chrome mirrors. The 17-inch American Racing Torque Thrust wheels are wrapped in Dunlop 255/45ZR17 tires in back and 235/40R17s up front. The car also gets tubular upper and lower control arms, an aluminum radiator, power steering, and power front discs with slotted and drilled rotors. Inside, the black vinyl interior includes factory bucket seats, a center console, a sport steering wheel, and a Retrosound radio. So while we speculate on the return of the Camaro, consider looking to the past to get the edge off with this low-mile time capsule.

HLTH 2026: GLP-1 costs remain a challenge. A new CVS study aims to identify the right price" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Cost and access to GLP-1s remains a challenge, but the benefits of these drugs aren't in doubt.

Sources indicate that A new study from CVS Health aims to quantify at what price a GLP-1 drug has generated enough savings elsewhere through improved clinical outcomes. The healthcare giant used anonymized claims data from Aetna members in fully insured intends and found savings from reduced hospital and medical spending, as well as improved health outcomes.

But those benefits weren't enough to offset the increased pharmaceutical spending at the current price point, the study found.

The study tracked a mix of members who took GLP-1s from 2023 to 2025, so some patients had three years of follow-up care and management.

Sources indicate that amy Compton-Phillips, M.D., chief medical officer at CVS, told Fierce Healthcare that part of the challenge in this equation is that these drugs gained steam as a treatment for obesity at a high price. And while those costs have come down, the reductions haven't yet been enough to offset the expenditures.

Another challenge for employers in particular—where GLP-1 coverage has been most in flux—is turnover, she said. While GLP-1s do drive significant improvements, an employer may not reap the benefit of the reduced cost if an employee moves to a different organization before those are realized, even though they paid for the medication initially.

The study sought to identify a price point where those savings would be felt and landed at $350 per month over a three-year period. Achieving that, Compton-Phillips said, would likely lure employers into embracing broader GLP-1 coverage.

"For them, it might be really worthwhile to say, 'Hey, at this price point, I can afford to cover this for my employees, knowing that in the near term the savings will pay for my investment,'" she remarked.

Recent findings suggest that the study found obesity rates declining after a 2022 peak, as well as a reduction of between 34% and 42% in hospitalizations over three years. Patients also had 14% lower odds of a serious cardiac event.

For patients who remained on the drugs for three years, their total medical spending decreased by $9,400, but associated pharmacy spending increased in tandem by $13,300, the study found.

Clinical improvements also fell off when patients were not able to remain adherent to the medication over several years, highlighting the importance of a wraparound approach that supports broader care management rather than simply prescribing a patient a GLP-1.

Compton-Phillips said CVS' own weight management program brings nutrition, peer coaching and other supports into the fold, in addition to the prescription. This is especially critical, she said, as evidence suggests weight gain is common after a patient stops taking their GLP-1, making behavior change key.

"At the moment, there's not great evidence that if you come off the drugs, you will maintain the weight loss," she stated.

The CVS researchers mentioned that the ultimate goal of the study was not to demand that all GLP-1 prescriptions repay their own costs, but to ensure that drug costs align with patient benefits and the broader cost of access. By lowering the net price of these products, more people can access them, the study concludes.

It has been revealed that "These drugs make people's lives better, and I want to give them out," Compton-Phillips said. Doing so becomes a challenge, though, "at the price they are today," she said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rapid Growth in Energy Storage Is Helping Stabilize Electricity Prices and Strengthen Grid Reliability; Industry Urges Congress to Pass Permitting Reform to Accelerate Deployment.

In a recent development, LAS VEGAS — The U.S. energy storage industry installed 14.3 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of newly introduced capacity in Q3, bringing total installations in the first nine months of 2026 to 48.3 GWh, according to the U.S. Energy Storage Market Outlook Q4 2026 (ESMO) released today by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.

Sources indicate that U.S. energy storage capacity installed has now exceeded 200 GWh to date as grid operators, utilities, and energy buyers turn to storage to lower energy costs and strengthen grid reliability. After voters sent a clear message in the midterm elections that lowering energy costs must be a priority, the U.S. solar and storage industry is urging lawmakers to send the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) to the President’s desk.

Last week, more than 300 solar and storage companies sent a letter to Congressional leadership urging swift passage of BAAJA. The legislation will accelerate energy storage deployment, reduce project costs, and expand access to lower-cost, reliable electricity for households and businesses.

“Voters made it clear that they want lower prices, and the growing deployment of energy storage is helping make that happen. We’re urging Congress to pass BAAJA to build out America’s energy infrastructure and put downward pressure on prices,” said SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty.

The outlook for energy storage continues to strengthen, with the report increasing its 2030 cumulative U.S. deployment forecast by 3.7% to 708 GWh across grid and BTM. The revised forecast reflects sustained industry momentum, with U.S. installations up 20% year over year through the first nine months of 2026.

Texas led the nation in utility-scale storage deployment through Q3, adding 12.3 GWh of capacity. Arizona and California followed with 7.7 GWh and 6.8 GWh, respectively. Recent SEIA analysis shows that rapid growth in solar and energy storage helped drive down average wholesale electricity prices by 42% in Texas and 51% in California from summer 2021 to summer 2026.

11 states surpassed their previous annual energy storage installation records in Q3, even with three months remaining in 2026: Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois.

In a recent development, “States are moving from targets to centralized procurements,” remarked Pete Tillotson, Senior Analyst at Benchmark Minerals. “Across utility mandates and bulk capacity contracts, energy storage pipelines are growing as a result of both investment appetite and flexibility requirements.”.

According to recent reports, U.S. storage manufacturing continues to accelerate, ensuring that more of the batteries being deployed to strengthen the grid are made in the United States. In July, a newly introduced battery cell manufacturing facility opened in Tennessee. In October, a new cell manufacturing facility opened in Indiana, bringing total cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, a 50% increase.

Utility-scale projects accounted for the vast majority of Q3 installations, with 12.2 GWh deployed, followed by 1.3 GWh of commercial and industrial storage, and 746 MWh of residential storage.

Breaking: When your gut bacteria run out of fiber, they may start eating your gut lining

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that eating more plants is widely associated with better health, but scientists are still uncovering exactly why.
  • Sources indicate that plant-based diets support digestive health, immune function, metabolism, and cardiovascular health.
  • Fiber is particularly important because it provides food for gut microbes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that eating more plants is widely associated with better health, but scientists are still uncovering exactly why. New research suggests that fiber is only part of the story. Certain plant proteins that resist digestion may also play a surprisingly key role in shaping gut bacteria and determining whether they produce beneficial or potentially harmful substances.

Sources indicate that plant-based diets support digestive health, immune function, metabolism, and cardiovascular health. One reason is that they help maintain a diverse community of microorganisms in the intestines, collectively known as the gut microbiome. Many of these bacteria are beneficial, helping break down food components that the human digestive system cannot process on its own.

Fiber is particularly important because it provides food for gut microbes. Plants also contain phytochemicals, natural substances that often give fruits and vegetables their vibrant colors and help protect them from environmental threats. These compounds can also contribute to human health. Yet researchers have only begun to understand the complicated chemical interactions that occur when gut bacteria digest plant foods.

Two studies led by Jenna AbuSalim and Joshua Rabinowitz, director of the Princeton Branch of the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, provide important upcoming insights. One, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, shows how plant fiber and certain proteins influence gut bacteria to favor the production of beneficial compounds over potentially harmful ones. The other, published in Nature Metabolism in June, challenges the longstanding belief that many important chemical compounds circulating in the body originate exclusively from intestinal microbes.

According to recent reports, "There's growing interest across medical disciplines in manipulating the human microbiome or using its metabolic products themselves for therapy," said Rabinowitz. "Diet holds great promise for controlling the microbiome and its outputs. But to devise effective therapeutic interventions, we need to understand what aspects of the diet control which microbial outputs.".

How Plant Foods Change the Chemicals Your Gut Produces.

In the PNAS study, researchers examined a group of substances called phenol metabolites. Metabolites are chemicals formed when the body or microorganisms break down and process nutrients. Some are essential for normal biological functions, while others can contribute to health problems when they accumulate.

The phenol metabolites investigated by the team are produced when gut bacteria process two amino acids, tyrosine and phenylalanine. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, but the compounds they ultimately produce can have very different effects on health.

Industry observers note that two metabolites derived from phenylalanine, phenylpropionate and hippuric acid, are associated with healthy body weight and better gut health. In contrast, two compounds derived from tyrosine, p-cresol sulfate and phenol sulfate, have been linked to worse outcomes in cancer patients and harmful effects throughout the body in people with kidney disease.

The researchers wanted to understand whether different components of plant foods could influence which of these substances gut microbes produce.

"Our studies highlighted that both the fiber and indigestible proteins from plants -- which we call 'proteins imitating fiber,' or Prif -- shift the balance of phenol metabolites from the harmful kind made from tyrosine to the healthful variety derived from phenylalanine," remarked AbuSalim.

An Overlooked Plant Protein Works Alongside Fiber.

Although the health benefits of dietary fiber have been studied extensively, scientists have paid much less attention to plant proteins that pass through the digestive system without being fully broken down.

Sources indicate that the researchers found that these indigestible proteins, which they call Prif, can reach the gut microbiome and serve as material for bacterial metabolism. In doing so, they influence which microbes thrive and which chemical compounds are produced.

In a recent development, importantly, these proteins do not work in isolation. They cooperate with plant fiber to change how gut bacteria process nutrients, shifting their activity toward the production of beneficial phenol metabolites.

In a recent development, this discovery suggests that the nutritional value of plant foods may depend on more than their familiar concentrations of fiber, vitamins, and minerals. The amount and type of protein that escapes digestion could also help determine how food influences the gut microbiome.

When Gut Bacteria Run Low on Fiber, They May Feed on Your Gut's Protective Mucus.

One of the most intriguing findings concerns where gut bacteria obtain the raw materials used to produce harmful metabolites.

To investigate, the researchers labeled proteins with stable (non-radioactive) isotopes, allowing them to track exactly where the proteins traveled and how they were processed in the digestive systems of mice. This technique works by giving molecules a detectable chemical signature without making them radioactive.

The experiments revealed an crucial difference between the sources of beneficial and harmful phenols.

It has been revealed that the potentially harmful phenols came from gut bacteria breaking down proteins belonging to the host, including proteins found in the mucus layer that coats the intestines. This protective mucus helps separate intestinal microbes from the cells lining the gut and forms part of the body's natural defenses.

Meanwhile, the beneficial phenols were produced almost entirely from indigestible proteins supplied by food.

It has been revealed that fiber helped suppress the bacterial breakdown of the gut's protective mucus, reducing the production of harmful phenols. The indigestible plant proteins (Prif), in turn, supplied more dietary protein to gut bacteria, encouraging them to produce beneficial compounds instead.

Together, the findings reveal two complementary ways plant foods can influence intestinal chemistry. Fiber helps discourage bacteria from consuming proteins in the gut's protective mucus, while Prif provides an alternative source of nutrients that supports the production of healthier metabolites.

"We think Prifs represent an emerging class of dietary nutrients that shape the composition of the gut microbiome and could have a far-reaching influence on metabolic health," said AbuSalim.

The implications could eventually extend to nutrition labels and dietary recommendations.

"Food packaging may eventually list Prif right below fiber," noted Rabinowitz.

A Second Discovery Challenges What Scientists Thought About Gut Bacteria.

The companion study in Nature Metabolism addressed another crucial question: Are gut bacteria really responsible for producing all the metabolites traditionally attributed to them?

Along with phenol metabolites, the researchers examined indole metabolites, which are formed from tryptophan, another amino acid found in dietary proteins.

Industry observers note that these substances have attracted considerable scientific interest because they participate in biological processes linked to inflammation, immune activity, and disease. Researchers have investigated their involvement in inflammatory bowel disease, neurodegenerative disorders, and cancer. Some indole metabolites have also been found to influence the spread of cancer and the immune system's ability to attack tumors.

In a recent development, scientists have generally assumed that gut bacteria are the source of these compounds. That belief has encouraged efforts to develop probiotics and dietary interventions that increase the production of potentially beneficial indole metabolites.

However, this approach depends on an key assumption: that intestinal microbes are responsible for producing most or all of the compounds researchers want to influence.

If the body's own cells make substantial amounts of these metabolites, changing the microbiome may not be the most effective way to control their levels.

Your Body Can Make Compounds Once Attributed to Gut Microbes.

To investigate, the research team used isotope tracing in mice, rats, and human cells to follow how different metabolites were produced.

The results challenged conventional thinking. Mammalian cells were capable of generating numerous phenol and indole metabolites independently of intestinal bacteria.

Among these were indole-3-lactate and indole-3-acetate, two biologically vital compounds previously considered products of microbial metabolism.

The researchers also examined what happened when antibiotics disrupted the intestinal microbiome. If certain metabolites depended entirely on gut bacteria, their concentrations would be expected to decline sharply when those bacteria were depleted.

But many metabolites remained at substantial levels in the blood of antibiotic-treated mice. A similar pattern appeared in samples from patients receiving antibiotics, including people undergoing cancer treatment.

Industry observers note that other compounds behaved differently. Levels of indole-3-propionate and p-cresol sulfate, which are produced exclusively by microbes, declined following antibiotic treatment.

These results provided further evidence that some metabolites depend on intestinal bacteria, while others can also be manufactured by the body's own metabolic processes.

The distinction matters because it could change how researchers develop treatments intended to increase beneficial metabolites or reduce harmful ones.

What These Discoveries Mean for Nutrition and Future Treatments.

Together, the two studies offer a more detailed understanding of how diet, gut microbes, and the body's own metabolism interact.

Industry observers note that the first identifies an overlooked category of plant proteins that works with fiber to influence bacterial activity, potentially helping shift the balance away from harmful metabolic products. The second demonstrates that the body itself can produce many compounds once believed to originate exclusively from gut bacteria.

Both findings have implications for research into metabolic disease, digestive health, cancer, and other conditions involving the microbiome.

They also suggest that attempts to manipulate gut chemistry through diet, probiotics, or other therapies will need to account for both microbial activity and the body's own metabolic capabilities.

Much of the experimental evidence comes from animals and laboratory studies, so additional research will be needed to determine how these mechanisms influence long-term health outcomes in people.

Nevertheless, a better understanding of the relationship between different food components and microbial metabolism could eventually make dietary advice more precise and help researchers identify new therapeutic strategies.

"Beyond that," mentioned Rabinowitz, "a clearer picture of how different foods interact with the microbiome to modulate the production of bacterial metabolites will help sharpen the guidance nutritionists and doctors can give to people for disease prevention and therapy.".

These studies were funded by the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, the National Institutes of Health, the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the Princeton Alliance for Collaborative Research and Innovation, Princeton University.

Aside from his post as Director of the Princeton Branch of the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, Joshua Rabinowitz is Professor in the Department of Chemistry & Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics and a member of the Rutgers Cancer Institute.

Breaking: Humana launches national provider Gold Card program

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fiercehealthcare

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Humana is continuing its push to reform prior authorization with the launch of a national provider gold card program.
  • The program will go into effect on Dec.
  • Humana estimates that about 50,000 providers will qualify for the program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Humana launches national provider Gold Card program" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Humana is continuing its push to reform prior authorization with the launch of a national provider gold card program.

The program will go into effect on Dec. 1, the firm revealed Tuesday. It will focus initially on MRI, CT and MRA imaging as well as physical and occupational therapy. Through the program, eligible providers will no longer need to secure a prior authorization approval and can instead use a streamlined process.

Humana estimates that about 50,000 providers will qualify for the program. Eligible providers must be able to demonstrate a proven track record of high-quality care and patient outcomes.

Traci Granston, M.D., vice president of clinical innovation and trend at Humana, told Fierce Healthcare in an exclusive interview that prior authorization and other utilization management approaches are key in ensuring that patients receive the appropriate care.

Industry observers note that however, lengthy decision times and other barriers can create a painful friction. So for providers that consistently demonstrate that they are aligned with clinical guidelines, the gold cards can remove that guardrail.

"If they're following those guidelines and providing appropriate care, prior auths don't really serve a purpose for them," Granston remarked.

The insurer conducted a pilot earlier this year with about 400 provider organizations and approximately 8,000 clinicians. Through that process, the team conducted interviews with clinicians and office staff who shared their desire for fewer administrative burdens and a simpler experience.

In a recent development, those insights shaped the broader launch, Humana remarked, and the insurer intends to continue to iterate and evolve the gold card program over time, including by adding fresh service lines. It's not uncommon for a program to roll out that aims to support providers, but their voice is less often at the table in shaping what the experience looks like to ensure that their pain points are being addressed.

Granston mentioned that the team is examining more time-sensitive services that could fit within the program, for example.

"For our top-performing providers, we would like to essentially get out of the way and let them continue to care for our members," she noted.

Industry observers note that the gold card program builds on Humana's existing work to reform prior authorization, including a streamlined approval process for electronic submissions that took effect in January of this year. Under this initiative, Humana responds within one business day in 95% of electronic prior authorization cases.

Sources indicate that the insurer also announced earlier this month that it would join forces with athenahealth to accelerate the use of electronic prior authorization. Through the partnership, more of the process is embedded directly in the provider's workflow, streamlining the experience for them at the point of care.

Granston stated that the goal is to make it easier to surface the data necessary to make an approval and enable that to occur in real time. This also means that fewer people have to be dedicated to the work of submissions and approval.

"When the information exists, you don't really need all these people to be touching it," she said.

Mercedes Is Auctioning Off A C111 For The First Time Ever, And It'll Be Your Last Chance To Buy One For At Least 25 Years

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Back in 2022, Mercedes-Benz brought a chosen group of collectors to its Museum for a secret auction, at which one of the two 1955 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupés was sold for a record-breaking €135 million, about $143 million according to exchange rates at the time.
  • Turns out the next thing is another completely unexpected sale.
  • Recent findings suggest that while I don't think the C111 will touch the Uhlenhaut's record hammer price, you really should never say never.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Back in 2022, Mercedes-Benz brought a chosen group of collectors to its Museum for a secret auction, at which one of the two 1955 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupés was sold for a record-breaking €135 million, about $143 million according to exchange rates at the time. Most people, myself including, thought there was no way Mercedes would have ever sold one of the Uhlenhauts, not to mention many of the other slightly less rare and iconic cars in its collection. Now that it had auctioned off its most valuable car, it opened up so much speculation: What could be next?

Turns out the next thing is another completely unexpected sale. On Tuesday night, at an event kicking off the week's Rétromobile Latest York festivities, Mercedes-Benz confirmed that in just a few months it will be selling one of its groundbreaking C111 prototypes. This will be the first time Mercedes has ever sold a C111, and unlike the Uhlenhaut, it will be a public auction held at RM Sotheby's Rétromobile Paris sale in February, with all proceeds going towards funding the future of the Mercedes-Benz Museum.

Recent findings suggest that while I don't think the C111 will touch the Uhlenhaut's record hammer price, you really should never say never. There's no precedent for how much this car could go for, especially given that Mercedes-Benz has promised it won't sell or auction off another C111 for at least 25 years. If you want one, now might be your only chance, and the C111 in question is perhaps the best one of the bunch.

Recent findings suggest that as a bit of a memory refresher, the first C111 was introduced to the public at the 1969 International Motor Show in Frankfurt, though a few were already built by then, and an updated version was shown the following year in Geneva. It was strictly an experimental vehicle, a testbed for future technology, design and powertrain ideas. Prospective customers handed Mercedes blank checks to get a C111 of their own, and Mercedes says there was "enormous public interest," but the C111 was never put into production. The company cites the 1973 oil crisis, new emissions standards and high production costs as the reasons why, but that didn't stop Mercedes from continuing to build more new versions.

Industry observers note that between 1969 and 1978, Mercedes built 17 different C111s across three iterations of the model: the C111-I, the C111-II, and the C111-III. The C111 was originally conceived with a rotary powertrain, first a three-rotor Wankel with later versions getting a four-rotor engine. One was built with a V8 and another has since been converted to have a V8, and the last few C111-IIIs had five-cylinder turbodiesels with which they set a bunch of records at Nardò. Three of the C111s were dismantled after testing, and one was destroyed in crash testing; the rest have remained in Mercedes' collection ever since, with only a couple of them being still functional.

As Mercedes continued building upcoming iterations of the C111, the overall design and various details evolved, but every C111 was spectacular and clearly part of the same family. The tech giant had never made a mid-engined sports car, not to mention anything such a wild wedge shape, so it's no surprise they were show-stoppers everywhere. Some C111s had their glass-fiber-reinforced plastic bodywork originally painted white, and the last few were metallic silver, but the cars are best known for the Weißherbst paint worn by the vast majority of them — "white autumn" in German, named after a traditional copper-tinted rosé.

Industry observers note that the C111 being sold is a C111-II, car number 33, which Mercedes indicates is "only of internal significance." Production began in March 1970 with the car being completed in August, when it became the second C111-II to go into the test fleet. It was fitted with a 2.4-liter four-rotor Wankel engine that produced a massive 345 horsepower and 289 pound-feet of torque, sending the 2,734-pound car from 0 to 62 mph in 4.8 seconds and on to a top speed of 186 mph (300 km/h), making it the fastest car in the world at the time. In fact, chief test engineer Hans Liebold once hit 188 mph on the Autobahn heading towards Baden-Baden.

Recent findings suggest that mercedes notes Car 33 "was used to test a fluidic component designed to ensure even emptying of the two side fuel tanks, which have a combined capacity of 30.6 gallons, to carry out temperature measurements in the rear trunk, and to conduct test drives at the Hockenheimring." It was featured on the first German concern of Playboy in 1972, and since 1975 it has been retired, part of Mercedes-Benz's collection. When the museum opened in 2006, the car has been on display in the Fascination Design area, floating on a plinth surrounding a curved staircase.

In 2024, the Mercedes-Benz Classic team in Fellbach gave Car 33 a full restoration, making it one of just a couple C111s that actually still run, and the only running car with a rotary engine. The mechanical restoration was completed without messing up the car's lovely patina, the only addition to the car being a fire extinguisher. It has the original paint and houndstooth cloth seats, and a Becker Europa radio that actualy works.

There are 24,766 kilometers on the odometer (about 15,389 miles), and Mercedes notes that while Car 33 was used to test anti-lock braking systems, the ABS at the moment doesn't work. The car comes with its original magnesium racing wheels, sized 10x15-inch in front and 13x15-inch in the rear, but they are "not only suitable for display purposes," so Mercedes created a new set of 8x15 light alloy wheels that the car can actually be driven on. The rear trunk tub, which is designed to hold luggage, is fitted and able to be removed.

I'm particularly excited to see how much this car goes for because I've had a few very special experiences with C111s, including this specific one. Mere days before the world shut down in 2020, I was given a tour of Mercedes' secret "holy halls" warehouses in Germany, where I saw half of all the C111s all lined up together. (The photo you see below, which Mercedes graciously let me take on a film camera.).

Industry observers note that at Monterey Car Week in 2022 I got to ride shotgun the V8-powered C111 on the Tour d'Elegance, which was incredible even when we were stuck in traffic and slightly overheating. In 2024, I got to ride up and down Massive Sur in this particular car, number 33, fresh off its restoration with a fully functioning rotary engine. The V8 C111 already felt extraordinary, but the four-rotor motor's totally unique buzzy sound and character really takes it to the stratosphere. There's no other car in existence quite like it.

Apart from other C111s, of course. Yes, it's pretty nuts that Mercedes is selling one of these things, but it will still have 12 others in the collection. I'm sure now that the Classic team got this one working, it will be able to restore one of the other rotary-powered C111s in the collection. Don't think this is the last the world will see of this C111, either. Part of the buyer contract for the Uhlenhaut was that its upcoming owner must bring the car to events and shows, and that Mercedes gets to use it for things when it wants, and I'm sure the same will be the case for this sale.

Whoever buys it really should use it, too. For all of its fantastical styling and engineering, it's a proper car. Sure, the rotary doesn't really like sitting around at low speeds, instead egging you on to keep reaching the red mark at 7,000 rpm on the tachometer, and there's no air conditioning so your only respite from in-cabin heat is to open the small vent windows (or just open the gullwing doors). It's pretty comfortable, though, and pretty easy to get in and out of. The engine isn't so loud that you can't hold a conversation with your passenger, and the interior just feels like any other Mercedes from the '70s.

The C111 be will be sold on February 3, 2027, at the Salles du Carrousel underneath the Louvre, where RM Sotheby's typically has its Rétromobile auction. RM Sotheby's notes bids can be placed by phone or in person at the auction, after reigstering ahead of time of course, and if you're interested you can go to the Mercedes Classic Center website to learn about "the terms and conditions of participation, bidder registration and opportunities for pre-inspection." Given the C111's existence as a forward-thinking experiment, I think it's fitting that the money goes toward making the automaker's museum even better for future generations. Says Mercedes:.

The aim of "Mercedes-Benz Museum 2.0" is to bring the brand's unique heritage to life for future generations and make it accessible worldwide. To this end, Mercedes-Benz is continuously developing both the Museum in Stuttgart and its virtual offerings. A key component is the Museum's digital twin. This makes the Museum experience accessible regardless of physical location, thereby extending its reach far beyond Stuttgart. It will give people all over the world greater access to the Mercedes-Benz brand heritage. The virtual twin is being developed in collaboration with The Classic Car Trust (TCCT) and its digital platform, Roarington.

"With 'Mercedes-Benz Museum 2.0' , we are consistently taking our Museum to the next level. We are continuing to write our tech giant and brand history right up to the present day, creating new exhibition experiences and providing space for topics that are of particular interest to our visitors – from more recent classic cars to the latest innovations. With a digital twin, we are also opening up the Museum to people all over the world. Visitors can also experience the exhibits interactively here. The first results will be visible as early as 2027." -Bettina Haussmann, Director of the Mercedes-Benz Museum.

Sources indicate that so, how much could it go for? Who the hell knows. The collector car market is so absurd these days — McLaren F1s are $35-million cars now — and there's no prior sales of cars that you can really compare the C111 to. Last year the Indianapolis Motor Speedway auctioned off a Mercedes-Benz W196 R race car that become the second-most-expensive sale ever, also in parnership with the automaker and RM Sotheby's. The most expensive public sale of a Ferrari 250 GTO has been just under $52 million, while private sales have been rumored to exceed $70 million, and I think the C111 could easily clear that mark.

It has been revealed that for its part, Mercedes claims that "for at least 25 years, this will remain the only opportunity: Mercedes-Benz has contractually committed not to sell any further C111s during this period." That's definitely an incentive for people to keep raising their paddles. I'm also going to take this sale as confirmation that Mercedes is definitely working on a C111-inspired supercar in the vein of the Vision One-Eleven concept from a few years ago.

💡 Key Takeaways
