Leatherman Behavioral Care Pavilion in Florence. Cole also maintained MUSC’s U.S. News & World Report accolade as the “Best Hospital” in South Carolina.

In a recent development, "To have had the opportunity to lead and serve this remarkable institution has been one of the great privileges of my life," Cole mentioned in a statement. "MUSC stands today as one of the nation’s leading academic medical centers, a testament to what can be achieved when people are united in service to patients, students, families, communities and one another.”.

Sources indicate that >Alice Rigdon of Mayo Clinic in Florida will join Deaconess Health System as senior vice president and chief financial officer, effective this fall. She will succeed Cheryl Wathen, who is retiring after more than 36 years with Deaconess, including 16 years as the system's CFO.

Recent findings suggest that at Mayo Clinic Florida, Rigdon drove capital and finance transformation initiatives, including standardization, automation and workforce development. Prior to joining Mayo Clinic, she served as VP of finance at SCL Health's Saint Joseph Hospital in Denver and as director of outpatient strategy and development and CFO of Piedmont Medical Center in South Carolina.

Wathen was initially named senior vice president and CFO of Deaconess in 2010, after serving as manager of internal audit, manager of finance, CFO of The Women's Hospital and controller of Deaconess Health System.

"What I am most proud of is the people I have hired and mentored who have excelled in their roles and will be the leaders that take Deaconess into the future,” Wathen noted in a statement.

According to recent reports, >The American Hospital Association named Steve Walsh as its upcoming president and CEO, taking over for the retiring Rick Pollack. Walsh comes from a similar role at the Massachusetts Hospital Association, and will stay there until the appointment takes effect this fall. Read more here.

>Symplr, a provider of enterprise healthcare operations software, appointed Andrew Langford as Chief Financial Officer, effective immediately. As symplr continues to scale its investment in AI-powered innovation, Langford is poised to help drive the firm’s next phase of value creation and operational excellence, the company said. He succeeds Tom Fink, who has served as interim CFO since early 2026, and will ensure a smooth leadership transition.

Langford was previously an executive vice president at Zelis, where he oversaw financial strategy, treasury, enterprise pricing and operational planning for the healthcare and financial technology company. Prior to Zelis, he spent nearly a decade at Global Payments, Inc. in a series of progressively senior finance leadership roles.

“Andrew brings the strategic perspective, financial discipline and operational acumen that will help guide symplr through its next phase of growth,” said Venkat Kavarthapu, symplr CEO, in a statement. “His expertise in scaling global organizations, executing strategic transactions and partnering across the business will be instrumental as we continue to invest in AI-powered innovations that reduce complexity, enhance care quality and deliver value for our customers.”.

>President Donald Trump declared on his social media platform, Truth Social, that Chris Klomp has been tapped to serve as Deputy Secretary for the Department of Health and Human Services.

In a recent development, klomp, who heads the Department of Medicare at the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, has made a rapid rise through the agency to a potential role as its second-in-command. The Deputy Secretary post has been vacant since February, when Jim O'Neill departed the agency. At the same time, Klomp was elevated to a senior adviser to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.

In the Truth Social post, Trump noted that Klomp's career trajectory "proves that he is a potential STAR." He said that he, Kennedy and CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., chose Klomp as a nominee "together.".

Recent findings suggest that "Chris is a Strong and Inspiring Leader and a Highly Successful Entrepreneur," Trump wrote in the post. "Everywhere Chris goes, he earns TRUST. He is a person of principle, and is deeply committed to serving the AMERICAN People — and fixing our broken Healthcare System.".

Industry observers note that >Michael Wagner, MD, the President and Chief Executive Officer of Care New England Health System (CNE), will step down as CEO and transition to become Chair of the Board of Directors. The Board has begun the process to search for CNE’s new CEO and President, aiming to have new leadership by early 2027.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Wagner joined Care New England in 2022, and he was responsible for implementing an Epic electronic health record program and a strategic planning initiative. Wagner also secured $100 million in capital in order to expand the system and restored the organization to positive operating performance. He intends to remain President and CEO until the successor has been selected and onboarded, which will ensure a smooth transition.

Gary Furtado, the current Chair of the CNE board, will continue to serve in his role until the transition is complete. Furtado mentioned in their release that: “Mike’s leadership has been transformative for Care Upcoming England. His vision, commitment, and steady leadership have strengthened the organization clinically, strategically, and financially. The Board is grateful for his service as CEO and pleased that he will continue to support the organization as Board Chair.”.

>Rush University System for Health and Rush University Medical Center announced today that Omar Lateef, D.O., president and CEO, intends to retire from his role in June 2027. The Rush Board of Directors also announced that it will begin a national search for the next system leader in early fall.

In a recent development, lateef has been connected to Rush for over 25 years, completing his fellowship training in Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine at Rush University Medical Center in 2005 and joining the faculty afterwards. In 2019, he became the chief of pulmonary and critical care medicine, and in 2022, he became the CEO of the system.

Recent findings suggest that in these leadership positions, Lateef led Rush’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic, earning both him and the system widespread recognition. Under Lateef’s leadership, Rush University Medical Center’s standing among the nation’s premier academic medical centers has grown significantly, including repeated placement on the U.S. News & World Report Honor Roll, according to the organization. He helped establish national benchmarks for quality and safety through Rush’s leadership in Vizient quality outcomes.

It has been revealed that “Omar’s career at Rush exemplifies extraordinary dedication to our mission and our patients,” noted William Downe, Chair of the Rush University System for Health Board of Directors. “From his arrival as a fellow more than two decades ago to his service as President and CEO, he has helped shape Rush into the organization it is today.”.

>Madeline Bell, the CEO of Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP), will retire on October 1, 2026, after almost 40 years with the organization. CHOP's current president, Joseph (Joe) Mitchell, M.D., will succeed her.

It has been revealed that bell, who has served as CEO for 11 years, announced her intent to retire in 2024, beginning the search for CHOP’s fresh leader. In April 2025, Mitchell joined CHOP and began to work closely alongside Bell, the Board, and their C-suite to ensure a smooth transition.

Mitchell brings over 20 years of healthcare leadership experience, including roles at both Boston Children’s Hospital and Franciscan Children’s Hospital. At Franciscan, he secured approvals and capital to support its 10-year institutional master blueprint. Prior to this, he worked at McKinsey & Organization for 14 years, including seven years as partner.

Recent findings suggest that “Joe brings a fresh perspective, a patient-first approach and a strong strategic mindset," Greg Davis, chairman of CHOP’s board, remarked in the announcement. "We are confident he will guide CHOP into its next chapter with continued excellence and impact.”.

>Kevin Leahy, the CEO of nonprofit Catholic healthcare ministry Franciscan Alliance, will step down from his position on December 31.

He plans to stay with Franciscan as an internal consultant until the end of 2027, to facilitate the leadership transition. Following this, he will retire after 48 years of service at Franciscan.

"It is our responsibility to continue Christ’s ministry in our Franciscan tradition by serving the needs of all who seek healing of body, mind and spirit, especially the most vulnerable among us," Leahy said in a statement.

>MultiCare Health System announced its CEO, William (Bill) Robertson, will retire on Dec. 31. The current president, Florence Chang, will become the health system's newly introduced President and CEO beginning on Jan.1 2027.

Chang and Robertson will continue to work closely together this year to ensure a smooth transition.

Robertson has been part of the MultiCare team since 2014, serving as CEO since 2022 and growing MultiCare to become the largest community-based nonprofit health system in the region. He was largely responsible for their expansion across Washington state, creating a comprehensive and clinically integrated system there.

It has been revealed that chang joined MultiCare in 2006 as senior vice president and chief information officer. She has won multiple accolades for MultiCare, including the HIMSS Davies Organizational Award of Excellence. As executive vice president and chief operating officer, she was responsible for the smooth operation of eight hospitals and over 180 clinics.

Industry observers note that “On behalf of the Board of Directors, I want to thank Bill Robertson for his extraordinary leadership and the lasting impact he has had on MultiCare,” stated John Wiborg, board chair for MultiCare Health System, in the announcement. “As MultiCare moves forward into this next chapter, the board has full confidence and trust in Florence Chang as she steps into this leadership role. She is a highly effective servant leader with a great passion for MultiCare’s mission, as well as a deep knowledge of the organization’s capabilities and areas of opportunity.”.

>Komodo Health changed its leadership structure as part of the company's long-term vision for enterprise-wide adoption of AI. Miles Ennis, former chief operating officer, has been appointed as president, while co-founder, Web Sun, will assume the role of co-CEO. They will both work alongside co-founder and CEO Arif Nathoo, M.D.

Ennis initially joined Komodo Health as chief revenue officer in 2024, leading one of the strongest growth periods in organization history and accelerating the adoption of Marmot, which is an AI-native platform that builds evidence sets for complex questions, according to the company. In his new role as President, he will continue to scale Komodo's growth opportunities, while aligning innovation with industry needs and strengthening the company’s execution.

In the firm's recent press release, both Sun and Nathoo emphasize that healthcare is moving in the direction of full AI adoption, as opposed to the previous phase of AI experimentation. Sun further states that “Miles has consistently demonstrated the ability to connect strategy, product innovation, customer needs, and execution, a capability that becomes even more important as AI reshapes what is possible in healthcare and Life Sciences.".

Sources indicate that >Jamie Sharp, M.D. and Chris Rigg have joined Strive Health's executive team. The value-based kidney care company tapped Sharp as its upcoming chief medical officer and Rigg joined as chief financial officer. Sharp will oversee the clinical strategy, while Rigg will assist with scaling the business and deploying new AI technologies.

In a recent development, sharp previously served as chief medical officer at dementia care platform Rippl, and she held senior executive roles at Aetna, naviHealth and Evolent Health. "Drawing on this experience, Sharp will advance clinical outcomes and care model transformation at Strive," organization executives said in a press release.

Rigg most recently served as chief financial officer and senior vice president of commercial health benefits at Elevance Health, supporting more than 32 million consumers across individual and employer group projects. In his early career, he was a healthcare-focused analyst at Deutsche Bank, Susquehanna International Group and Merrill Lynch.

"Sharp and Rigg’s leadership will help accelerate Strive’s ability to deliver measurable outcomes for patients, providers and payers as Strive continues to expand its value-based kidney care model nationwide," Chris Riopelle, CEO and co-founder, mentioned in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that >R1, a healthcare revenue management leader, announced that Eric Tagliere will join the firm as Chief Information Officer. During his over 30-year career, Tagliere has served as Chief Technology Officer for both Humana and Marriott, leading both companies’ technological integration.

At Humana, Tagliere spearheaded operations to advance their cloud and technology modernization strategy, according to the company’s press release. At Marriott, he was a key part of the technological integration of Starwood Hotels & Resorts and oversaw digital engineering. In his latest role at R1, Tagliere will assist in R1’s transformation “from a labor-first to technology-first paradigm.” This work is in line with R1’s pioneering Healthcare Revenue Operating System that combines AI with human intelligence to improve the revenue cycle.

In a recent development, in his statement, Chief Executive Officer of R1, Joe Flanagan states, “I am pleased to welcome Eric to R1 as we continue to strengthen our technology capabilities and position the Company for long-term, AI-enabled growth. With more than three decades of experience leading large-scale technology transformations, Eric is a proven leader who brings unique insights and capabilities to advance our technology strategy.”.

>Travis Moore will join Xealth, a leader in digital health, as the company's upcoming Chief Revenue Officer. As CRO, Moore will lead Xealth’s revenue organization, expanding their overall footprint in healthcare, according to their recent press release.

Industry observers note that moore brings over 20 years of health technology leadership experience to Xealth, in fields including product management, marketing and sales. In previous roles, including as SVP of Sales & Growth at Kyruus, he oversaw the addition of commercial teams, revenue growth, organization and execution. In his statement, Moore says “Xealth has a unique opportunity to provide the missing link for digital health expansion, and now with the backing and broader vision of Samsung Health, I’m looking forward to helping our commercial team scale that impact.”.

Industry observers note that >During an induction ceremony at the Healthcare Financial Management Association (HFMA) conference, Matthew Cox officially assumed the role of National Chair. HFMA is a non-profit, nonpartisan organization that strives to offer finance professionals in healthcare spaces with guidance.

Recent findings suggest that as chair, Cox aims to prioritize collaboration and community building to take on healthcare industry challenges. As CFO of Corewell Health, Cox focuses on making care and coverage affordable while maintaining financial integrity of the system, the organization noted. C. Ann Jordan, president and CEO of HFMA states that this expertise, and his “dedication to supporting healthcare leaders nationwide make him exceptionally well suited to serve as HFMA’s next chair.”.

Other executives joining HFMA as Board officers and members are as follows:.

Chair-Elect Marcus Whitney, CHFP, co-founder and CEO of Jumpstart Health.

Secretary-Treasurer Scott R Harwig, CPA, CMA, MBA, Executive Vice President and CFO at BJC Health System.

Board Members (three-year term ending in 2029).

Ash Shehata, Managing Director at Impact Advisors.

Kevin Smith, CFO of SSM Health.

Jeremy Friese, MD, Founder, Chairman, and CEO of Humata Health.

Industry observers note that >Morrison Foerster, a top global law firm, confirmed the addition of two latest partners in the firm's Intellectual Property Litigation Group and Life Sciences + Healthcare divisions. Ching Lee Fukuda and Tom Broughan provide nearly five decades of combined experience in patent and trade secret law regarding medical devices, medtech, life sciences, and technology.

Sources indicate that fukuda previously served as Sidley Austin’s co-leader of global IP litigation and a member of their Global Life Sciences leadership team. She was a partner there for over a decade, winning trial victories before district courts, the Federal Circuit, the International Trade Commission and the Patent Trial and Appeal Board. Fukuda’s work has been recognized by many legal publications, and she was named Patent Lawyer of the Year by Women in Business Law Americas in 2024.

It has been revealed that broughan also joins Morrison Foerster from Sidley Austin, bringing similar experience in IP litigation in district court. In Patent Trial and Appeal Board proceedings, he regularly serves as a lead counsel and has been recognized in Best Lawyers for his work there. The two of them have worked together extensively, according to Morrison Foerster’s press release.

Brian Nash, the chair of Morrison Foerster’s global Intellectual Property Group, notes that Fukuda and Broughan will continue to work together to “enhance and expand our IP litigation footprint.”.

>According to a recent LinkedIn post, Maynd Jolly has been named the CFO of Health Care Delivery for CVS Health. Previously, he worked as CFO and SVP of Growth and Client Partnerships at enGen, and Global CFO of Digital Oncology and Head of Finance at Enterprise Services.

> The American Medical Association has named Sandra Adamson Fryhofer, M.D., as its next president-elect, a decision that comes as the current holder of that title, Willie Underwood III, M.D., takes the place of outgoing president Bobby Mukkamala, M.D.

In a recent development, fryhofer is a board-certified internal medicine physician with a full-time practice in Atlanta and an adjust associate professor of medicine role at Emory University School of Medicine. She's been a member of the group's House of Delegates since 1999, elected to its Board of Trustees in 2018 and served as the board's chair from 2022 to 2023. She also previously had leading roles at the American College of Physicians as its president and a member of its Board of Regents.

It has been revealed that fryhofer has been a prominent voice in public health. Alongside serving as the AMA's liaison to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (CDC ACIP), she has been a regular medical correspondent and contributor for CNN and Medscape.

“Medicine is at its best when we put patients first and remain guided by science and evidence," Fryhofer said in the organization's announcement. "We have a tremendous opportunity to improve public health and ensure every patient has access to high-quality care. I am honored to serve as president-elect as we continue that work together.”.

According to recent reports, the AMA's members elect presidents for one-year terms that turnover every June during its Annual Meeting of the House of Delegates. Underwood, a urologic surgeon with expertise in healthcare disparities and policy, was selected in last year's vote and will begin his term this week.

In a recent development, >Rajneesh Kumar is joining Staritas, an independent health supply chain data provider, as the firm's new Chief Technology Officer. It marks the company’s first major leadership hire and demonstrates Staritas’ commitment to investing in decision making technology, according to a press release.

Staritas’ CEO, Emmet O’Gara states: “Raj has the technical depth and operational leadership to accelerate our AI investments, expand our platform, and advance our mission of helping healthcare leaders make every choice clear, and we are thrilled to be adding him to our team.” His twenty-five years of experience in enterprise technology transformation leadership will allow him to accelerate product innovation that assists organizations in their informed decision-making process.

Recent findings suggest that >Transcarent, an access platform for high quality, affordable medical and pharmaceutical care, confirmed that Anjali Jameson joined the tech giant as Chief Product Officer. In previous roles, she led product and technology teams at Rally Health, UnitedHealth Group and Apple, building digital health products that serve employers, payers and providers.

Jameson will utilize her background to oversee Transcarent’s WayFinding platform, which is “the first agentic AI-powered health and care platform designed to guide owners through the healthcare system and take action.” This platform aims to improve quality of care for self-insured employers by offering an easily navigable healthcare experience.

In the organization’s press release, Glen Tullman, CEO of Transcarent, noted that, “She understands how to use AI to do what technology has done in every other industry - deliver higher quality at dramatically lower costs - and how to bring that to health and care.” This move will position Transcarent to continue leading in AI powered healthcare solutions, executives mentioned.

It has been revealed that >AdvancedMD, a cloud-based healthcare software provider, appointed Stephanie Cho as Chief Marketing Officer and unveiled Move Care Forward, a brand platform that gives independent practices tools to reduce administrative work and focus on patient care. Cho’s appointment and this launch will power accelerated investment in the tech giant, AdvancedMD said in a press release.

Cho formerly worked as the vice president of marketing at Simple Practice, leading customer marketing for their mental health care platform and delivering a multi-million-dollar revenue impact. She has previously held marketing leadership roles at Wells Fargo and American Express, and she holds an MBA from Stanford Graduate School of Business.

“She’s the right leader to make sure every practice in ambulatory care knows what AdvancedMD can do for them — and that Move Care Forward isn’t a tagline, it’s how we operate,” says AdvancedMD CEO Amanda Sharp.

>Ben Nielsen will succeed the retiring CEO of Ridgeview Medical Center, Mike Phelps. Ridgeview, a nonprofit regional health care system that serves part of the Twin Cities, initiated a comprehensive process in early 2026 to select the organization's latest President and CEO.

According to the Board, in this process, they “recognized Ben’s strategic capabilities, operational leadership and his experience developing and implementing many of Ridgeview’s key business priorities.” He has held multiple leadership roles at Ridgeview from 2010 onwards, including as chief operating officer, where he coordinated the health system’s ambulatory operations across campuses and locations.

Sources indicate that mike Phelps will remain with Ridgeview through Jan. 2, 2027, to assist with a smooth transition. He emphasizes that “Ben’s character and appreciation for our strong culture — centered on ensuring everyone we care for matters here — will help sustain our commitment to caring for our communities while keeping Ridgeview a strong, healthy organization where staff can invest their valuable time and careers.”.

>Anant Vinjamoori, M.D., will serve as the fresh Chief Medical Officer for the Hims brand, an online comprehensive care platform. With more than a decade of clinical and executive experience, Vinjamoori brings expertise in preventive and longevity care that incorporates diagnostic and therapeutic technologies.

Industry observers note that prior to joining Hims, he founded Next Generation Medicine, which combines medical education with AI technology to assist clinicians with incorporating longevity medicine. He is also the author of several peer-reviewed publications, and Vinjamoori received his MD from Harvard Medical School and his MBA from Harvard Business School.

In a recent development, >The Melanoma Research Alliance (MRA), a nonprofit funder of melanoma research, announced that beginning on July 1, 2026, Stephanie Kauffmann will serve as the organization's Chief Executive Officer. Joining MRA in 2022 as Chief Operating Officer and President, she oversaw growth in research investment and philanthropic and corporate partnerships.

It has been revealed that kauffman will replace Marc Hulbert, Ph.D., who is leaving MRA to become CEO of the National Kidney Foundation. The Board recognized Dr. Hulbert’s contribution to strengthening the position of MRA as a melanoma research funding leader, and notes that he will continue to serve as a member of MRA's Scientific Advisory Panel.

According to Debra Black, Co-Founder and Chair of the Melanoma Research Alliance, in Kauffman’s previous role she “has earned the trust and respect of our Board, staff, researchers, donors, and patient community through her leadership, vision, and unwavering commitment to our mission.” Under Kauffman’s leadership, MRA plans to continue expanding their investments in groundbreaking rare melanoma research and patient centered innovation to improve conditions for patients worldwide.

>Ardent Health President and CEO Marty Bonick "has stepped down to pursue other opportunities," the for-profit health system revealed this week. Replacing him immediately is Dave Caspers, who had been serving as chief operating officer.

Recent findings suggest that bonick helmed the firm through a string of challenges, including the COVID-19 pandemic and its 2024 initial public offering. Board Chairman Mark Sotir noted that work in the announcement and said the former head executive had positioned Ardent "for sustained long-term growth and help[ed] build a strong foundation as the Company continues to navigate industry headwinds with a focus on disciplined execution. We wish him all the best in his next chapter.".

Caspers, meanwhile, joined Ardent in March 2025 but has spent decades in operational roles. These include senior healthcare leadership positions at Walmart Health, Banner Health and Target. He's spent the past year in the weeds of Ardent's IMPACT (Improve Margins, Performance, Agility and Care Transformation) Program.

Sources indicate that "Over the past year, I have had the privilege of working closely with Marty, whose leadership and guidance have been instrumental in laying the solid footing on which Ardent Health now stands," stated Caspers, who has also joined Ardent's board. "Today, Ardent Health and our best-in-class team are well-positioned to accelerate our next phase of growth, and I am eager to build on this momentum with a continued focus on delivering high-quality care to the communities we serve.”.

>Drew Altman, M.D., founding president and CEO of the influential heath policy research, polling and news nonprofit KFF, will retire from his roles at the end of this year.

He formed the organization in 1990 out of the Henry J. Kaiser Family Foundation, and has since expanded its scope to include the country's largest newsroom focused on health policy, KFF Health News.

“With two small grandkids in Sacramento and Atlanta and another on the way, after what will be almost 37 years of very hands-on leadership since I founded KFF, and with KFF at the apex of its effectiveness, and the opportunity for a perfect transition, the clock in my head is telling me it’s time,” Altman mentioned in this week's announcement.

Following the recommendation of a search committee, KFF has unanimously appointed two in-house leaders to take on Altman's titles: Larry Levitt, at the moment executive vice president for health policy, as CEO; and Mollyann Brodie, Ph.D., currently executive vice president and chief operating officer, as president.

The pair have a combined six decades of experience at KFF already under their belt, and will take on board positions with their newly introduced roles. They will work with Altman to ensure a smooth transition through the end of the year, officially stepping into his shoes in January 2027.

>Visory Health, a prescription savings program, has promoted two executives: Alexandra Robertson to chief growth officer, and Brittney Tierce to chief technology officer.

Industry observers note that robertson started as vice president of growth, driving the organization's expansion and presence in more than 38,000 pharmacies nationwide. She will now oversee growth strategy, partnership development and program innovation.

"Visory is positioned to redefine what prescription access looks like for underserved populations, making affordability and access the norm, not the exception," Robertson mentioned in a press release shared in advance with Fierce Healthcare.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, Tierce created the tech underlying Visory. She will now drive the tech strategy company-wide, including security, tech and AI innovation.

Sources indicate that "Technology should be a bridge, not a barrier," Tierce mentioned in the announcement. "My focus is raising that bar continuously by creating smarter systems, faster delivery and infrastructure that scales access to the communities we serve.".

It has been revealed that > Healthcare AI tech giant Abridge brought on board a new chief technology officer, San Oo, as it expands its technology into more health systems. Oo joins Abridge after previously holding leadership roles at Slack and Notion, two popular workplace and productivity software tools.

In a recent development, at Notion, Oo set engineering goals and directions, with a strong focus on reliability, developer velocity and agentic engineering, according to an Abridge press release. At Slack, he helped build the engineering organization during the "hypergrowth years" that defined modern workplace collaboration. Earlier, he served as CTO at ShopBack, a unicorn in the Asia-Pacific region. He was also a founding member of two companies that were later acquired: Mumbo Inc., acquired by LinkedIn in 2012, and Astro Technology, acquired by Slack in 2018.

"The platforms San helped build altered the texture of work with thoughtful technology and exceptional craft that facilitate human connection,” Shiv Rao, M.D., CEO and founder of Abridge, mentioned in a statement. “Healthcare is the next industry that needs that kind of care and platform-level rethink, and San is the rare engineering leader who's done it multiple times.".

Recent findings suggest that abridge is rapidly scaling its AI scribe and clinical decision support technology. It is live in more than 270 of the largest health systems in the U.S., including Duke Health, Johns Hopkins Medicine, Sutter Health and Yale New Haven Health. The platform will support more than 100 million patient conversations in 2026.

"I've spent my career building products and platforms that people love to use that are secure and reliable. Now I want to do the same for healthcare, where the stakes are even higher,” Oo mentioned in a statement. “Abridge already sits at the center of the most key moment in healthcare, the conversation between a clinician and a patient. The opportunity now is to extend that intelligence across the entire system.".

> Alignment Healthcare has announced multiple leadership changes that it says will power up the company for long-term growth.

In the role, Konowiecki will provide critical enterprise-wide leadership as the team looks to build scale, Alignment noted in the announcement. Konowiecki is a veteran healthcare executive.

“Together, these leadership additions strengthen Alignment’s operating model and position the tech giant well for sustained growth and execution at scale,” Kao noted in the announcement.

Premier has the scale, the data and the relationships to help providers make better decisions and deliver better outcomes. This is where we can make the greatest impact.”.

In his new role, Billioux will spearhead Cityblock's clinical strategy and care operations as the company looks to continue advancing its care model.

> Blue Shield of California has named Hayley Park as its fresh senior vice president and chief pharmacy officer.

In the role, Park will lead the charge on Blue Shield's Pharmacy Care Reimagined initiative, which eschews traditional pharmacy benefit management models for an "unbundled" approach that leans on multiple solutions to offer different elements of the benefit.

Blue Shield said Park brings more than 25 years of experience to the position, and that she served most recently at Kaiser Permanente Northern California as president of pharmacy operations and services.

“What drew me to Blue Shield is that it’s a mission-driven nonprofit health strategy that’s committed to improving member health and their lives—not just lowering costs for medications,” Park said. “As pharmacy care shifts to support individuals in a more connected and personalized way, I am excited to join an organization that is transforming healthcare to make it more accessible for everyone.”.

That approach brough national recognitions and designations to its facilities, plus new developments like a genomic program bringing precision medicine into patient care.

> Centene Corporation has created two latest positions to lead key segments of its insurance business.

The company remarked in an announcement that it has named Daniel Finke as group president for markets and commercial and Michael Carson as its group president for Medicare and specialty. Both executives will report to CEO Sarah London, per Centene.

Industry observers note that finke is an experienced insurance executive and will be tasked with overseeing and scaling the firm's Medicaid and commercial segments. > Cory Mead was named CEO of HCA Florida Palms West Hospital, effective March 30. With more than a decade in leadership roles with HCA Healthcare, Mead most recently served as CEO of HCA Florida Woodmont Hospital.

Recent findings suggest that elevance said the new leaders will help expand and scale Carelon, which reaches over 90 million healthcare consumers. The Health Benefits segment provides coordinated solutions to more than 45 million Elevance members.

CareFirst, meanwhile, is a nonprofit with 3.5 million members primarily living in the District of Columbia, Maryland and Northern Virginia. On deck is Winjie Miao, who is presently senior executive vice president and chief operating officer. She's set for a promotion to president on April 5, priming her to step in as CEO in September when Berdan steps away. Miao has been Texas Health Resources' chief operating officer since 2022, but first joined the organization in 2000.

#30062. Breaking: 2027 Subaru Forester Wilderness Hybrid Is The Happy Wanderer

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1547 w)

Breaking: 2027 Subaru Forester Wilderness Hybrid Is The Happy Wanderer

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1547 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that subaru has a knack for making its vehicles incredibly capable right out of the box, but it also knows how to add extra garnishes to take things to the next level, like when it Wilderness-ified the standard Forester by bumping up the ride height and giving it all-terrain tires, more underbody protection, tougher exterior body panels and a slew of copper accents.
  • Industry observers note that the hybrid powertrain offers more power, better fuel economy and a more refined drivetrain experience than the standard Wilderness' 2.5-liter boxer four-cylinder, while also affording the Forester a bit more off-road capability thanks to the added torque of an electric motor.
  • It has been revealed that it makes it a bit hard to understand why the regular Forester Wilderness exists at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that subaru has a knack for making its vehicles incredibly capable right out of the box, but it also knows how to add extra garnishes to take things to the next level, like when it Wilderness-ified the standard Forester by bumping up the ride height and giving it all-terrain tires, more underbody protection, tougher exterior body panels and a slew of copper accents. Now Subaru is taking that notch up another notch by hybrid-ifying the Wilderness-ified Forester, resulting in — you guessed it — the 2027 Forester Wilderness Hybrid.

Industry observers note that the hybrid powertrain offers more power, better fuel economy and a more refined drivetrain experience than the standard Wilderness' 2.5-liter boxer four-cylinder, while also affording the Forester a bit more off-road capability thanks to the added torque of an electric motor. Making things even sweeter is the fact that choosing the hybrid only adds $1,000 to the Forester Wilderness' MSRP, a delta that Subaru says will be overcome in just 2 years, or about 30,000 miles.

It has been revealed that it makes it a bit hard to understand why the regular Forester Wilderness exists at all. The added fuel efficiency and comfort mean the Forester Wilderness Hybrid can do a seemingly endless amount of driving, exploring and wandering around, and it's absolutely happy to do so.

In a recent development, full Disclosure: Subaru flew me out to central California, put me up in a very nice hotel and fed me, all so I could drive the 2027 Forester Wilderness Hybrid. They sourced me a lovely 2026 Ascent Touring to drive all the way from Chicago to New York when every flight in the U.S. was grounded, and I faced the prospect of spending a few days sleeping on the floor at O'Hare. For that reason, I am eternally grateful to both Aaron Cole and Miranda Jimenez.

There isn't much of a difference between the Forester Wilderness and Forester Wilderness Hybrid outside of the hybrid powertrain, but it does a hell of a lot to transform the character of Subie's compact crossover. Like in the non-Wilderness Forester Hybrid, Subaru teamed up an Atkinson-Miller-cycle 2.5-liter boxer four-cylinder with two motor-generator units inside the continuously variable transmission. One is used to stop and start the gas engine and charge the battery, while the other handles regenerative braking and sends actual drive power to all four wheels. They're fed by a 1.1-kWh battery that lives where the spare tire once was, which may be disappointing to some off-road enthusiasts who also love busting tires. However, that positioning means the hybrid has the same exact amount of rear cargo room as a regular Forester, which normal people are going to appreciate.

They're also going to appreciate the extra power. The Forester Wilderness Hybrid pumps out 194 horsepower, a 14-hp improvement over the normal Forester Wilderness. Subaru gives no combined torque figures, but the gas motor puts out 154 pound-feet, and the electric motor produces its own 199 lb-ft. Either way you slice it, the numbers are stronger than the 178 lb-ft of torque from the normal Forester Wilderness. In typical Subaru fashion, the symmetrical all-wheel-drive system sends internal-combustion power to all four wheels — unlike the RAV4, which has no mechanical connection between the front and rear wheels — and that makes a huge difference off-road.

Gas mileage has never been a Subie strong suit, but the hybrid's fuel economy is also much improved to go along with its added performance. According to the EPA, the Forester Wilderness Hybrid will get 33 mpg city, 29 mpg highway and 31 mpg combined, improvements of 9 mpg, 1 mpg and 5 mpg, respectively. The EPA-expected driving range is also bumped up from 432 miles to 515 miles. Happy wanderer, indeed.

Recent findings suggest that the Forester Wilderness' lovably ugly looks are still present, and the hybrid maintains the same 9.3 inches of ground clearance as its gas-only counterpart. It also gets the same 235/60R17 Yokohama Geolander All-Terrain tires, raised roof rails with 800 pounds of capacity, bronze interior and exterior design elements, and redesigned front and rear bumpers with increased approach, departure and breakover angles.

In a recent development, hill descent control and Subaru's X-Mode system with Snow/Dirt and Deep Snow/Mud settings mean it's pretty much impossible to get this thing stuck; those two modes can basically be summed up as stuck and absolutely biffed. They allow the Forester Wilderness Hybrid to do pretty much anything off-road; at the very least, it can do things far beyond what anyone would expect from a car without a locking rear differential.

According to recent reports, the majority of the time I drove the Forester Wilderness Hybrid was without any pavement below me on the seemingly endless acreage of Rancho Quien Sabe, and I've got to say, it was nearly boring in the way the SUV saw any obstacle in front of it and just traversed it without fuss or hesitation. The Forester happily trudged along, unbothered by what sort of terrain it was forced to deal with. In the rare moments where I found myself a bit more stuck than I thought I should be, all that was needed was a little bit of extra power, and the added torque of the electric motor pulled me out with ease. Aiding in that was the 180-degree front view monitor that helped me see where I was going, but while it was undoubtedly helpful, I can't help but think the resolution left a bit to be desired.

I'm no fool, and I know that for all of its off-road prowess, the Forester Wilderness Hybrid will spend the majority of its life on road. Luckily, it's quite good there. Subaru did a good job of insulating the cabin so not too much road noise or rattly boxer sounds enter the cabin, and the more powerful drivetrain means it's even better at getting up to speed than the slightly anemic normal Forester Wilderness. It also comes as standard with all sorts of safety features, courtesy of Subaru's EyeSight suite of tech like emergency lane-keeping assist, emergency steering assist, blind spot detection, rear cross-traffic alert, reverse automated braking, and full-speed adaptive cruise control. (I was able to truly experience the highs of EyeSight during my 820-mile drive home in the Ascent).

In a recent development, changes to the Forester Wilderness Hybrid are decidedly minimal on the inside, too. Drivers are still treated to a 10-way power seat, and in front of the steering wheel is a fairly customizable 12.3-inch gauge cluster screen that can display a full-screen map. Beside that in the middle is an 11.6-inch vertical infotainment screen, which is getting harder and harder to justify as the years pass — especially now that the newly introduced Outback is out, and its system is so good. Luckily, you can hook up wireless Apple CarPlay or Android Auto, but even they are a bit laggy, and glare is still prevalent when it's super sunny.

Industry observers note that screen woes aside, the animal-free interior is fairly well appointed for this type of vehicle. Dual-zone climate controls, a panoramic-ish sunroof, TomTom navigation, a heated steering wheel, four heated seats, a power tailgate, all-weather floor mats and an 11-speaker Harman/Kardon stereo are all standard on the Forester Wilderness Hybrid.

In a recent development, space is also very solid for the class. I had more than enough room to fit comfortably behind myself at 6-foot-1, and there's 33.1 cubic feet of room behind the second row for all of your Outdoor Activity Crap. If you somehow need more room for your Outdoor Activity Crap, drop the second row, and that space increases to 64.1 cubic feet. If that somehow still isn't enough for your Outdoor Activity Crap, you can strap 800 pounds to the roof (statically). There are enough interesting materials choices and quality-feeling items that you won't feel too silly about the cost.

Subaru states the 2027 Forester Wilderness Hybrid starts at $41,970, including destination, and that's pretty much where pricing ends, as well. Outside of a few optional paint colors, there aren't any packages you'll be able to add to the Wilderness Hybrid. What you see is what you get. Nice and easy. And as I mentioned before, it's just $1,000 more than the standard Forester Wilderness. There's a hard deal to beat.

In a recent development, the Forester Hybrid Wilderness has a real can-do attitude to it. It's a real billy goat of a car — one that takes a licking and keeps on kicking, happily coming back for more. When driving, it was as if the Forester was whistling a little tune to itself as I mashed the throttle, forcing it to traverse up a hill a compact crossover has no business going up.

In a recent development, no, it doesn't have the best infotainment in the world and it's not a classically "beautiful" vehicle, but it has something most cars don't: character. The Forester Wilderness Hybrid wants to get lost with you, and all you need to do is make sure you've got the time to get lost with it, because with over 500 miles of driving range, you can get lost for a long, long time.

From Social Leasing to Social Fleets: A Proposed Law Lends Credibility to the Goal of One Million Affordable Electric Cars

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (594 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, social leasing could soon change in scale, name, and business model.
  • It has been revealed that several presidential candidates have made reaching one million vehicles (or even more) one of the hallmarks of their campaigns¹.
  • Sources indicate that the current system cannot simply be scaled up twentyfold.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, social leasing could soon change in scale, name, and business model. The bill introduced by MP Christine Arrighi aims to create a public service offering one million “low-cost electric vehicles” (ALM). Scheduled for December 3rd in the National Assembly, its examination is expected to place at the heart of the debate a now crucial question: how to make social leasing sustainable and widespread?

It has been revealed that several presidential candidates have made reaching one million vehicles (or even more) one of the hallmarks of their campaigns¹. While this convergence is excellent news, the battle of figures notes nothing about how to achieve this goal.

Sources indicate that the current system cannot simply be scaled up twentyfold. Its cost per vehicle, intermittent financing, imperfect social targeting, lack of a guaranteed solution after three years, and the resale risks borne by dealerships are all structural limitations. The 2026 edition also revealed its dependence on Renault and Stellantis, which can at any time restrict volumes to favor more profitable traditional sales.

The proposed law changes its approach. Sponsored by MP Christine Arrighi, it draws inspiration from the proposals of T&E France and Bernard Julien, stemming from their study on the future of social leasing, published in June 2026.

In this new model, the government would directly purchase the vehicles at an average net cost of €15,000. These vehicles would be kept for twelve years in a public fleet and leased successively to one or more households for an average monthly rent of €150 before being resold. The day-to-day management of the fleet would be delegated to groups of public or private operators within the local areas.

In a recent development, the initial investment to build the fleet would be financed by borrowing, with a maximum outstanding amount of €7.8 billion in 2035. Lease payments and resales, supplemented by €350 million in annual public support (equivalent to the current social leasing budget), would cover service costs and repay the debt within eighteen years. By then, the system would be self-financing, and the state would own one million cars worth approximately €10 billion.

“This model is much more beneficial for public finances,” explains Diane Strauss, director of T&E France. “It requires an initial funding effort, but it eventually pays for itself. Instead of subsidizing at a loss, we build up an asset that generates its own revenue. This is what makes the move to a million vehicles financially viable.”.

Sources indicate that in addition to providing long-term protection for low-income motorists against rising and volatile fuel prices, the proposal represents a genuine industrial planning policy. The announcement of a public order for two million vehicles over twenty years (including fleet renewal) would indeed give the French automotive sector the visibility necessary to invest and prepare for the future.

“This will also allow us to direct our production towards the vehicles that households truly need: affordable, fuel-efficient, repairable electric cars, produced in France and Europe,” concludes Léo Larivière, automotive transition expert at T&E France. “This proposal must now open a substantive discussion among all stakeholders. It is high time to prepare the next steps for one of the rare examples of policies that reconcile climate, social justice, and industrial planning.”.

Industry observers note that ¹ Raphaël Glucksmann and Marine Tondelier aim for one million vehicles. Jean-Luc Mélenchon proposes a public fleet of 1.4 million cars by 2032, and François Ruffin raises the target to three million. Gabriel Attal and Dominique de Villepin also advocate expanding social leasing, without specifying a target.

#30059. Stronger flu shot linked to nearly 55% lower Alzheimer's risk

📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1350 w)

Stronger flu shot linked to nearly 55% lower Alzheimer's risk

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1350 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A higher dose of the annual flu vaccine may offer older adults an unexpected benefit: a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease.
  • Recent findings suggest that in a large study led by researchers at UTHealth Houston, adults ages 65 and older who received a high-dose influenza vaccine were less likely to develop Alzheimer's than those given the standard-dose version.
  • Industry observers note that the discovery grew out of an unexpected conversation between a UTHealth Houston physician and local public health officials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A higher dose of the annual flu vaccine may offer older adults an unexpected benefit: a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease.

Recent findings suggest that in a large study led by researchers at UTHealth Houston, adults ages 65 and older who received a high-dose influenza vaccine were less likely to develop Alzheimer's than those given the standard-dose version. The findings, published in the medical journal Neurology, suggest that the strength of a flu vaccine could matter for more than just protection against influenza.

Industry observers note that the discovery grew out of an unexpected conversation between a UTHealth Houston physician and local public health officials. What began as a visit to discuss earlier vaccine research eventually led scientists to investigate whether different flu vaccine doses might be associated with different levels of Alzheimer's risk.

A Surprising Connection Between Flu Vaccines and Alzheimer's.

Industry observers note that alzheimer's disease is the leading cause of dementia and an increasingly serious public health concern. In 2025, more than 7 million Americans ages 65 and older were living with the disease, representing approximately 1 in 9 people in that age group. That figure is projected to more than double by 2050.

Researchers have been exploring whether common vaccines might influence the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's. In a 2022 study, a team led by Paul Schulz, MD, found that flu vaccination was associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer's among adults 65 and older.

Schulz is a professor of neurology at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston and director of the Neurocognitive Disorders Center at UTHealth Houston Neurosciences.

Three years after that earlier investigation, Schulz and his colleagues published upcoming research examining a more specific question: Could receiving a stronger flu vaccine be associated with an even greater reduction in Alzheimer's risk?

The idea came from public health officials who had learned about the team's previous findings and invited Schulz to discuss them.

Sources indicate that "The public health department had seen our vaccine research and asked if I could come down to talk to them about it," said Schulz, who is the senior author of the study and the Rick McCord Professor in Neurology and Umphrey Family Professor in Neurodegenerative Diseases at McGovern Medical School. "We went through the findings, and they asked if there was a difference with different dosages; I was confused.".

Why Older Adults Receive Stronger Flu Shots.

Sources indicate that as people grow older, their immune systems gradually become less effective at recognizing and fighting infections. This age-related decline can make influenza particularly dangerous for seniors.

To help address that vulnerability, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends high-dose influenza vaccines as a preferred option for adults ages 65 and older. These vaccines contain four times as much influenza antigen as standard-dose shots. Antigens are the components of a vaccine that stimulate the immune system to recognize and defend against a virus.

The higher dose is designed to produce a stronger immune response in older adults, whose immune systems may respond less effectively to conventional vaccines.

Schulz had not previously realized that this stronger formulation was available.

"I was stunned that, as a physician, I didn't know a higher dose was offered," Schulz said.

Recent findings suggest that annual flu vaccination is recommended broadly, but preventing influenza is especially important for people with Alzheimer's disease. Flu infections and their complications can pose serious health risks for individuals already coping with cognitive impairment.

Before 2022, the CDC did not express a preference for one type of injectable influenza vaccine over another for people ages 65 and older. Instead, the guidance emphasized receiving a flu shot every year, regardless of the specific formulation.

According to recent reports, previous research from UTHealth Houston had already linked inactivated influenza vaccines, which use viruses that cannot cause influenza infection, to a 40% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. However, researchers had not yet determined whether a higher vaccine dose might be associated with additional benefits.

Another practical problem made the question particularly relevant. As the population of older Americans continues to grow, demand for high-dose flu vaccines sometimes exceeds the available supply. Consequently, some seniors receive standard-dose vaccines instead.

This variation gave researchers an opportunity to compare Alzheimer's outcomes among older adults who had received different formulations.

According to recent reports, "So we started looking, and sure enough, we were able to put together thousands and thousands of people over the age of 65 who got the high- or low-dose vaccine. They're more at risk for Alzheimer's than anybody else, of course, because it's age-related and we could look at high-dose versus low-dose and see if there was a difference," Schulz said.

Nearly 200,000 Adults Reveal a Significant Difference.

To investigate the potential connection, the research team analyzed data from nearly 200,000 men and women ages 65 and older.

The results indicated that people who received high-dose influenza vaccines had a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease than those who received the standard-dose formulation.

The researchers reported that standard-dose influenza vaccination was associated with a 40% reduction in Alzheimer's risk, while high-dose vaccination was linked to a reduction of nearly 55%.

The association was particularly pronounced among women, who appeared to experience a greater reduction in Alzheimer's risk with the stronger vaccine.

These findings add to growing evidence of a possible relationship between influenza vaccination and brain health. They also raise key questions about whether the immune response triggered by vaccination might influence biological processes involved in Alzheimer's disease.

In a recent development, however, the findings demonstrate an association rather than establishing cause and effect. Additional research is needed to determine whether high-dose flu vaccination directly reduces the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's and to understand the mechanisms that might explain the connection.

What the Findings Could Mean for Alzheimer's Prevention.

With Alzheimer's affecting millions of Americans and the number of cases expected to rise sharply in the coming decades, researchers are searching for practical ways to reduce risk.

The possibility that an existing vaccine could have benefits extending beyond influenza prevention is particularly intriguing. Unlike an entirely fresh treatment, flu vaccination is already widely used, and higher-dose formulations are specifically designed for older adults.

The new findings suggest that vaccine dosage could be an vital consideration in future studies exploring the relationship between the immune system and Alzheimer's disease.

For now, the research provides another reason to investigate the potential benefits of influenza vaccination while emphasizing the need for further studies before drawing conclusions about Alzheimer's prevention.

Research Team and Study Contributors.

Avram Samuel Bukhbinder, MD, a graduate of McGovern Medical School who is at the moment a clinical fellow in neurology at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard University, served as a corresponding author of the study.

Schulz is also a faculty member of The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center UTHealth Houston Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences.

Other contributors from McGovern Medical School included Elizabeth He, visiting scholar in the Department of Neurology; Kristofer Harris, MPH, research coordinator in the Department of Neurology; Mya Rodriguez, graduate research assistant in the Department of Neurology; Kamal Phelps, MD, an alumnus of the Department of Neurology; Jenna Thomas; Gabriela Cruz, MD, resident in the Department of Neurology; and Lauren Jhin.

Researchers from the McWilliams School of Biomedical Informatics at UTHealth Houston also participated. They included Xiaoqian Jiang, PhD, associate vice president for medical AI, chair of the Department of Health Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, and Christopher Sarofim Family Professor in Biomedical Informatics and Bioengineering; Yejin Kim, PhD, assistant professor in the Department of Health Data Science and Artificial Intelligence; Luyao Chen, researcher; and Yaobin Ling, PhD, postdoctoral research fellow.

In a recent development, materials provided by University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Share the story of the first time you ever drove a car in the comments section below.

RuPaul actually inspired this question. On social media he recently told the story of the first time he ever drove a car at 11-years-old, when he stole the keys to his dad's 1966 Toyota Corona and drove it around Cerritos, California. RuPaul describes himself as someone who's obsessed with cars, and I know most of us Jalops would describe ourselves in a similar fashion. That's why we want to know the story of the first time you ever drove a car.

According to recent reports, I'm not sure that I've even shared this story with my friends or family, but sharing it here seems like a good idea. I don't remember my exact age at the time, but I know I was in middle school, so it was definitely before I should have legally been behind the wheel. Still, I'd been practicing my driving in my conscious and unconscious mind for at least a decade before this, so I felt ready.

One fateful summer day at Model Boat Shop (don't laugh, it was really fun), a friend's older sister came to pick him up, but her boyfriend was the one who drove. Along with my brother, our conniving, car-obsessed minds hatched a brilliant proposal to strongarm this poor high school kid into letting us drive his green second-generation Nissan Altima. We convinced him it would earn him brownie points with his girlfriend if he'd let her little brother and his friends drive his car, and he bought it, hook line and sinker.

Recent findings suggest that he took us to a nearby parking lot and let us loose, and I have the most distinct memory of doing incredibly safe and not-at-all dangerous acceleration runs and panic brake evaluations in that parking lot while the owner of the car looked on in horror. Thankfully nobody got hurt and nobody got sued, but that joyous memory was the first time I drove a car. What's your story?

According to recent reports, commercial property owners invest in solar and battery storage to manage energy costs and strengthen resilience. One question can shape that investment from the start. Who pays when equipment needs repairs years after installation?

Solar Insure today expanded its SI-Commercial Suite with two fresh warranties. SI-Commercial Battery is a 20-year limited warranty for commercial battery storage systems, and SI-Commercial Total covers solar and battery storage under one warranty. Together with the existing SI-Commercial Solar warranty, these additions allow Certified Providers to offer protection tailored to each project, whether it includes solar, battery storage, or both. Solar Insure protects more than 100,000 systems nationwide.

Industry observers note that “Commercial projects are built for the long term, and their protection should reflect that,” mentioned Ara Agopian, CEO of Solar Insure. “By expanding our commercial warranty suite, we’re helping solar companies offer protection that fits the systems their customers are investing in. It’s about giving property owners greater confidence not just in the installation, but in the years of ownership that follow.”.

A failed inverter or declining battery capacity can lead to costs an owner did not budget for. Even when a manufacturer covers replacement equipment, the owner may still be responsible for labor and service costs. The expanded suite helps Certified Providers explain which repair expenses are covered so customers can evaluate their potential repair costs alongside system performance and installation price.

In a recent development, “Commercial battery owners are making a long-term investment, but some of the most significant expenses can emerge years after installation,” said Dean Chiaravallotti, Chief Revenue Officer at Solar Insure. “A battery replacement or unexpected repair can change the financial picture of a project. When providers can explain how they address those costs before the customer signs, they help buyers make a more informed investment decision. That’s the value we’re bringing to commercial storage.”.

Solar companies must become Solar Insure Certified Providers to offer SI-Commercial warranties. Certification includes a review of the manufacturer’s qualifications, business practices, and commitment to customer service.

Industry observers note that for qualifying claims, Solar Insure pays covered repair costs directly to the Certified Provider or service provider performing the work. If the original installer is no longer available, Solar Insure helps coordinate next steps, which may include identifying another qualified service provider. When a property changes hands, coverage transfers to the new owner at no cost.

“A lot can change over the life of a commercial energy system. Properties change hands, service providers change, and equipment eventually needs attention,” mentioned Chiaravallotti. “Property owners need to know what happens w          hen those changes occur. Our goal is to give them a clearer path forward, with protection and support that extend well beyond the original installation.”.

Solar companies can contact Solar Insure to learn about becoming a Certified Provider. Commercial property owners can speak with a Solar Insure Certified Provider about which warranty fits their project.

In a recent development, solar Insure is a leading provider of solar and storage warranties, focused on protecting long-term system performance and elevating accountability across the renewable energy industry. #30053. Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1538 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tick-borne illnesses are becoming increasingly common across the United States, and Lyme disease remains the most frequently reported.
  • In a recent development, now, one of the longest-running studies of Lyme disease ecology is challenging several assumptions about what makes the disease more likely to spread.
  • A new study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences brings together nine of the project's most surprising discoveries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tick-borne illnesses are becoming increasingly common across the United States, and Lyme disease remains the most frequently reported. Nearly 500,000 Americans are diagnosed each year. The infection is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, which typically reaches humans through the bite of an infected blacklegged tick. Antibiotics can treat Lyme disease, but without treatment, the infection may affect the joints, heart, and nervous system. Some patients also experience symptoms that persist over time.

In a recent development, now, one of the longest-running studies of Lyme disease ecology is challenging several assumptions about what makes the disease more likely to spread. For more than 35 years, scientists at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in Millbrook, Newly introduced York, have tracked the complicated relationships among ticks, mice, oak trees, predators, and weather. Their research has uncovered unexpected patterns that could help predict when people face greater exposure to infected ticks.

A new study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences brings together nine of the project's most surprising discoveries. The findings show how decades of observations can reveal connections that shorter studies might miss.

"On balance, these surprises have enriched our knowledge of this system, helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk," stated lead author Richard Ostfeld, a disease ecologist at the Cary Institute who leads the research program alongside Shannon LaDeau.

According to Ostfeld, the extensive data collected over the years have been essential for separating meaningful ecological patterns from coincidences and statistical fluctuations.

Industry observers note that "Studies of this depth and length are incredibly rare," said LaDeau. "This research has followed an ecological community -- including oak trees, mammals, and microorganisms -- examining how interactions like predation, parasitism, and competition shape the system over time. The evolution of understanding summarized in this paper is something you simply cannot get without such a long-term and system-focused study.".

Deer May Play a Smaller Role in Lyme Disease Risk Than Expected.

Industry observers note that when Lyme disease first gained recognition in the United States during the 1980s, white-tailed deer were considered a likely driver of rising tick populations. Hunters frequently encountered deer carrying numerous adult ticks, suggesting that areas with more deer might also produce more ticks.

Sources indicate that the reasoning seemed straightforward. Although deer cannot pass the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks, they provide blood meals for adult female ticks. Scientists suspected that larger deer populations would allow more female ticks to reproduce, eventually increasing the number of young ticks capable of spreading the infection.

But decades of monitoring have produced a different picture. On the Cary Institute's 2,000-acre forested research property in Dutchess County, Upcoming York, researchers found no statistically significant connection between deer numbers and the abundance of nymphal ticks. Nymphs are immature ticks responsible for much of the Lyme disease transmission to humans.

"We had detected a weak positive relationship between deer and subsequent nymph abundance over short subsets of the data," stated Ostfeld, "but the whole data set in its entirety shows no such thing.".

Mice Are a Much Stronger Predictor of Tick Surges.

While deer populations failed to predict the abundance of nymphal ticks, mouse populations showed a much clearer relationship.

It has been revealed that years with especially large mouse populations were followed by approximately 40% more nymphal ticks the next year. White-footed mice are particularly key because they provide excellent blood meals for tick larvae and are highly effective at transmitting Borrelia burgdorferi to those feeding on them.

Once infected as larvae, ticks can retain the bacteria as they develop into nymphs. When these nymphs take another blood meal, they can pass the infection to humans.

The findings suggest that tracking mouse populations could provide a valuable early warning of unusually high tick numbers.

How Acorns Can Predict Tick Populations Two Years Ahead.

One of the most unexpected discoveries involves something that might seem entirely unrelated to Lyme disease: acorns.

In a recent development, oak trees periodically produce exceptionally large crops of acorns in synchronized events known as acorn masting. These unusually productive years provide an abundance of food for forest rodents, allowing mouse populations to expand during the following year.

That increase in mice then supports larger numbers of young ticks. As a result, the researchers found that a particularly heavy acorn crop can reliably predict an increase in nymphal ticks two years later.

The relationship reveals a remarkable sequence of events in which the reproductive cycle of forest trees helps determine future tick abundance. It also offers researchers another potential tool for anticipating periods of greater Lyme disease exposure.

Why More Mice Don't Always Mean More Infected Ticks.

Although mouse abundance helps predict how many nymphal ticks will appear, the researchers discovered that it does not consistently predict what percentage of those ticks will carry Lyme disease bacteria.

Initially, scientists expected both measures to rise together. Because mice are efficient transmitters of B. burgdorferi, an increase in mice seemed likely to produce not only more ticks but also a greater proportion of infected ticks.

Early observations appeared to support that idea. However, as additional years of data accumulated, the apparent relationship gradually disappeared.

"It kept me up at night," remarked Ostfeld, "because it meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong.".

The explanation appears to involve the other animals that share the forest with mice. Skunks, squirrels, and opossums also serve as hosts for feeding ticks, but most are much less effective at passing the Lyme disease bacterium to them.

When these animals are abundant, more larval ticks may feed on hosts that are unlikely to infect them. This can reduce the percentage of nymphal ticks carrying the bacteria, even when mouse populations are high.

It has been revealed that "So the infection prevalence in the nymphs really depends on how all the larval tick meals are distributed across all the hosts," explained Ostfeld. "It would have been convenient if one host predicted that for us, but that has not been the case.".

This finding highlights an crucial distinction between the total number of ticks in an environment and the proportion carrying the pathogen. Predicting the risk of infection requires understanding the broader community of animals that ticks feed on, not simply counting mice.

Extreme Heat and Cold May Not Kill Ticks in the Wild.

Weather has also produced some unexpected results.

Earlier laboratory experiments suggested that exposure to intense heat or severe cold could kill blacklegged ticks. Yet observations in natural habitats revealed that ticks are surprisingly capable of surviving these conditions.

Researchers believe ticks protect themselves from temperature extremes by retreating into deeper soil layers or hiding beneath fallen leaves, where conditions are less severe than at the surface.

However, the long-term data also revealed a more complicated relationship with temperature. Years that are warmer overall tend to be followed by fewer nymphal ticks than usual, despite the ability of individual ticks to withstand short periods of extreme heat.

Industry observers note that at the same time, warmer conditions generally favor mouse populations, which can lead to more ticks. These opposing effects make it difficult to predict how changing temperatures will ultimately influence Lyme disease risk.

What 35 Years of Research Mean for Lyme Disease Prevention.

Taken together, the discoveries show that Lyme disease risk depends on a network of ecological interactions that is complicated but not entirely unpredictable.

Sources indicate that mouse abundance, for example, provides a stronger indicator of future nymphal tick numbers than deer abundance at the study site. Similarly, unusually harsh winters may not reduce tick populations as dramatically as previously expected.

By understanding these patterns, public health officials may be better equipped to anticipate periods of increased tick exposure and develop more effective prevention strategies.

Still, vital questions remain, particularly about how climate change will affect ticks, the animals they feed on, and the oak trees that influence rodent populations.

"You would expect that a warming climate, which makes life better for the mice, would eventually make life better for the ticks, but we have not seen that so far," remarked Ostfeld. "We need to know what to expect from the different manifestations of climate change, which are sometimes warmer and drier, and sometimes warmer and wetter. The time of year when it's very warm also matters to ticks, oaks, and acorn production.".

The research site in Dutchess County has undergone significant environmental changes since monitoring began in 1991. Climate shifts, changes to the surrounding landscape, and the arrival of invasive species have all altered the conditions in which the forest's plants and animals live.

Researchers intend to continue following these changes to determine how ticks and their hosts respond over time. Their work could provide increasingly valuable insights into how future environmental changes will influence human exposure to Lyme disease and other infections carried by ticks.

CMS proposes sweeping Medicare integrity rule it says will save $90B
