Can America Build More Housing Without Gutting Historic Protections? Inside the Senate’s Permitting Battle

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1400 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A sweeping permitting reform package moved closer to a final Senate vote Monday, when lawmakers voted 70–27 to limit debate on legislation that could weaken a federal safeguard for historic places.
  • At issue is Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which requires federal agencies to consider how projects they fund, approve, or permit might affect historic properties—and consult with those affected before proceeding.
  • The proposed changes would exempt most projects whose only federal connection is financial assistance, while imposing tighter deadlines and restricting legal challenges.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A sweeping permitting reform package moved closer to a final Senate vote Monday, when lawmakers voted 70–27 to limit debate on legislation that could weaken a federal safeguard for historic places.

At issue is Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which requires federal agencies to consider how projects they fund, approve, or permit might affect historic properties—and consult with those affected before proceeding.

The proposed changes would exempt most projects whose only federal connection is financial assistance, while imposing tighter deadlines and restricting legal challenges.

As the nation confronts a shortage of 4.03 million homes and an aging energy grid, supporters argue that reducing regulatory hurdles will accelerate infrastructure development. But preservation advocates warn the changes could leave communities with less influence over what gets built—and what gets lost.

Recent findings suggest that "Preservation is not a hindrance to progress," Heather Veneziano, director of Tulane University's Historic Preservation Program, told Realtor.com® during a recent walking interview through Bayou St. John, one of Newly introduced Orleans' oldest neighborhoods.

Rather than keeping neighborhoods frozen in time, she argued, preservation can help communities determine how they evolve.

"Keeping things static is impossible," Veneziano mentioned.

New Orleans provides a particularly salient standpoint from which to understand Veneziano’s perspective.

Industry observers note that the city is home to 26 nationally recognized historic districts encompassing more than 45,000 properties and roughly 40% of its urbanized area, according to the city. Indeed, its architectural heritage is so extensive that it became the only entire city included on the World Monuments Fund's Irreplaceable America list.

Veneziano helped lead the nomination, informed in part by the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina and the connections to place that could not be rebuilt elsewhere.

Sources indicate that "You lose all your really strong ties and connections to place, but also to people," she said of the communities uprooted after the devastating 2005 superstorm. "And places don't matter without people.".

But Veneziano sees the buildings themselves as part of what makes those communities viable.

In a recent development, "It's an economic driver for the community, it's housing at a basic level for the community," she mentioned. "Those are the containers for all of the services that happen in your community.".

Along Bayou St. John, Veneziano pointed to the Pitot House, built in 1799, as an example of another kind of value older buildings retain.

Its elevated living quarters reflect a time when residents built knowing water would eventually come, while its surviving materials offer lessons in constructing homes suited to Louisiana's flood risks.

"You have to build for place," she said.

Yet, those lessons might have been erased had preservationists not found a way to accommodate another pressing community need.

In 1964, the religious order that owned the property needed land for a girls' school. Rather than allow its demolition, preservationists raised money to move the house 220 feet down the street on flatbed trucks.

The compromise allowed both the school and the house to continue serving the community. And today, the deal serves as a reminder of how preservation can accommodate development rather than prevent it.

Not every historic property can be relocated, however, and the expense of finding alternatives can test even the most committed to protecting a neighborhood's housing resources.

In March, Jane Place Neighborhood Sustainability Initiative, a community land trust dedicated to permanently affordable housing, sought permission to demolish a century-old shotgun house in Mid-City.

The nonprofit argued that rehabilitation would be prohibitively expensive and higher-density construction would better serve the property.

Preservation authorities disagreed, finding insufficient evidence that the house was beyond repair. Jane Place eventually withdrew its appeal without a finalized replacement development plan.

The spat concerned local demolition rules, not Section 106. But it exposed competing interpretations of how best to protect a neighborhood's housing resources: Preserve an existing home or make room for more?

Veneziano acknowledged that unclear local requirements can frustrate homeowners trying to maintain or renovate their properties.

"If your municipality doesn't have their act together and isn't clear about what their guidelines are," she noted, "it can be very challenging to homeowners.".

In a city facing an estimated shortage of 44,000 affordable rental units, the case for preserving old buildings can be difficult to reconcile with the urgent need for newly introduced homes. But elsewhere in the Big Easy, a long-vacant public building offers another approach.

In September, a century-old firehouse reopened after decades of vacancy, transformed into seven affordable apartments above an early-childhood education center.

The mixed-use redevelopment cost approximately $8 million, including $1.35 million in state historic tax credits and $725,000 in federal disaster recovery funds.

"The Louisiana Avenue Firehouse shows us that demolition of historic buildings is not always the answer," Louisiana Housing Corporation Executive Director Kevin Delahoussaye stated.

But the very public investment that helped save the building also triggered Section 106 review—and that additional requirement is what housing advocates argue can make federally assisted developments more expensive and difficult to finance.

Their argument is simple: More reviews take more time. More time costs more money. And combined, that can make a project not worth it.

YIMBY Action, which supports the proposed Section 106 exemption, estimates that at least $10 billion annually in federal housing and community development funding could move faster under the broader permitting package, citing delays that can jeopardize financing or discourage developers from accepting public money altogether.

Veneziano emphasized that preservationists aren't simply trying to "save this fancy house." Their work, she explained, is "really community engagement"—helping residents recognize and protect histories that might otherwise be overlooked.

That concern brought hundreds of preservationists, civil rights advocates, and tribal representatives to the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 9 to oppose changes to Section 106.

"Our sacred places are living places of prayer," Harry Antonio Jr., governor of the Pueblo of Laguna in Fresh Mexico, told the crowd.

The Senate proposal would narrow consideration of certain effects on historic places, including noise and visual impacts, raising concerns about the protection of sacred landscapes, burial grounds, and other culturally significant sites.

Veneziano pointed to a conflict farther upriver in Wallace, LA, where federal scrutiny exposed problems with a developer's assessment of a proposed grain terminal.

There, descendants of enslaved residents opposed the project, which would have been built near historic plantations, burial grounds, and their predominantly Black community.

A ProPublica investigation revealed that an archaeological consultant's original findings about potential harm to historic sites had been stripped from a report prepared for the developer. The Army Corps of Engineers subsequently rejected the assessment as insufficient and demanded further investigation.

In April 2024, the Corps determined that noise, light pollution, and the terminal's industrial appearance would adversely affect Wallace's historic character—precisely the kinds of impacts the Senate proposal would subject to a narrower standard of review.

Sources indicate that the manufacturer behind the terminal abandoned the project later that year, blaming prolonged permitting delays. Residents celebrated the outcome as a victory.

Such lengthy reviews, however, may be the exception rather than the rule.

An October analysis by Virginia's Department of Historic Resources found that 85% of nearly 9,900 projects completed Section 106 review within 30 days. Just 6% took longer than 90 days, primarily because they required additional surveys or involved potential harm to historic properties.

Those figures aren't necessarily representative nationwide, nor do they establish whether reviews actually delayed construction.

"If you're trying to get a project through, yeah, it's annoying," Veneziano acknowledged.

Still, Section 106 doesn't prohibit development. It requires agencies to consider the consequences and potential alternatives before proceeding.

And as Congress weighs how to accelerate construction, lawmakers will also confront a more fundamental question: Who gets to determine what a community can afford to lose?

Veneziano posed a question of her own: "How do we take the best of what we have, and build upon it into the future?".

HLTH 2026: Teladoc Health's weight care program lets employers partially contribute to GLP-1 costs" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Teladoc Health is expanding its Comprehensive Weight Care program with a new option that allows employers to contribute to GLP-1 costs outside of traditional pharmacy benefit designs.

Through the new offering, employers can give access to medications from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk—accompanied by support from licensed professionals, personalized lifestyle coaching, artificial intelligence-enabled food logging and more.

It has been revealed that with each blueprint year, employers will set a fixed payment per employee per fill that applies consistently across covered medications, the organization said. Employees then pay the remaining balance for each fill. Teladoc manages eligibility, program oversight and consolidated invoicing.

Pharmacy claims are administered on a 100% pass-through basis, including eligibility verification and audit-ready claims documentation.

Moreover, employers can opt in to tie contributions to program engagement, using metrics like food logging and regular weigh-ins, executives say.

The offering is available now, with initial contracted clients slated to launch programs for their employees beginning Jan. 1, 2027.

“Employers want to provide benefits that help their workforce achieve their health goals and need flexible strategies that work for their organizations,” said Kelly Bliss, Teladoc Health U.S. Group Health president, in a statement. “We are helping employers meet the needs of their employees while providing greater predictability and transparency around healthcare spending. Importantly, we give people a trusted path to high-quality care and affordable access to FDA-approved, authentic medication for meaningful, sustained health outcomes.”.

Alongside the announcement, the company also unveiled new research examining two years of weight-loss outcomes among nearly 23,000 members enrolled in its programs.

According to recent reports, results indicated “clinically meaningful weight loss” increased over time, with 47.7% of members achieving at least 5% weight loss by 24 months. And among those who lost weight during their first year, 53% continued losing additional weight during the second.

#30021. Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1094 w)

Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1094 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A common class of drugs used to treat osteoporosis may have an unexpected benefit: lowering the risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
  • The medications, known as nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (NBPs), are widely prescribed to prevent bone loss and fractures.
  • Recent findings suggest that more than 55 million people worldwide right now live with dementia, and that number is projected to climb to 139 million by 2050.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A common class of drugs used to treat osteoporosis may have an unexpected benefit: lowering the risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. In a study involving more than 120,000 older adults, researchers at the University of Hong Kong (HKUMed) found that patients taking certain medications to strengthen their bones were significantly less likely to develop dementia.

The medications, known as nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (NBPs), are widely prescribed to prevent bone loss and fractures. The findings suggest that these established treatments could potentially serve a second purpose by helping protect the aging brain. The research, conducted by scientists in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at HKUMed's LKS Faculty of Medicine, was published in Alzheimer's & Dementia.

Recent findings suggest that more than 55 million people worldwide right now live with dementia, and that number is projected to climb to 139 million by 2050. The World Health Organization has identified dementia as a major global health priority. Although the first medications designed to slow the progression of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) have recently gained approval, their high costs, limited suitability for some patients, and questions about their effectiveness remain key challenges.

It has been revealed that these obstacles have increased interest in finding affordable ways to prevent or delay dementia before symptoms develop. One promising approach is to identify existing medications that might offer benefits beyond the conditions they were originally designed to treat.

The Surprising Connection Between Bone Health and Dementia.

Recent findings suggest that osteoporosis and dementia often affect the same older adults. Osteoporosis causes bones to become weaker and more vulnerable to fractures, while dementia progressively affects memory, thinking, and the ability to carry out everyday activities. The two conditions also share several risk factors, including older age, being female, and low levels of physical activity.

Previous research by the same HKUMed team established that osteoporosis and fractures are independent risk factors for dementia. The researchers also found that people already living with dementia face an increased likelihood of falling and breaking bones.

This relationship raises an intriguing possibility: medications that treat osteoporosis might also help reduce dementia risk.

According to recent reports, among the most commonly prescribed osteoporosis treatments are alendronate and zoledronate, both of which belong to the NBP drug class. These medications work by slowing the breakdown of bone tissue, helping maintain bone strength and reduce the likelihood of fractures.

According to recent reports, scientists have also begun uncovering evidence that some of the biological processes influenced by these drugs may be involved in the development of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. This overlap has prompted researchers to investigate whether NBPs might provide benefits for the brain as well as the skeleton.

Study of 120,000 Patients Finds Up to 24% Lower Dementia Risk.

It has been revealed that to explore this possibility, the HKUMed researchers examined electronic medical records from across Hong Kong, analyzing data from more than 120,000 patients aged 60 and older. All participants had osteoporosis or fragility fractures, which are breaks that can occur after relatively minor injuries because the bones have become weakened.

The records covered the period from 2005 through 2020, allowing the team to investigate how different osteoporosis treatments were associated with dementia risk over time.

The results revealed a notable difference. Patients taking NBPs had a 16% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease and related dementias compared with patients who received no osteoporosis medication.

The association was even stronger when NBP customers were compared with patients taking other types of osteoporosis drugs. In that comparison, dementia risk was 24% lower among those receiving NBPs.

Women and patients who had experienced hip fractures appeared to show particularly strong associations between NBP treatment and reduced dementia risk.

The researchers also estimated that treating 48 patients with NBPs over five years could potentially prevent one case of dementia. If future research confirms that the medications directly reduce dementia risk, the implications could be substantial, particularly for older adults who already need treatment for osteoporosis.

Because the findings come from an observational study, they do not establish that the drugs themselves prevent dementia. However, they provide evidence supporting further investigation into whether these medications could help delay or prevent cognitive decline.

Could Existing Osteoporosis Drugs Help Prevent Alzheimer's?

Professor Cheung Ching-lung, Associate Professor in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at HKUMed, believes the findings highlight the possibility that a familiar osteoporosis treatment could deliver two important health benefits.

"Our study provides evidence that NBPs may offer dual benefits in strengthening bones and reducing fracture risk, as well as potentially preventing ADRD. Their potential neuroprotective role provides an empirical basis and supports future research on the actual effectiveness of this medication in preventing or delaying cognitive decline associated with ADRD.".

Sources indicate that the potential advantage of this approach is that NBPs are already widely available and have an established history of use in treating osteoporosis. Rather than developing an entirely new medication from scratch, researchers could investigate whether these existing treatments offer additional protection for people at elevated risk of dementia.

The findings are particularly relevant as populations around the world grow older and the number of people affected by dementia continues to rise.

"These findings are significant as they demonstrate a potential approach for reducing dementia risk in a vulnerable population using safe and widely available NBPs. In our rapidly aging society, these findings suggest that while waiting for the novel therapies, existing medications can also provide additional protection for high-risk populations," mentioned Professor Cheung.

Further studies will be needed to determine whether NBPs can directly prevent or delay Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. Nevertheless, the results suggest that medications already prescribed to protect aging bones may also have an important role to play in protecting brain health.

The research was led by Professor Cheung Ching-lung of the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at HKUMed. Dr Sing Chor-wing, from the same department, served as the study's first author.

Additional researchers included Professor Chan Koon-ho, Dr Patrick Chiu Ka-chun, and Professor Kathryn Tan Choon-beng, all from the Department of Medicine in the School of Clinical Medicine at HKUMed.

Builders Are Slashing Mortgage Rates To Win Buyers, but Hold Firm on Sticker Prices

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that prices for new homes have been stagnant for years.
  • The latest Realtor.com® quarterly construction insights report shows that prices on latest homes are holding steady, but builders are having to get creative to attract buyers, relying on rate buydowns and other incentives as the 30-year fixed mortgage rate stays above 7%.
  • Industry observers note that the median listing price for upcoming builds hit $451,071 in the third quarter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that prices for new homes have been stagnant for years. That leaves room for potential homebuyers if they're on the hunt for good incentives.

The latest Realtor.com® quarterly construction insights report shows that prices on latest homes are holding steady, but builders are having to get creative to attract buyers, relying on rate buydowns and other incentives as the 30-year fixed mortgage rate stays above 7%.

Industry observers note that the median listing price for upcoming builds hit $451,071 in the third quarter. It's been right around that number since late 2023. Builders are starting fewer homes in the inflation-plagued economy.

Increased labor and material costs and decreased buyer demand led to the completion rate of fresh single-family homes falling 11.0% year over year in September.

Meanwhile, existing-home prices came in 1.5% below 2025 levels, landing at $402,883. Newly introduced homes have to compete with existing homes for buyers, and the rise in existing-home sales demonstrates that some cost-conscious buyers who might have built new are choosing existing, instead. Existing-home sales just hit a 16-year low.

Sources indicate that "Builders were quicker to adjust to the realities of muted buyer demand in this high-rate environment, while existing-home sellers had pricing expectations based on the market from 2021 and 2022 that were slower to dissolve," Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner writes in the report. "The overall price softness we’ve seen through 2026 is driven primarily by the existing-home segment.".

In a recent development, that's led to more builders and sellers tempering their expectations. Resellers cut prices on 21.6% of homes this quarter. Builders are doing the same for 20.9% of their stock.

"The growing incidence of price reductions for newly introduced and existing homes is an indication of softness in the housing market in general and gives reason to expect that the diminished pace of inventory growth will continue," writes Berner.

Recent findings suggest that homebuilders this year are reporting that the difficult housing market is eating into margins. Some have retooled to the higher end of the market, which is less affected by affordability concerns. Others have dangled more incentives to bring buyers calling.

That's led to some oddities, and it means the market for latest homes is, in a lot of ways, buyer-friendly.

It has been revealed that for instance, existing homes are more expensive than new ones based on the price per square foot: $218 for new homes, $219 for existing ones. That's because, while there's a $50,000 gap between the median new-home price and the median existing-home price, new homes are bigger: a median of 2,056 square feet compared to 1,790 square feet. So, adjusting for size, this price gap disappears.

Sources indicate that also, new builds are concentrated in the South, where land is cheaper. Existing-home sales in the much more expensive Northeast, meanwhile, drives up the data. So, nationally, the median sales price for new homes was $400,400 while for existing homes it was $417,500.

For builders, reduced rates are the most common type of buyer incentive, helping homebuyers cut down on the total cost of ownership. This quarter, the average starting mortgage rate for newly introduced-home buyers was 5.01%. For existing-home buyers, it was 6.15%.

Recent findings suggest that "In today’s environment of higher-for-longer mortgage rates, this is an enticing marketing strategy. Builders often have strong relationships with mortgage lenders to whom they send lots of their buyers, and in exchange for this volume of loan origination, the lenders can offer below-market rates.".

Sources indicate that but the savings aren't always permanent. But even with temporary benefits, like the popular 3/2/1 step-down, buyers still see a big benefit in cost savings.

With inflation high and mortgage rates elevated, what's going to break the cycle?

It has been revealed that the housing market over the next year will remain challenged, Goldman Sachs stated in its latest forecast. It predicts home prices will keep growing at an "anemic" 1% in 2027.

“In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity,” economists Ronnie Walker and David Mericle wrote. “The combination of mortgage borrowers refinancing at low rates en masse in 2020 and 2021 and the high current level of mortgage rates has created a significant financial cost to moving.".

Sources indicate that if mortgage rates do start to come down next year, that could bring buyers off the sidelines and cause housing activity to pick up. Goldman projected that could be the case in late 2027.

According to recent reports, some areas are more immune. Maor Greenberg, co-founder and CEO of structural engineer Spacial, notes builders feel squeezed by rate hikes, as carrying costs go up on houses that are already under construction. Then, the buyer deals with a higher mortgage rate. The higher end of the market and booming areas like the tech-awash San Francisco Bay Area are rare exceptions.

Industry observers note that "Even in a soft market, there’s a point where starting to build a house makes more sense than waiting for more favorable conditions, because you’re paying money to hold on to land," Greenberg indicates. "That moves the problem down to selling: To do that, builders offer incentives and cut prices. Margins get tighter, but you’re not losing as much money.”.

Ryan Serhant, speaking exclusively to Realtor.com, recently offered his own advice on the market: Don't wait for lower rates.

While it might seem like the housing market will stay frozen forever, there are some cities where buyers can get a good deal. And a whole lot of other people are thinking the same thing.

“Everyone wants low rates, they never want what comes with it," he stated. "You know what'll happen if rates come down? There will be no houses for sale.”.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

Earlier this year, Optum Rx teased the rollout of newly introduced pharmacy tools designed to address medication cost and access.

Now, the tech giant is offering a look at how those tools work.

In a recent development, the pharmacy benefit manager said Tuesday that the tools build on Optum's latest and more transparent pharmacy model, which the tech giant announced in May and shifts to a fee-based structure. The model moves away from more traditional approaches linked to manufacturer pricing and prescription volume and offers clients a clearly defined fee structure.

The first platform, called Shop MyScript, allows members to compare prices for their medications as well as their options for pharmacies or delivery before the prescription is dispensed. The tool will notify members of potential cost savings shortly after a script is written.

In a recent development, in addition, Shop MyScript embeds in the prescribing workflow, Optum mentioned, so that the member does not have to make comparisons after the fact. If they choose to keep the existing prescription, it will then be sent to the pharmacy.

Optum stated that early adopters have averaged $28 in savings through the program.

"People should have clear information about their medication costs and options when they can actually use it, not after a decision has already been made," stated Katte Carey, president of Optum Rx, in the announcement. "These tools give people more information earlier in their journey, so they can make choices that work for them and get the support they need along the way.".

It has been revealed that in addition, the pharmacy benefit manager revealed Optum Assistant, a conversational AI guide that helps members complete routine tasks and track down key information. The tool can triage concerns on a range of topics, from questions about medication and benefits to pharmacy experience challenges.

In a recent development, if the AI guide can't address the individual's needs, they can choose to be connected to live support to find a solution. Optum said about 80% of conversations using the tool led to a resolution without needing a live advocate.

The final upcoming launch aims to support cash-pay options, according to the announcement.

Optum Price Wise will offer members a complete cost breakdown, including the price of a drug and any fees. That total, all-in price allows members to fully understand what their options may be, and make the choice that works best for them at the pharmacy counters.

The PBM said fresh tools like these build on Optum's new and more transparent pharmacy model, which the company confirmed in May and shifts to a fee-based structure. The model moves away from more traditional approaches linked to manufacturer pricing and prescription volume and offers clients a clearly defined fee structure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:27 EST / NOVEMBER 17 2026.

Sources indicate that enterprises have spent the AI boom racing to secure graphics processing units, or GPUs, but the harder decisions now sit above the hardware. Token bills, data sovereignty and model choice increasingly decide which AI pilots reach production, a shift on display at the SC26 supercomputing conference.

Sources indicate that dell Technologies Inc. has spent the past year pushing its AI Factory beyond servers and storage. Customers now want a full-stack outcome that covers software, open-source tools, models and operations, according to Brad Maltz (pictured), senior director of AI solutions at Dell.

“The hardware’s key because that drives the tokens,” he noted. “You really, truly need a full-stack AI factory view above and beyond just the hardware stack.”.

In a recent development, maltz spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how token bills and data sovereignty are steering enterprises toward open-weight models and a full-stack AI Factory. The interview came as Dell rolled out AI Factory updates at the conference. (* Disclosure below.).

Many enterprises are still stuck in pilot mode, and coding assistants are often the easiest place to start. Employees have already tried tools from Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC, so teams want to apply that experience to business use cases. Once those pilots grow, the bill arrives, Maltz explained.

“The token spend right now in the frontier labs and the hyperscalers — that’s a little more than we expected,” he stated. “We didn’t expect to spend $10,000, $20,000 per person per month.”.

Sources indicate that cost is only one trigger. Data sovereignty, intellectual property leakage, security and governance all have to be addressed before a pilot goes live. Those requirements are steering many enterprises toward open-weight models they can fine-tune and run on-premises, including U.S. options such as Nvidia Corp.’s Nemotron, according to Maltz.

“There will always be frontier labs. There will always be open-weight models,” he said. “The question is going to be: do we have enough diversity with the open weights to meet the enterprise use cases?”.

Industry observers note that to keep pace, Dell introduced its AI Ecosystem Program to validate software partners on its AI Factory. About 60 more partners have applied or are under evaluation, and each addition lets Dell solve 10 to 30 more customer problems, Maltz noted. For sovereign deployments, that often means disconnected, on-premises systems that keep models next to the GPUs and data enterprises already control.

It has been revealed that “People understand data is the lifeblood of AI,” he mentioned. “It’s the thing that trains the models. It’s the thing the models operate against. It comes from your enterprise business applications.”.

#30015. Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover

Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (905 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A widely available nutritional supplement derived from vitamin B5 may offer a promising upcoming approach to treating psoriasis, according to research from China.
  • Sources indicate that the findings, published October 27 in the Journal of Experimental Medicine (JEM), reveal an unexpected connection between cholesterol production and the immune system.
  • How Overactive Immune Cells Contribute to Psoriasis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A widely available nutritional supplement derived from vitamin B5 may offer a promising upcoming approach to treating psoriasis, according to research from China. Scientists found that pantethine can calm immune cells involved in autoimmune inflammation, preventing psoriasis from developing in mice and improving symptoms in a small human clinical trial.

Sources indicate that the findings, published October 27 in the Journal of Experimental Medicine (JEM), reveal an unexpected connection between cholesterol production and the immune system. By interfering with this process, pantethine may help reduce the excessive immune activity responsible for psoriasis and potentially other autoimmune diseases.

How Overactive Immune Cells Contribute to Psoriasis.

Recent findings suggest that at the center of the discovery are dendritic cells, specialized immune cells that help organize the body's defenses. These cells act as coordinators, identifying potential threats and directing other immune cells to respond.

In a recent development, dendritic cells perform this role by capturing foreign substances called antigens and presenting them to T cells, which are immune cells that recognize specific threats. They also release chemical signals that recruit additional immune cells and trigger inflammation.

Although these activities are essential for fighting infections, problems can arise when dendritic cells become excessively active. Instead of helping protect the body, they can contribute to persistent inflammation and autoimmune diseases such as psoriasis.

"Emerging evidence highlights that metabolic pathways and their associated metabolites play vital roles in regulating immune cell function and autoimmune progression," notes Wei-Na Zhang, a researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing. "But therapeutic strategies targeting metabolism in inflammatory diseases remain underexplored.".

Zhang led the research alongside Qing Xia, Ai-Ling Li, and Tao Zhou, also from the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis, and Cheng-Xin Li from The First Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital in Beijing.

Scientists Discover a Hidden Link Between Cholesterol and Psoriasis.

In a recent development, the researchers identified unusually high levels of enzymes called Vanins in dendritic cells from people with psoriasis and several other autoimmune diseases. These enzymes help regulate the processing of certain substances involved in cellular metabolism.

Industry observers note that when the scientists reduced Vanin levels, dendritic cells became less active and were less capable of stimulating T cells. They also found that a drug designed to inhibit Vanins prevented psoriasis from developing in mice.

Further investigation revealed why these enzymes might play such an important role.

Vanins convert pantethine into vitamin B5, an essential nutrient that cells need to produce energy. Pantethine is already sold as a nutritional supplement and is commonly used to help lower blood cholesterol because it can reduce cholesterol production.

Recent findings suggest that this connection is particularly interesting because cholesterol does more than circulate in the bloodstream. It also influences how immune cells function. Previous research has shown that cholesterol can stimulate dendritic cell activity, while elevated blood cholesterol is a major risk factor for developing psoriasis.

The team discovered that excessive Vanin activity reduces the amount of pantethine available inside dendritic cells. As pantethine levels fall, cholesterol production increases, causing these immune cells to become unusually active.

Restoring pantethine levels interrupted this process. The supplement reduced cholesterol accumulation within dendritic cells and helped suppress the excessive immune activation associated with inflammation.

"We found that pantethine administration effectively alleviated psoriasis in mice, suggesting that insufficient pantethine levels may be the crucial contributor to hyperactivation of dendritic cells and autoimmune inflammation following the up-regulation of Vanins," Zhang says.

Common Supplement Highlights Promise in Human Psoriasis Trial.

Encouraged by the laboratory and animal findings, the researchers investigated whether pantethine might also benefit people living with psoriasis.

They conducted a small clinical trial involving 24 patients with the condition. All participants received a topical ointment containing calcipotriene/betamethasone, a combination treatment used to control psoriasis symptoms. Calcipotriene is a vitamin D derivative that helps regulate skin cell growth, while betamethasone is a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation.

Half of the participants also took pantethine tablets, allowing researchers to examine whether adding the supplement improved the results of standard treatment.

After 12 weeks, the patients who received pantethine alongside their prescribed ointment showed greater improvement in psoriasis symptoms. The benefits were especially noticeable among participants who had high blood cholesterol levels before treatment.

These findings suggest that pantethine could potentially serve as an additional treatment for psoriasis, particularly in patients whose cholesterol metabolism may be contributing to inflammation.

However, the trial included only 24 people, and the researchers emphasize that larger studies are necessary to confirm the supplement's effectiveness. The human results also do not establish that the same biological mechanism observed in laboratory experiments is responsible for the improvement in patients.

Sources indicate that "Our investigator-initiated clinical trial demonstrated encouraging therapeutic efficacy of pantethine as an adjunctive therapy in psoriasis, but these findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept for clinical feasibility rather than direct mechanistic validation," Zhang says. "Overall, our study uncovers the Vanin-pantethine-cholestrol axis as a key metabolic pathway governing dendritic cell activation and provides a foundation for therapeutic strategies targeting several dendritic cell-mediated autoimmune diseases.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Betsey Johnson has relisted her California property with an $140,000 price cut—putting its upcoming asking price at $6.8 million.

The iconic fashion designer, 84, snapped up the 4,300-square-foot abode on April 11, 2025, paying $6.85 million.

Just over a year later, on July 27, 2026, Johnson listed the home for $7.5 million. By Sept. 15, the price had been slashed by half a million dollars, asking $6.99 million. A month later, on Oct. 17, the listing was removed.

Now, the home has once again appeared on the selling block with a reduced asking price, being listed with Chris Cortazzo of Compass.

The property, which was built in 1957, boasts five bedrooms and 4.5 bathrooms.

"Tucked behind gates on Eldorado Meadow Road, this single-level contemporary residence enjoys an exceptional vantage point within Hidden Hills, with expansive views of rolling hills, distant mountain ridgelines, and beautiful open meadows," the listing reads.

Surrounded by lush greenery, the home boasts a spa-inspired pool and plenty of space for entertaining.

Upon entering the home, guests are greeted with an expansive floor strategy and a chic lounging area that flows effortlessly into the dining space and opens up to the outdoors.

The kitchen is surely the crown jewel of the property as it comes complete with a black marble island and state-of-the-art appliances.

It has been revealed that "Inside, wide-plank wood floors and exposed beams carry through the open living and dining areas. A glass-front wine display sits just off the entry, while a wall of pocketing glass opens the living room to the pool and mountains beyond. French doors beside the dining area lead to a covered terrace. In the kitchen, richly veined black marble extends from the backsplash to a waterfall island with counter seating. Woven pendants, wood cabinetry, a six-burner range with double ovens, Thermador appliances, and a concealed bar complete the space," adds the listing.

The bedrooms are the perfect place to relax and boast enough space for a queen-sized bed.

The primary bathroom features a large soaking tub and a glass-enclosed shower.

The property also comes complete with a large walk-in closet and an office space.

Sources indicate that "Beyond, the primary suite occupies nearly an entire wing. A fireplace and white-painted beams frame the bedroom, and a sunlit sitting area opens directly to the poolside deck. The dressing room is lined with built-in cabinetry. In the bath, slatted wood walls complement a floating black stone double vanity, a glass-enclosed shower with dual showerheads, and a freestanding soaking tub set against a broad garden-facing window," the description continues.

Moving outside, the grounds offer a lovely area to kick back and enjoy the California sunshine.

Industry observers note that "A poolside sun deck and outdoor shower complete the garden. Additional amenities include integrated audio, home automation, a two-car garage, and gated driveway parking for approximately 10 to 12 vehicles," adds the listing.

The designer's real estate portfolio has an impressive track record.

In 2019, the designer—who had previously spent 55 years living in New York City—sold her one-of-a-kind pink mobile home for $1.95 million.

The Malibu dwelling was located in Paradise Cove Mobile Home Park, which is considered to be one of the most famous and luxurious trailer parks in the country.

The picturesque community of 270 homes has attracted many notable residents, including Sarah Paulson, Stevie Nicks, and Pamela Anderson.

Sources indicate that before offloading the mobile home, Johnson spent over $500,000 turning it into a playful wonderland decorated with countless bohemian prints, florals, and electric colors. There was even a fully functional outdoor tub.

“I would like people to think of this as a funny little museum,” she told People magazine in 2018, referring to the expansive collection of antiques and vintage finds she had displayed in the home.

The mobile home had two bedrooms and two bathrooms, and plenty of room for her daughter, Lulu Johnson, 41, and two grandchildren, Layla and Ella, who reportedly also lived in Malibu, visiting frequently.

“I’ve made lots of mistakes with boyfriends and husbands,” said Johnson, who has been married three times. “I don’t think I’ve made more than two mistakes with my houses, purchases for my houses, or the clothes in my closet.”.

It wasn’t long before Johnson would find herself in yet another pink mobile home in Malibu, moving into a 2,300-square-foot home in the gated Point Dume Club.

“I love the idea that, with a trailer park, you’re in a kind of community,” she told the Upcoming York Times Style Magazine in 2021. “At my age, if I fall down in the middle of the street, I want someone to go, ‘Hey! What’s that girl doing in the middle of the street?’”.

Soon after moving in, Johnson papered the walls with vintage wallpaper that perfectly matched the floral print from her childhood home.

Pink homes are somewhat of a tradition for Johnson, who famously lived in a bubblegum pink loft in Manhattan in the 1980s—the photos of which still regularly circulate on blogs and social media accounts dedicated to whimsical design.

And although the exterior is not pink, Johnson does also have a four-bedroom, six-bathroom vacation home in Guerrero, Mexico, where her half-punk, half-ballerina touch can be found in every room.

According to Elle Decor, the property—aptly named “Betseyvilla”—was previously offered as a rental through Airbnb, although the listing appears to no longer be available.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Medicare Shared Savings Program saved $2.5B last year: CMS" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Medicare Shared Savings Program has reached the highest savings number in its history, according to new federal data.

In a recent development, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services stated Tuesday that the program generated more than $2.5 billion in net savings to Medicare in 2025, making for the ninth year in a row that it led to cost savings. The agency added that every accountable care organization met or exceeded quality reporting requirements.

ACOs participating in MSSP earned $4.9 billion in shared savings payments during 2025, CMS noted, with 80% of organizations earning performance payments.

As of 2026, 511 ACOs representing more than 700,000 providers are participating in the Medicare Shared Savings Program, which represents 12.6 million people enrolled in traditional Medicare, another record.

"Patients want doctors who work together, care that puts their needs first, and fewer unnecessary hurdles — that is what accountable care is designed to deliver," said CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. "These record savings show the power of rewarding providers for quality and coordination. We want more people with Medicare, and more of the providers who care for them, to benefit from this approach.".

CMS said that it wants to make it easier for providers to participate in MSSP if they choose, especially given the program's results to date. It included changes in the latest Physician Fee Schedule to encourage participation, including increased opportunity for certain ACOs to earn shared savings and upcoming financial incentives to draw in first-time participants.

According to recent reports, in addition, CMS said that would create more predictable spending targets that make planning and participation straightforward. The agency is also aiming to streamline patient notices and simplify required technology.

“We are excited to see continued progress on both savings and enrollment for Medicare beneficiaries. Beneficiaries are best served when a provider is watching out for them and coordinating their care,” said Center for Medicare Director John Brooks in the announcement.

Emily Brower, CEO of the National Association of ACOs, remarked in a statement that the 2025 results "build on years of progress and underscore what the accountable care community can accomplish through collaboration, innovation and the widespread adoption of proven best practices.".

According to recent reports, "NAACOS looks forward to partnering with CMS to build on this momentum," said Brower. "Policies that unleash innovation, reduce burden, and create sustainability through fair and predictable budgets will allow ACOs to deliver even greater value for patients and the Medicare program.".
